TELE WINTER'S COMIN' ON, MI LASS. The winter's comin' on, ml lass; • The north wind's blowin' cowd : Avem sure we've cooarted long enough, It's time eawr tale•wer towd, The brids 'at sung i' yonder tree Are flown across the brine, An' aw've a cheery hooam for thee, Where love's breet sun can shine. Tha doesn'a want to ged Trio lost . Amon.," the moorland snow; Thi laugh belies tha when tha says Aw needn'd come at o. When t' weather's wild, we cornd ged eawt A-walkin' hale an hewr ; There's awlus summat rough abeawt, A snowstorm or a sheawr. An' when aw come an' stop i' the heawse, Yore lads mek sich a din That iv aw've bod two words to say Aw connod ged urn in. Thi favther will toke politics, An' likes a reawnd wi' me; He thinks aw come a-campin' him An' nod a-cooartin' thee! An' when there's.nobry else i' th' place, Yore Molly ceawrs th' nook, As quate an' wakken as a meawse, Wi' th' papper or a book. Hoo reads a deeal ; an' one would think Her common sense would tell 'At cooarters sometimes like an heawr To whisper hi their-se 1 • Thi fayther thinks when fooaks ged wed They should hey lots o' brass, A mon should hey his fortune med Afoor he claims his lass. Ay, well! aw'm wotla a field or two, A bonny cot an' o ; tin' when there's steady hands at th' plough Sich things are sure to grow. The sweetest charm o' wedded life Is nod i' *tunes grand; It's only known to th' mon an' wife 'Ats strivin' hand-in-hand. . The lark 'at builds her own wee nest Is merry wi' her mate, While mony a soul can find no rest 'lnside a palace gate! An' neau aw've welly done, mi lass, Mi stooary's getten towd; An' winter's comin' on, my lass, The north wind's blowin cowd, Come, show tby bonny e'en to me, ' Clasp thy two hands i' mine, An' say thall claim wod waits for thee, An' mek yon sweet cot thine! Higher Walton, Jan. 17, 1888.
GEORGE HULL.

He who would see his sons and daughters thoroughly and truly gentle must forbid selfishness of actioh, rude- ness of speech, carelessness of forms, impoliteness of con- duct from the first, and demand that in childhood and the nursery shall be laid the foundation of that good breeding which is as a jewel of price to the mature man and woman. _ _

_ It is in early life that the habit of promptness may most easily be acquired. Parents should accustom their children to choose and decide many things for them- selves, teaching them how to think quickly and effec- tively, prohibiting changes without sufficient cause, and allowing them to experience the natural consequences of their determinations. In this way they will gradually learn to bear responsibility and to acquire as much rapidity of thought and word as is consistent with its importance and effectiveness. "There are two sides to everything." said the lecturer. "I repeat it—there are two sides—" At this point a little tired-looking man stood up in the front seat to say, "Well, if you've no objections, I'll just step out and see if there are two sides to this hall. I know there , is an inside, and if I find there is an outside you'll know it by my not coming back. You needn't be alarmed if I shouldn't return." As he walked up the aisle he was /allowed by the admiring eyes of the whole audience. Their sympathies were with him, but they were deacienp in moral courage. "Yes, sir," went on Profa.mor X. to a gentleman to whom he had recently been introduced, "I have given some attention to the study of human nature, and I rarely fail to read a fswe. correctly. Now, there is a lady,' he continued, pointing across the rooom, "the lines of whose countenance are as clear ;to tne as type. The chin shows firmness of dispcsition amounting to obstinacy; the sharp-pointed nose, a vicious tempera- ment; the large mouth, volubility; the eyes, a dryness. of soul; the —." "Wonderful, Professor—wonder- ful "You know something of the lady, then ?" said the professor complacently. "Yes, a little; she's my wife." . . .

It is said that a genius has invented what is called an ilectrical lounge. The lounge is connected by wire with the parental bedroom. At 10 15 prompt the cruel father touches a knob in his room, and the seat of the lounge flies up and spills its occupants upon the floor. We can imagine a youth in the ant of proposing when the knob is touched. He is saying, "Oh. Jennie, I love you more than tongue can tell. Will you be mice? My own my very own? Will:you—n Just then, presto! change! tm flies the seat of the lounge, and the pair are sent spinning across the floor. How natural it would be for the young lady to say then, "Oh, George, this is so sudden!"

- THE SENSE OF Toucw IN Fisir.—Fish seem to have the sense of touch as their dominate faculty. They hear and see dimly when in the ocean; but by the least movement of fin or tail they can communicate vibrations to the water by means of which a whole family, a whole hatching of fifty or sixty little fry, will guide themselves and keep swimming with perfect unantmity, in the same direction and at precisely the same distance from one another, so that they form a certain figure which does not vary. Most commonly this figure is a globe or an ovaL It is the youngest fry who follow this habit. If one, observing or suspecting danger, wags a fin and darts off in another direction, all the others are instantly after him, so simultaneously aware of the new vibration and repeating the movement, that they do pot even for a moment alter the shape of their lfigure.—Jean Ingeloto, ix "Good Words." THE DFATH or MOSES.—For forty .years Moses had not been alone. The care and burden of all the people, the -weight of their woe, and guilt, and death, had been upon him continually. The multitude had been laid upon him as if ho had conceived them their tears had been his meat night and day, until he had felt as if God had withdrawn His favour from him; and he had prayed that he might, be slain, and not see his wretchedness. And now, at last, the command came "Get thee up into this mountain." The weary hands, that had been so long stayed up against the enpmies of Israel, might lean ags,in upon the shepherd's staff, and fold themselves for the shepherd's prayer—for the shepherd's slumber. Not strange to his feet, though forty years unknown, the Toughness of the bare mountain path, as he climbed from ledge to ledge of Abarim ; not strange to his aged eyes the scattered clusters of the mountain herbage, and the broken shadows of the cliffs, indented far across the silence of uninhabited ravines; scenes such as those among which, as now, with none teside him but God,he had led his flocks so often, and which he had left—how painfully l—taking upon him the appointed power to make of the fenced city a wilderness, and to fill the desert with songs of deliverance. It was not to embitter the last hours of his life that God restored to him for a day the beloved solitudes he had lost, and breathed the peace of the perpetual hills around him, and cast the 'world in which he had laboured and sinned far beneath Li s feet in that mist of dying blue—all sin, all wandering, soon to be forgotten for ever.—John Ruskin—Modern _Painters. div.head: CHAPTER IL
div.p: CHAPTER IL
TOM CHILTON.

If the tone of Simon Knight's voice was in ap- proval when he saw Tom Chilton, scarcely as much could be said for the expression of Phyllis's face. Phyllis's chief beauty consisted in bright colouring enhanced by dark brown lashes and brows, and the natural wavy curls that clustered on her forehead. When her eye fell on Tom Chilton all the colour forsook her cheeks and she looked as if she had a good mind to faint. No one, however, took any notice of her, and she thought better of it, and by the time the aforesaid Tom Chilton had shaken hands with Mr. and Mrs. Knight she was able to lay her little palm—icy cold though—in his, and give him a sort of half Imile, the ghastliness of which escaped him as the room was not very brilliantly lighted. " Come on, come on, my boy. Phyllis get another knife and fork and plate and let us refresh this stranger. Tom, let us see, two mortal years come Whitsuntide since we've seen you—sit down, lad, and tell us what you've been about." And as Mr. Knight lavished this, for him, most overpowering welcome, he pushed a chair to the new corner; Phyllis had meantime gone into the kitchen, and was much longer than was absolutely necessary fetching the things for which her father had sent her. When she returned she was bright and rosy as usual, though those who knew her well might note a troubled look in her eyes. . She set the plata, et cetera, before Tom, who was already sitting at the table, and as she did so, he looked up into her face, but she half closed her eyes, and turned away from him. _ _ _

Oh, how Phyllis wished that Tom Chilton were anywhere but there that evening, and yet there had once been a time when she had waited for his coming, and counted his footsteps as she heard him striding along the lane. But that was two years and more ago; she was only fifteen then—a girl does not know her own mind at fifteen, at all events Phyllis felt very sure that she had not known hers. Did she know it now? "Oh,yes," she would have answered most decidedly. , "Well, lad, new for your story; what is it?" asked Simon Knight once more when the prepara- tions an unexpected guest entailed had all been con- cluded. "Been to America, that's all," said Tom Chilton, laughing, "came back last night, and here lam." na" To Ameriky—well I never." It was Mrs. Knight who spoke. "Whatever did you go all that way off for, Tom, and . us has been often wonderin' whether you was drowned or not." "Did you think I was drowned?" asked Tom, looking straight at Phyllis, whom this direct q.uestion made very . red; while for the first time since Tom came into the room she opened her month to speak. "No, Tom, I did not think you were drowned. I always thought you would turn up again some time." Neither the certainty nor the indifference with which she spoke pleased Tom, who began to fear that if he had gained ground in one way during the two years he had been absent he had lost it in another. Simon Knight, without intending it, dashed into the breach, if breach it were. "You see she believes in you, Tom, she always did. Phyllis wouldn't think as you'd go to the bottom. You're sure to swim, my boy." By which remark there was not much difficulty in inferring that Simon Knght believed in Tom Chilton himself. Of course; he always believed in rising people, and Tom Chilton was sure to rise, he had lots of per- severance and acuteness; and moreover, when • his father died two years ago he had left him a i pretty little sum n the bank by way of capital. With the intention of doubling or trebling this sum Tom had gone off abroad, and to judge by his outward appearance on this occasion, his most sanguine expectations had beenzealised. Tom Chilton was rather a sallow-complexioned, sandy-haired young man who could scarcely be called handsome, though the exceeding intelligence of his face gained for him the appellation of good looking, while his keen eyes alone filled his whole countenance with light; seldom were such telling eyes seen as Tom's, while in them there was not one ray of cunning. Tom's chief weakness was perhaps vanity, he spent a great deal of time in striving to set off his not very prepossessing person, thinking thereby to impress those with whom he came in contact, whereas he ought to have allowed his brains to do the work. This* evening in honour of his visit to the Knights he had dressed himself with more than usual care,and would have been considerably taken aback could he have heard Phyllis's mental remark— "He does not look a bit of a gentleman, only a flashy imitation of one." Light trousers, dark coat and waiscoat, and a very blue cravat, these did not seem to be muck amiss, only. she felt instinctively that the whole thing was spunous. What did Phyllis—hard-working little suburb- living Phyllis Knight—know about what constituted a real and aspurionsgentleman? Perhaps Tom Chilton willek-now to his cost before he is many weeks older. For the present, instead of speculating on the sub- ject of Phyllis's knowledge, he contents himself with striving to make himself agreeable and give his old friends to understand, without exactly telling them how much money he has made, that he has been by no means idle during his ' sojourn in the new country. "And are you going out there again! Hoped yon was intending to settle a bit here," said Simon, when Tom Chilton finished a somewhat lengthy account of what he had been doing by saying he had bought a bit of land in Texas. "No, I ain't going back—that is, not to stay, 'I might pop over for a fewmonths to see how things are working; that is about all. I'm thinking of put- ting some money into a business here when I can find one to my liking." Simon Knights eyes sparkled at this piece of in- telligence, but he dal not say anything more, pro- bably feeling that the time was not yet ripe. "And how have you all been getting on!" asked , Torn Chilton, suddenly changing the conversation I from his own affairs to those of the Knights. "Times is always bad in this yere country," grumbled Simon, "folks never die .so as you can make a pound or two out o' bury-in' them, and they won't live so as you can make a bit out o' buiklin' their houses."
Tom Chilton laughed. , "Your were always a grumbler. My father used tu say there was as much grumble as gold in your coffers." - _ _ .. _. ... .

"Your father was a fool," said Simon, "because he I got money hisself he thought everyone else had. Hannah there knows what a twisted time we've had a-tryin' to keep things a bit straight, hardly able to 'pay for this girl's schooling, , shouldn't in fact if the mother hadn't scraped for it. ' " That was only, father, because you think women ought not to learn," broke in saucy Phyllis. "Of course there was no money for schooling, but Mr. Chilton is quite right, you—" The sentence was not finished, for the new comer burst into such an indignant protest at being called Mr. Chilton that Plies blushed, and became in- stantly silent, while her father went on "That's right, don't stand no nonsense, my boy. You call him Tom, ncrirl, and behave like a rew-ectable tradesman's daughter—none o' they simpering airs and graces you learnt at the Stanhopes'. Mr. this and MASS the other, it is. quite sickening." For a moment Phyllis looked as if she were o.cming to answer her father, but she bit her tongue and left Tom Chilton to inquire: " Ah, yes, what about the Stanhopes ? They used to be your great .patrons." "Patrons, mine! Never use that word in, con- nection with me," shouted Simon. "Hannah's if you like, she cringes to aristocracy. I loathe the very name of it." Torn Chilton stared in absolute astonishment at his host, mid for a moment looked as Phyllis had done as if he were about to make some retort, then he too bit his tongue, and decided to wait and discover cautiously and gradually what had been going on during his absence before he committed himself to any remarks. Not finding any one to quarrel with him, Simon Knight resumed the joviality of manner to which he had been treating them during a portion of the eve,ing. He took his pipe from his pocket and proceeded to fill and light it, suggesting to Tom if he was still a smoker to do the same. Torn at once produced a cigar-case, and offered a cigar to his host, saying he had not been in America for nothing —ncr did he wish it to be thought that he had left his manners there, for he looked at the two ladies and asked: "You do not object to smoking :if I remember right?" "I hate it," answered Phyllis, tossing her headf while she took up some of the dishes off the ta.ble,and strutted into the ,kitchen as though she wished to be quit of the whole concern.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,_ JANUART 28, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,_ JANUART 28, 1888.

Tom Chilton's eyes followed her. in some won- derment, and her father said gmffiy : "She's spoiled, lad, she's spoiled; it's all they Stanhopes, trying to make a lady of her." "She is more beautiful than ever,"remarked Tom, very earnestly. "Beautiful, aye; but beauty ain't everything. Howsomever, you go in and win, my boy—son of my oldest friend, and you shall have my blessing." Tom Chilton's eyes sparkled, but Mrs. Knight's voice jarred: "Yon shouldn't go throwin' your daughter at no man's head, Simon, nor yet speak of her as if she wasn't through and through beautiful, mind and body." "Hold your tongue, Hannah, and don't interfere with what you know nothing about," answered Simon, ahgry again the moment he was contradicted; and in- all probability Tom Chilton would have been treated to a domestic scene, only fortunately for him he was spared by a knock at the outer door, which by this tune had been shut. 'That's Greaves come for orders for to-morrow,"said Simon, getting up and going out to speak to his bead man, thus leaving Mrs. Knight alone with, Tom Chilton.

The young man began to laugh. " Ha'nt improved one * bit, my friend Knight hisn't, can't keep the top on his pepper-box,anyhow." Ft.." No, he's worse, much worse in many ways," answered Mrs. Knight, dolefully then looking cautiously around her, she drew her Chair nearer Tom Chilton's and almost whispered "If he asks you to put your money in and join him in the business, don't you .do it." "Ng, lam notlikely. But why not ? " "Don't ask—please don't ask, only mind my warn: ing. ' "All right, you are a gbod woman, Mrs.Knight,you always were very good to me." "And you'll be silent on the subject," she went on, interrupting, "you won't say a word to no one." "You may trust me, indeed you may, and now tell me about Phyllis. How beautiful she is! Still, he is changed, very much changed. She used to be so free and affectionate, calling me Tom, and making my rough name sound quite noble with her pretty lips ; now she looks coy and distant, an 4 says Mr. Clifton. She hasn't got a new lover has she, Mrs. Knight?" "Lover! law, not as 'knows on," and nervous Mrs. Knight began to tremble a little. , • "Then what has changed her?" "Father would say it was the Stanhopes. MiSs Irene Stanhope is Phyllis's foster sister, you know, and they're a great deal together." "But why Should this change Phyllis ?" "Well, you see, Miss Irene is a lady,a very great lady, and she ain't happy without our Phyllis, and has had her taught lots of very fine things she knows herself. It's a wonder to me, with her head so full of cleverness as it is, that Phyllis brings herself down to our bit of cooking and cleaning; but father will have her do it; he has took to hating they Stan- hopes." I always thought," said Tom Chilton, "it was either Mr. Stanhope or his father who set Knight up in this business." " Hush—forthe loveof Heaven, hush! Never within these four walls let such a word be said again." Tom Chilton looked very much astonished. There was altogether something wrong about the Knights, he was beginning to think. Then he came to the philosophical conclusion that he had not stood still for two years himself, therefore why should he expect them to have done so. He would just ask Mrs. Knight one or two more questions in order to find his way better about, and then he would go and join Phyllis in the kitchen. "Mrs. Purvis, the housekeeper—is she still at the Stanhopes ?" "Of course, why she's a fixture; nothing but death will ever move her. She ain't no good friend to me. I don't know for what cause, but she's always mighty civil to Simon; however, we don't come across one another much. Mr. Ferdinand is her boy. I don't believe there's anything in this life she thinks too good for him—and he is—but that ain't my business to repeat • "Let's see, Mr. Ferdinand,"thA's the second son?" "Yes, Mr. Oeoffrey is the eldest. Oh, he is a real gentleman—sometimes I think I love him almost as well as Miss Irene." "And Phyllis is a great deal with these people?" "Lor' bless you, yes, and she's at home with them, too—our Phyllis was born to be a lady." Tom Chilton did not respond, he looked very grave and thoughtful, and as Simon seemed to b returning from his colloquy by the door, he started off into the kitchen without vouchsafing another remark to Mrs. Knight. He found Phyllis standing gazing abstractedly at the fire,her arms hanging down,and her hands clasped together. "Why, Phyllis, one would almost think you were unhappy." Tom Chilton's voice startled her, and she turned round to him, a flush on her face. "Oh, lam happy enough," she answered," at least I was till—" "Till I came," he said, finishing her sentence for her.

"No, not that, I'm glad enough to see . you. You'll help me to cheer mother, she has a rough time of it every now and agai ,n and since father has taken to you he'll let you speak." "Is that all, Phyllis ? " "All what, Tom ? " "All that you are glad to have me back for ? " "0, that I don't know," she replied, throwing off her dejection and shaking herself back into her usual bright manner, "It is the only' reason I can think of just now—if any more crop up I'll let you know." "And I am to be content with that ?" "Why not?" "Because I want more, Phyllis; have been trusting to more all through the weary months I have been away." "von should not have gone away," she said in a very low tone, "have gone away without one word of good-bye ; long, silent ibsences somehow have tho knack of killing feeling, Torn?" "Not killing it. Don't say killing it, Phyllis—only nipping it so that a hot sun may draw it forth again. I could not do otherwise than I did. I could not ask any girl to be my wife till I had added to the bit of money my father left me and made up my mind whether I'd settle here or in the new country." She did not move or Flake any reply, so he strove to take her hand but she pulled it back. • "Oh," Phyllis, don't be unkind, haven't you one good word to say to me ?" • "I loved you once, Tom, or thought I did, perhaps I was deeeived,your coming back has brought no beat- ing to my heart." 0, Phyllis!" "I am sorry, very sorry, but I cannot help it." "And don't you think the old feeling will re-- ten?" _ _ _ _ _

She shrugged her shoulders. He went on— "I will wait—wait any time you like to name. Do you think it is going to the Stanhopes so much that has killed your love for me, eh, Phyllis ? " "Going to the Stanhopes—what do you know about my going to the Stanhopes ? " and her face'was all aglow, while something like the angry look that haunted Simon's eyes came into hers. When he saw the look he was sorry he had spoken so much to the purpose, and he at once tried to soothe her, and change the current of her thoughts, but she would have none of his amends, only said very resolutely— " Recollect, Tom, if you wish to rise in my favour never attempt to stand between me and my goings and comings with the Stanhopes." He would not, indeed he would not, he promised, but he fervently wished no Stanhope had ever been born, since they seemed to have bewitched all the Knight family. (To be continued.)

that across Arpley Fields is so much the more con- venient and expeditious ?" In answer to this ques- tion it is to be pointed out, first, that this new way to Stockton Heath will be a substitute for that be- tween Lower Walton and Wilderspool, which is to be closed ; and, second, that the road across Arpley Fields may not always be available at the moment it is required. It might be that at the very time the driver of a vehicle from the Higher Walton direction reaches Lower Walton, the swing bridge, which will carry the road to the left, that is to say, the Arpley Fields-road, over the canal, has been ' flung open to allow of the inward or outward pas- sage of some vessel. In that event, all vehicular traffic along the road at this point would, of course, for the time being be stopped. The driver might then avail himself of the alternative route to the right through Stockton Heath, cross the canal there, and by way of Wilderspool Causeway reach War- rington.

to" facilitate traffic it is provided that, before any portion of the present Warrington and Chester- road is stopped up, a signal box shall be erected on the south bank of the canal, for the purpose of showing the public whether the swing bridges on the new'road and on the Stretton-road are open or shut, or which of the bridges is open and which shut.

(To Le Continued) CADISREAD AND fILAM SECTION. Br LOOKER ON. As yet, there is not much to be seen in connec- tion with the construction of the canal in the im- mediate neighbourhood of the villages of Cadishead and Irlam, which adjoin each other, and which have interests in common. Beyond preliminary prepara- tions, active operations cannot be said to have yet commenced here. Indeed, to an uninterested observer walking through this part of the district, there is little to call his attention to the subject of the canal. There is a near prospect, however, of an active state of affairs. Workmen are engaged in laying a temporary line from Irlam station, where materials arrive for the Hollins Green and Warbur- ton sections. A private house situated a short distance of Irlam station has been engaged for the purposes of an office, where several gentlemen con- nected with the works are now located. . .

The inhabitants of the district express great satisfaction at the prospects of a revival of trade consequent upon the cutting of the great waterway, as their staple trade, the fustian cutting industry, has for some time been in a depressed condition. House accommodation is not plentiful enough to meet the demand for lodgings that will, no doubt, soon arise, and preparations are being made, as at other places on the line of route, for the building of huts for the navvies to occupy. An evangelist, it is said, with his wife and family, has already ar- rived in this district..

The Cadishead and Irlam section commences at Butcher's Fields, behind Rixton Old Hall, and con- tinues to Irlam locks. At present preparatory work is being carried on in the meadows, skirting that part of the river where the Mersey and t'lrwell Regattas used to be held. A steam navvy, built by Dunbar and Euston, is here ready for work, and rails are expected daily. They will be laid without delay. The meadows are to be used Its a "tip," are to be raised to the height of the land round about, and, the soil having been deposited on the surface. the land will then be good for farming purposes. The route crosses the Warburton Bridge-road, near Rye Park Farm, and thence passes through Skeer Rock. This site has been chosen as a yard, and has been 'named Pope's Dock. A kind of Jetty has been erected, and already a steam crane is at work unloading materials that arrive in barges on the river close to.

After leaving Skeer Rock the course follows the bed of the river, just in front of the old Boat House and Ferry, which used to be the only means of getting into Cheshire, except one took the trouble of journeying round by the old bridge at Warring- ton, before the present bridge at Warburton was erected. A bend in the river at the mouth of the Glazebrook takes a small slice off the Cheshire side, the course then comes again on the Lancashire side opposite Mill Bank, skirting the fields close to the river until near Albert Works, when another bend again takes a slice off the Cheshire bank. The course, then crossing the river direct, will go into the meadows and under the Stockport Line of the Cheshire Lines Committee Railway. A large embankment, rising from the present level of the railway to a height of say 70 or 80 feet will have to be constructed in order to carry the line of railway over the canal. The railway now in use will be required for the conveyance of the traffic of the docks, which will be built on the north side of the line. These docks will be mostly used for the coal traffic from the Wigan Junction, via Glazebrook, on the Lancashire side, and the Derbyshire and Yorkshire traffic on the Cheshire side. At this point the canal will take an NO), bend to the left, leaving the great meadow known as the Weatee, on the Lancashire side, and pass thence through Flixton Byes, where it meets the circuitous stream of the Mersey, and under the Cheshire Lines Railway from Manchester to Liverpool. Here again, an embank- ment, similar to the one to be erected at the Stock- port Line, will have to be constructed. A short distance from here will be erected the Irlabi Locks. The route then will bs on to Calamanco Lock,where it will touch the bed of the Irwell, near the Royal Oak Farm. This will be the end of the section. it is expected that in a few weeks the work of cutting will be in full swing on the land adjoining the Mersey near Warburton, on the Lancashire side Even now the Scene here is a busy one, as a railway 1 line of censiderable length, touching the river at , two points, has been laid, and three locomotives are puffing about. There are at present about 150 men working in this neighbonrhood. As soon as the steam navvy is put in use more men will be taken on. Although it is only two or three weeks since work was commenced here, a transformation is rapidly being effected. The building of a large storeroom has nearly been completed, it now only requiring the finishing touches, and a neat, com- pact little office has also been erected. Foundations are being made for the erection of huts for the nav- vies. By means of a travelling steam crane heavy goods can be lifted from the river flats and carried to any part of the railway. There is also a saw mill, which is kept busy at work supplying the car- penters with planks. Visitors arrive in the neigh- bourhood to look at the works every day, and much interest is manifested in the operations that are be- ing carried on. At Latchford wharf two new locomotives, called the Latchford and the Eccles, have arrived during the week, and fresh timber, machinery, wheels, &c., occupy the wharf. A large quantity of barrows, timber, &c., have been transhipped to the Irlam section.

div.head: RUNCORN, _NORTON, &c..
div.p: RUNCORN, _NORTON, &c..

So far there are no indications that the engineer- ing works in Runcorn proper will be commenced for many months to come, though there is no telling what a few weeks may bring forte; but on the Run- corn section, in the township of Norton, the work of preparation for the actual • cutting of the canal is rapidly being completed, and in a few days Mr. Gregson, who exercises control over Runcorn section will have his forces in full operation. In the first place, Mr. T. Kirkham, of Runcorn, has completed his contract for the erection of a tipping bridge at the Big Field. To the unprofessional eye, the eree- tion of such a structure, which is over 300 feet in length, is not without difficulties and dangers, and Mr. Kirkham is to be congratulated on the fact that only one accident at all serious, has occurred, al- though more than one workman has had a ducking in the far from pare water of the Old Quay Canal. It was understood that Mr. Kirkham is under an engagement to build three sirailiar bridges between Norton and Warrington; but the precise points where they are to be raised are not yet decided Upon. llis men have also completed the construc- tion of the offices, sore rooms, and workshops at the Big Field, and judging from the expedition used in other districts, blacksmiths, fitters, joiners, &c., will have soon taken up the quarters designed for them. It may be Mentioned that the engine shed is capable of holding no leas than nine locomotives, and that four are already on :the spot, and these have emblazoned on their sides the familiar names of Runcorn, Frodsham, Ditton, and Ince respec- tively. Last week attention was drawn to the fact that a steam navvy had commenced its work of "destruction," and during the past five days the locomotives have been busily occupied in removing wagons as rapidly as they were filled with clay by, this wonderful machine. Already the "Navvy' has made a cutting about 18 feet deep, and next week another machine will be set to work along- side. There is also a third " navvy " on the spot, but it has not yet been fixed. A portion of the ex- cavations is taken over the bridge, and " tipped " on to the marsh, and the remainder is being used in the construction of railway lines, which now run in several directions. At present about 100 men are employed by the contracter. There were also a similar number employed by Mr. Kirkham, but in a few days these will be transferred to Bob's Bridge, where 40 workmen's dwellings have to be
built. Each house will have sufficient capacity to accommodate a family and six lodgers, so that an enormous increase in thq population of the locality may be anticipated. _ ••

6ne curiosity is the turf or mud hut which has been erected for the use of the labourers for meals. fitted up with stove, &c., and made tolerably com- fortable for them. At Bob's Bridge, near Moore, the German navvy has been put together, and will, it is expected, be at work in the course of a few days. Another large locomotive has arrived, called the Lingoln, and was conveyed by road from Latchford station by a powerful traction engine. The cutting which has been made for some distance contains a large quantity of water, owing to heavy rains and drainage. It is being disposed of by the pumping engine. Large quantities of machinery and other materials have arrived; and at Bell House Lane, Acton Grange. The men employed on the works have not been making full time on account of the unfit state of the weather, which has been very stormy.

On the route of the canal, the district under t4el supervision of Mr. Superintendent Hollingworth reaches from Weston Point .to Orappenhall, and within this area it is highly probable that some thousands of navvies and handicraftsmen will be massed within the next two years. Without dis- paraging the character of these labourers, it would seem that the present police force is not sufficitnt to cope with this excess of the ordinary population, and it is stated that the authorities have had under consideration the desirability of increasing the force. Mr. Meadowcroft, the Runcorn agent to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, had an interview with Colonel Hamersley, the chief constable of the county, on Monday last; but whether their de- liberations were upon this subject or not we are, of course, unable to throw any light.

div.head: SHIP CANAL WORKS
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL WORKS
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 2-FROM HIGHER WALTON TO WARRINGTON.

Last week we drew a sketch of the.ckanges which the construction of the Ship Canal will bring about within the area •of Arpley Fields. at Warrington; this week it is our object to forecast the intended alterations and re-arrangements to be made, consequent on the ntaking of the canal, in the means of approach to Warrington from the direction of Chester. With this aim in view, let us forestall the future by a few years, till a time, in fact, when the canal is completed and in full operation, and then let us, in imagination, mount a vehicle which is being driven from a point on the Chester-road— say at Higher Walton—in the direction of Warring- ' ton. It will matter little to our purpose whether we perch ourselves on the rapidly-moving carriage of a county magnate on his way to town, on busi- ness or pleasure bent, on a farmer's cart laden with produce for the local market, or, even, on the barrels of a Wilderspool dray. To the right, as we move along, there will be little that is new to note, and indeed nothing that can be said to be the direct con- sequence of the making ef the Ship Canal. There will still be the grey and massive structure of the village church, which, to judge from appearances, will stand for centuries to come as ti monument of the piety and wealth of its founder ; and, further down, the pleasant residence of Alderman Crosfield at Walton Lea.

To the left, however, the changes will be of the most marked and striking description. The fields in this direction somewhat rapidly descend from the level of the road to the level of the land which bor- ders on the Mersey, and on the more low-lying ground, though well within view, and, indeed, only a short distance away, there run at the present time the embankments of the railways from Warrington Bank Quay station to Chester. &c., and to Crewe and the south; and more in the direction of War- rington there are to be seen Walton Arches, which carry the rails over the Mersey and Runcorn and Latchford Canal. At the future time of which we are speaking, however, the railway embankment of to-day will have disappeared, or at all events will be disused. The most conspicuous of the things that will have taken its place will be an immense via- duct, towering high above the level of the ground. Under this viltduct will run the Ship Canal, and over it will run the trains from Chester, Crewe, and the south to Warrington and the north, and, of course, also the trains from Warrington and the north to the south. It will be seen that from both ends of this large viaduct there are new and much higher embankments which carry the trains down to the level from which they had been raised in order to cross the canal.

From the Warrington end of the viaduct there will, as we explained last week, be p new line of rails, in place of the old ones, crossing the Mersey by another new bridge to be constructed a short distance to the west of the present Walton Arches. These Arches willremain, and from the Chester road a conspicuous object will be the new embankment branching off in a north-easterly direction from the north end of the Ship Canal viaduct, and by a some- what sharp descent bringing trains for Arpley Sta- tion, or for the new railway to be made across the Arpley Meadows to Warrington docks, down to the level of the present line of metals over the Arches.

The viaduct over the Ship Canal will be 200 yards in length from end to end, and in height will be 72 feet above high water level at ordinary spring tides, and 78.6 feet above the intended water level of the canal. The new railway bridge over the Mersey will, on the Lancashire side, be 38.5 feet above high water at ordinary spring tides, but, as the railway will be gradually nsing towards the bridge over the canal, the Mersey bridge will, on the Cheshire side, be 406 in height. In length it will be 110 yards.

MORLEY COMMON, &c. In passing along the road, it will not fail to be noticed that the footpath across Morley Common— so useful as a short cut from the Bank Quay end of Warrington to Walton, Daresbury and other places in that direction and so pleasant and con- venient at all times, but especially in summer, for a stroll from the close and smoky environs of the town has been effectually closed by the broad expanse of the new canal. There is, it is said, no sweet without its bitter, and, however Warrington may benefit in- dustrially and in other ways from the Ship Canal, there will be drawbacks, and one of these will be found in the ruthless sweeping away of some pleasant walks. In the neighbourhood of Morley Common, or of what remains of it, there will however, be in existence a ferry for the use whenever required—whether it' be night or day— of Sir Gilbert Greenall and his tenants, and -agents and other people authorised by him. To thislerry there will be convenient approaches, and it will be capable of accomodating all descriptions of vehicu- lar traffic and of conveying fifteen ton loads. Some- where in the same locality, there will be a wharf on each side of the canal for the use, free of wharfage dues and charges, of Sir Gilbert Greenall, his ten- ants, &c,

But, pursuing cur journey in the direction of Warrington, we shall find on reaching Lower Wal- ton that some changes of a very radical and exten- sive nature have been made. At the present time, there is a straight road through Lower Walton carrying the traveller over Tom Paine's bridge, which spans the Runcorn and Latchford canal, and past Wilderspool brewery on to the Causeway lead- ing direct into Warrington. When, however, all the contemplated changes in connection with the Ship Canal are carried out, this road will come to a sud- den stop near the spot where now stands the Stag Inn at Lower Walton; and that part of the present road which lies between this spot and some point on the Wilderspool side of Tom Paine's bridge will cease to be road at all, and what is left of it after the canal has been cut through it will, ultimately, no doubt, be broken up:and enclosed in the adjacent fields as either pasture or arable land. NEW ROADS.

In place of the old road that has been stopped, the traveller will have the choice of two entirely new ways by which to reach Warrington one to the left, the other to the right. That to the left will be the new road, which, as we mentioned last week, is to be constructed as a continuation of the River Road 'near Wilderspool level crossing at Warring- ton, and which is to skirt the seuthern bank of the diverted channel of the Mersey across Arpley Fields and finally to branch off, cross the canal, and open out on the Chester road near the Stag Imi. This will be the shortest route to War- rington from Lower Walton, and will, in fact, be considerably shorter than that which at present exists. The new road to the right, of which we ha.veTsaid the traveller will have the choice, is one to be con- structed from Lower Walton across the fields, and which will open out near St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, on to the road from Northwich and Stretton to Warrington. The question may arise in the reader's mind, "Why this other new road, when

div.head: WESToiNi'
div.p: WESToiNi'

Operhtions are about to be commenced upon this section, which extends across Frodsham Marsh. The engineer in charge possesses a name peculiarly ap- propriate—Mr. John Weston. At present there is only an office in course of erection on the Weaver wharf, but tenders have been invited for the con- struction of the customary workshops, and also for twelve workmen's huts, with the usual accommoda- tion. .

div.head: CAPSIZING OF A RAFT.-S MEN IN THE RIVER.
div.p: CAPSIZING OF A RAFT.-S MEN IN THE RIVER.

Mr. William Lamb, farmer, Wash-lane, Latch-' ford, gives the following account of an alarming accident on the Mersey. lie says :—On Wednesday morning I started from the storerooms at Latchford with a load of tools to • Statham-hey, near Lymm, which is between Lymm and Warburton. They started cutting the ship canal there after I had ar- rived—about 40 or 50 of them. I left my cart on the Statham side of the river and crossed the water with a number of tools. There was another man with me. On each side of the river is a pulley, over which a rope • runs, and we pull ourselves across by the rope. After putting down the tools I returned and gave my horse something to eat, but I had to cross again to see 's, gentleman on the other side. The river is very wide at this point. Five men had got on the raft, including myself, and we were moving away when three more men jumped on, making eight of us altogether. We pulled along for a considerable distance, but they began to be unsteady, and the raft got-under the water. Somehow the men got all on one side and the raft upset. Those who had hold of the rope stuck to it. I had hold of it. but most of us went under the water, and I don't believe any of us could swim. Some of the men floundered about, and one or two seized hold of the raft as it came to the sur- face. One man seized hold of my collar and clung fast to it. I broke his hold and held fast tothe rope, and assisted him to the rope. I missed that man directly after, although he should have been on my left. I assisted to save another young man who was making for the raft, and I saw the other man's head coming up just behind it. I collared him be- hind the neck, and dragged him along and we were pulled ashore. This man was in a rather bad state. and if we had not seized the rope nothing would have saved us. One man failed to get any hold at all, and would have been drowned but for a trian who put out a boat and dragged him in. Of course- we were all thoroughly saturated and starved. I made my way home in my cart, and lam thankful to say I feel no worse. I don't know how the other men went on, but those in charge of the works placed a man at the river, with instructions to see that only a limited number passed over at one time.

div.head: SPECIAL CONSTABLES.
div.p: SPECIAL CONSTABLES.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. Meadowcroft, Runcorn agent to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, applied to the magistrates to have 26 men sworn in as constables under the Canal Constables Act, 3 and 4 Victoria, chap. 50, to act on the Bridgewater Canal, the Runcorn and Weston Canal, the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, and the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr. Meadowcroft said he was authorised to make the application by the Board of Directors. The oath was then adminis- tered to the constables. The men have acted as constables for many years, but it was necessary to have them again sworn because of the inclusion of the Manchester Ship Canal length within the area of their duties.
THE POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY AND

IRWELL, A conference of local authorities was held at the Manchester Town Hall on Tuesday, under the pre- sidency of Lord Egerton of Tatton, to consider what means can be taken to prevent the pollution of the rivers Mersey and Irwell and the streams within their watershed. The conference was convened by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and deputa- tions were present from 16 corporations, 48 local boards, and ten rural sanitary authorities. The , Chairman explained that the Ship Canal Company had no feelings of hostility to the local authorities, 'but they had a great undertaking in hand, the success of which they could not allow to be pre, judiced by foul water. The water would be gathered in the docks, and if the present pollution went on ' the docks would be a pestilential place. He moved a resolution that in the interests of public health, as well as of the canal, the time had arrived when the various local authorities should take steps to prevent the pollution of the rivers. The resolution was seconded by .Mr. Alderman Thompson (Man- chester), and adopted. A second resolution adopted asked the authorities to communicate to the chair- man of the meeting before the 25th March the steps resolved upon. A third resolution asked manufac- turers and the public to co-operate with the local authorities in _preventing, Rollution,

div.p: ilair l FIRST -ARBITRATION.

- At Chester Castle, on Monday, Judge Horatio Lloyd and a special jury commenced an arbitration upon a dispute between Mr. Peter Pyne Brownrigg, of Liverpool. and the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany, as tc the value of some land at Ellesmere Port required by the Company. Mr. Brownrigg bought some land at Ellesmdre Pert in 1884, for be- tween MO and £9OO, without, it was stated, ,dny idea that any of it would be wanted by the Ship Canal Company. On his behalf witnesses were now called who valued the land. ' required by the Coin- pany—after allowing for compulsory sale and for consequent depreciation of the remaining land—at nearly ..£5,000. The' inquiry was adjourned until Tuesday morning. Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., in- structed by Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw. and Co., re- presented the Company. The proceedings were re- sumed on Tuesday, at Chester Castle, before Judge Lloyd and a special jury. On the conclusion of the case for the clainant.(Mr. Brownrigg), Mr. Balfour Browne addressed the jury on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, and then called evidenee to show that Mr. Brownrigg had placed an exaggerated value upon the land in question. In the end the jury awarded the claimant .£soo—a sum nu,ich be- low that which his witnesses had said the land wall worth—that amount including compensation for any possible depreciation in the value of the re- mainder of Mr. Brownrigg's land.

div.head: CLAIM BY THE WIRRAL HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: CLAIM BY THE WIRRAL HIGHWAY BOARD.

Al—th7Co's u—nnty --M—agiSt-ra—tes' Court, Birkenhead, on Thursday morning, before Mr. T. H. Jackson and other magistrates, Mr. Thomas A. Walker i contractor for the Manchester Ship Canal Company appeared in answer to a Zimmons issued by the Wirkal Highway Board, to re- cover £199 17s 8d for damages done to certain highways within the district of the Board, leading from Wootton Station to Eastham Ferry, by reason of the damage caused by excessive weights passing along the same and extrawdmary traffic thereon. Mr. W. H. Churton, clerk to the Wirral Highway Board, appeared on behalf of the Board; Mr. Durandu, instructed by Messrs. Perks, Wat- kin, and Company, Manchester, represented the defend- ant.—Befere the case was called, Mr. Churton called their worships' attention to it, as he wished to relieve them of it for the day, after consulting with the defend- ants. He wished the hearing adjourned fas other claims would necessarily follow, and it would be well if the whole matter could be thrashed out at one sitting. Under the circumstances he asked that the matter might stand over for four weeks.—Mr. Durandu consented, adding that the defendant did not deny liability, and was quite willing to pay anything reasonable.—Their worships agreed to the application. BARTON, &c. The Surveyor to the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority. Mr. C. C. Hooky, 0.E., is now preparing a system of

main drainage for these hamlets, in face of the growth ,of the population through the construction of the Ship Canal. At Barton, preparations are being pushed for- ward to proceed with the construction of the soction of the canal from Salt Eye Barton, to Weaste. The build- ing formerly used as a Primitive Methodist Chapel, be- low the Rock House at Barton, has been taken by the contractor, and is being fitted up for use as an office. By order of notice a number of tenants of cottage pro- perty on the banks of the river have vacated them, which indicates that operations of a practical nature will be shortly commenced.

THE NAVIGATION OF VIE SHIP CANAL AND THE RIVER MERSEY. IMPORTANT DECISION, The monthly meeting of the General Purposes 'Committee of the Manchester City Council was held at noon on Thursday, in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, the Mayor LAlderman Harwood), presiding. The proceeding; of the Parliamentary Sub-com- mittee stated that at a recent meeting of the sub- committee the deputy town clerk reported that, under the direction of the Mayor, Alderman Thomp- son, and Messrs. Leach and Southern, all necessary arrangements were ,made for conducting the in- quiry before Admiral Nares, which took Place on the 15th and 16th of November last. Mr. Pemlier. Q.C., ap- peared on behalf ot the Manchester Corporation and the Manchester Ship Canal Company in oppo- sition to the proposal ,of the Liverpool Corporation. to lay pipes in the existing bed of the river, and re- quested that they should be placed at such a level as would permit the river to be hereafter improved. and made as (leer) as the ship canal. The following communication had since ' been received from the Board of Trade upon the subject : , ~ Board of Trade (Harbour Department), 18th January, 1888. Sir,—With reference to my letter of the 22nd October, relative to the aqueduct`authorised by the Liverpool Corporation Waterworks Act, 1880, to be con- structed under the bed of the river Mersey, lam direc- ted by the. Board of Trade to enclose, for the information of the Corporation of Manchester, a copy of the order they have made under the powers conferred upon them by the 16th section of the Act, prescribing the depth at which the aqueduct is to be laid under, the Mersey.--I am, your obedient servant, C. CECIL TREVOR." The order was as follows :—" In the exercise of the powers conferred upon them by section 16 of the Liverpool Cor- poration Waterworks Act, 1880, the Board Of Trade hereby prescribe that so mush of the Vyrn7y aqueduct as will be situate below the bed of the river Mersey shall be laid throughout ilke whole breadth of the navigable channel thereof atk ouch a depth as to provide that the Upper portion of an protecting connected with the aqueduct shall not be le han 17 feet below ordnance datum. Signed, C. CECIL EVOE, Assistant Secretary to the Board of Trade." In moving the adoption of this portion of the pro- ceeedings. ~ . Alderman Thompson said the Liverpool Corporation were prepared to insert a clause in their Act whereby they were to lay their watercourse in a tunnel below the bed of the riverNersoy. The object the Liverpool Cor- poration had was to lay pipes in the bed of the river it- self. That seemed a very simple thing, and it was alleged that it would save a very great expense, but the Corporation of Manchester and the Corporation of War- rington felt it their duty to strenuously oppre that measure, and they had very good cause to rejoice over what had happened. The Liverpool Corporation pro- posed to carry the pipes at a higher levkl, and the conse- quence would have been that if at any future time the Ship Canal Company wished to widen their canal, which was very possible and very probable 'in the future, they would have had to obtain a new Act of Parliament to enable them to do so. He did not wish to appear sus- picious or churlish, but it really looked as if the object of the Liverpool' Corporation was to have the Ship Canal ' Company in their firm iron grip. It came out in evi- dence that the people of Warrington could only have ships of 200 tons burthen at the time of the high spring tides. It also came out that if the Corporation of War- rington, or any other power, would spend £130,000, they might so deepen the channel permanently that they 'would be able to get ships of 600 tons burthen there at any high tide. In Manchester they were very thankful for the enormous boon a the Ship Canal. Let them carry back their minds to what Manchester was 100 years ago, and think of the enormous growth of the city and the district ; and let them Carry their minds for- ward 100 years hence; it was almost impossi- qle to realise the enormous traffic that would then exist. They felt that, for the sake of pos- terity, they were bound to leave every approach . possible open. The Dwell navigation would remain in the hands of the Ship Canal Company, and at a veq moderate outlay the watercourse could be alter to admit of vessels of 400 or 500 tons burthen being ,) brought to Manchester. In consequence of what had been done the waterway would be kept open for ever. Mr. Leech, in seconding the motion, said he thought they might well be satisfied with the award made by the Board of Trade. Vessels would be able to pass along the channel without interfering with the pipes as they other- wise would have done. The resolution was carried.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
THE STATE OF ETTROPR-WAR PREPARA- TIONS.

MERSIN, MONDAY NMHT.—A telegram from Warsaw states that General Gourko, while presiding at a Council of Ware declared that a.sum of. 20,000,000 roubles was needed to complete the frontier fortifications of Russia, to build bridges and mend roads, and to construct a second railway track on thq lines leading to the frontier. An offensive war in Russian Poland, the General is also reported to have said, would be impossible under present conditions. PEOLIPPOPOLTS, Mormsr.—ln anticipation of the arrival here of Prince Ferdinand and his mother (Princess Clementine), the town is ex flit. The streets are decorated with flags, and much enthusiasm prevails amongst the inhabitants. Deputations from different parts of the province have arrived here, and are awaiting the arrival of their highnesses. The Austrian Consul here has received instructions to take no official notice of the arrival of Prince Ferdinand, and the British and Italian Consuls have been directed to act in the same

manner as the Austrian Consul. A good deal of com- ment has been excited in official circles hero by the fact that the Preach Consul yesterday gave a dinner in honour of M. Gueshoff, a former political refugee who has only lately received permission to return to this city. The Italian Consul and a dragoman attached to the RuSsian consulate were also present at the dinner. ATTACK ON COLONEL LITTLE IN BLIRMAH. A telegram from Rangoon, under Sunday's date, gives particulars of a murderous attack on Colonel Little (brother of Major Little, Chief Constable of Preston), at Bhaino. As the colonel was entering his bathroom at night, his Madrassee servant cut him down from behind. When Little fell the servant wounded him again, and then bolted. The weapon used was Colonel Little's own dah. Both wounds are very serious, and one finger of the colonel's left hand was nearly severed while he was trying to protect himself from the second blow. The injured man succeeded in reaching the door and giving the alarm to the sentry, and the servant was -,und hiding in some long grass. He has confessed his crime, but gives no reason for com- mitting-it. , AMERICA AND fIAN.AI)A.

NEW Yol2b, SATtliDAY.—Careful estimates of the loss of life during the recent blizzard in the North-West States .show that 235 persons perished. Other reports have been received computing the fatalities at a higher total, Borne even Placing them 1,000; but they are unsupported by substantial facts. Sad accounts continue to come in from various parts of Dakota, narrating how people lost themselves in the blinding snowstorm near their own doors, and wandering off the proper track perished at last some miles away from their homes. NEW Yonx, Sumnair.—The Reform Club, a new organisation formed in this city since the appearance of the President's Message, for .the avowed purpose of ad- vocating tariff reform, held its first public banquet last evening. Nearly 500 persons attended, including the members of all political parties, showing in a striking manner the remarkable popular support Mr. Cleveland has. 'There were several members of Congress present, many manufacturers from various parts of the country, and eminent representatives of the commercial and pro- fessional classes of the city. It was announced that the _ .

club had over four hundied enrolled members, and had alreadydecided to build a clubhouse in the Fifth Avenue. The first allusion to Mr. Cleveland's name brought all present to their feet. The cheering lasted several minutes, winding up with three rousing cheers. Through- out the evening no speaker could mention Mr. Cleve- • ' land's name without producing a roar of applause. NW Yon, MONDAY.—A daring bank robbery, fol- lowed by a speedy retribution, is reported from' Lime- stone. in Indian territory. Four masked men broke into • the bank in broad daylight, murdered the cashier, who offered resistance to them, and finally carried off a con- siderable quantity of money and valuable papers. An alarm was, however, soon given, and a posse started in pursuit of the robbers, who were overtaken before they went far. A sharp Akirmish ensued, in which one of the thieves was killed and tour of the posse were wounded; but in the end the robbers were beaten. One of them was immediately lynched, and two others were brought back to Limestone to await their trial. Nrivs YORK, MONDAY.—The United States Supreme Court to-day, granted the motion of the Attorney General ' IA Missouri for the oismissal of the appeal of Brooks, alias Maxwell, who is under sentence of death for the murder of Mr. Preller. This decision has the effect of .confirming the sentence of death passed by the St. Louis 'Court
SHIPPING DISASTERS.
The steamer Galcorm Castle went ashore on Monday in Cushendun Bay. An explosion on a Russian schooner at Cardiff, on Monday, caused serious, probably fatal, injuries to four of the crew.

The Greenock barque Waverley has arrived at Queens- town with her decks swept, having lost one seaman and baving others injureld• • Lloyd's agent at Poti telegrr.phs that the Astrion h.as gone ashore at Anaelia, and will probably ba a total wreck. The crew were saved.

The ship Ardmore, from Java. which sailed from Queenstown for London on the Bth January, has put hack to Queenstown, with loss of bowsprit andlibbooms, having been in collision with the William Foss, Nor- wegian barpip-, for Hamburg, on the Bth inst., off Scilly. The latter vessel was sunk, but the crew was saved. The Ardmore will go into harbour for repairs. The White Star liner Republic, which arrived at Queenstown on Saturday, brought news of the wreck in the china seas during the typhoon on the 19th Dec. of thecessenger steamship Vortigern, of Liverpool. The typhoon raged with such violence that the ship's decks were b*rert in, and she 'filled. Eleven passengers and nine or the crew were drowned, but the remainder saved themselves in the boats. The vessel seen off Belt Head, on Friday evening last, foundered during the night, with all hands. She was perceived at about ten o'clock burning distress signals, and the lifeboats from Salcombe and elsewhere were manned; but no trace of her could be found. The coastguard were on duty with rockets until a late hour. A strong smell of petroleum—supposed to have been the cargo—was observed. The Anierimm Line steamer Indiana arrived at Queens- town from Philadelphia. on Sunday. with passengers and inails,and it was reported that at 10 a.m. on the 14th Inst. a fire was iiscovered in the after hold among the cotton. Great excitement prevsiled among the passen- gers, but extinguishers were immediately brought into requisition, and after a copious supply of Nrater had been poured into the burning hold the fire was extinguished. The Inman steamer City of•Riehmond, from New York, With mails and passengers, which arrivedat Queenstown on Monday, brings intelligence of the foundering of the OBritish barque Chopin, and the loss of Captain Hull and six of the crew. The vessel was bound from Turk's Island to Bostor, and foundered in a hurricane off Segue La Grade, on tlie 13th ult. The mate and four of the crew were rescued, after being four days in an open boat, aad.landed at Sague. 2 A dense fog prevailed on Saturday morning in the Bristol Channel, and :everal ,Fasualties were reported in consequence. Late on Friday night the steamer Elsie, owned by Greny, Taylor, and Cu., of Whitby and Cardiff, ran ashore on Lundy Island. The crew were all rescued, but the vessel became a total wreck. The tug Prairie Flower, of Newport, towed a Swedish barque on to the breaks.er. on SatuTday night. The barque was got off, but the tug had to be beached, as she was making water. • A derelict German barque has drifted ashore near Ilfra- combe, and now lies on the sands. The British Steam Navigation Ce.'s iron steamer Con- stance. 563 tons, was wrecked in Plymouth Sound on atarday, and three of her crew were drowned. She ieft Antwerp on the morning of the 19th lust., with a 4eneral cargo, fer Plymouth and Bristol. During a a dense fog, the vessel ran on the Stag Rock inside the new atone entrance to the Sound. Two boats lay alonsgide for two hours, when they were obliged to abandon one boat, and pulled ashore in the starboard lifeboat. . They landed at the Great Western Dock. of the crew, consisting of fifteen all told, the captain, chief •-)fEcer, second officer, carpenter, and eight others were saved. Edward Scarrill, quarter-master ; Thomas Fleas, fireman ; and William Wylds, able seaman, ell three belonging to the port of Bristol, were drowned. The Ccr.stance is now full of. water, and is likely to become a total wreck. A. later telegram states the Constance is broken in two just on the foreside of her bridge. iler forepart is rolling in the sea, and her after part is fired on the rock. The steamer's deck is covered with water at high tide.

The Ccurt of Appeal, on Monday reversed .Tustice Kay's judgment to restrain the London Evening ,Post from using that ti'Ve. The preprietors were ordered to pay their ".ewn wets. Mr. George Smith, partner in the firm of Insrie and Co., saed merchants, Ayr, has mysteriously disappeared. :de left a friend's house at Govan on Saturday.
