div.head: BOLTON THEATRE FIRE
div.p: THE BOLTON THEATRE FIRE

Robert Preston, described as a bill-poster, of Bury, was charged at Bolton Police Court, on Monday, with wilfully and maliciously setting fire to Bolton Theatre Royal, on the 3rd or morning of the 4th of January, that building, in consequence, being entirely destroy. Mr. Melding, prosecuting solicitor, said that no one actually saw the prisoner set fire to the theatre; but there were sufficient circumstances to connect him with the crime. The prisoner was seen near the theatre just before the outbreak of the fire, besides he had never been to his lodgings all night. Further, the theatre office had been broken into with a pickaxe from the lumber room, and in getting there the strap cutting off water from the sprinklers would have to be. passed. Again, four shillings worth of postage stamps had been stokin from the theatre office, and at eight o'clock on the morning on which the theatre was burnt down, the prisoner was found at Bolton Post-office, trying to change these into money. Evidence was given by a large number of witnesses in support of the prosecuting counsel's opening statement. One. woman, named Cunliffe, deposed to the) prisoner using threats about the theatre before the fire, and on the day after, saying it served Eiliston, the proprietor, well right, and he knew who fired the place; in fact could put his hand on the man in two minutes. The prisoner was committed' for trial.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
Mr. W. J. Lane, M.P., was on Monday removed from Cork Gaol to Tullamore.

Mr. Davitt has returned from the Arran Isles, and re- ports that acute distress prevails among the 609 people comprising the population. The Rev. James Mc.Fadden, of Gweedore, arrived at Letterkenny early on Saturday morning, under a strong escort, accompanied by the Rev. John Dohesty, of Rath- mullen. The local clergy met him, and walked with him tco the police barracks.

Lord De Freyne. on whose estates in counties Sligo and Roscommon the Plan of Campaign has been in opera- tion for 15 months, has at last conceded the reduction of rent demanded by his tenalts. This is regarded by the leaders of the League as their greatest victory for a long time past. A largely attended meeting of the Mitchelstown branch of the Irish 'National League, which was one of the branches first, suppressed under the Crimes Act, was held on Sunday, at which two of the East London Radical delegates to Ireland were present, and congratulated the members on their action. The meeting was not in- terfered with by the police.

News has reached Belfast of a shocking case of hydro- phobia, which has occurred near Carrigallan, co. Leitrim. Over 30 people ate of a pig which had been bitten by a rabid dog and about a week afterwards a whole family, named dog, was seized with hydrophobia. Mr. Stewart and three of his children are suffering terribly; one of the latter having to be held down by four people when the paroxysms are upon her. _ _

_ The BeZfast Morning News has received information that the Government have determined upon the imme- diate suppression of the National League in Donegal and other districts in Ulster, and that the arrest of the Rev. T. Mc.Fadden and Mr. Blane, M.P., is the commencement of an extensive campaign against prominent Nationalists in the province. The next batch of arrests will include Mr. Mc.Cartan, M.P., Mr. Reynolds, M.P., and the Rev. Father Convery, president of the Belfast Branch of the National League. Mr. J. R. Cox M.P., member for East Clare, was arrested in London on Monday afternoon by Detective Littlechild, of Scotland.yard. He was walking into the Golden Cross Hotel, Charing-cross, in company with Mr. J. Deasy, M.P., when Mr. Littlechild walked up, and, touching him on the shoulder, asked, "Are you Mr. Cox?" Mr. Cox replied in the affirmative, and Mr. Littledhild then informed him that he held a warrant under the Crimes Act for his arrest. Mr. Cox said he intended going back to Ireland to be arrested.

An explosion of gas, attended with fatal consequences, occurred shortly before four o'clock on Monday afternoon in Judge Boyde's Bankruptcy Court, Four Courts. Dublin. The effect of the explosion was to blow the roof off the court, smashing the windows and those in the adjoining buildings, besides knocking down several parti- tions. It seems that two workmen had entered a trap door in the ceiling to ascertain the cause of an escape of gas, when the gas ignited at a light. David Orr, plumber, sustained a fractured arm. His assistant was killed, while the office keeper and two clerks were injured. The judge immediately left the court, and business was suspended. _ _

The hearing of the charges against the Rev. Thomas Burke and the Rev. Patrick Francis, of haying taken part in an unlawful assembly on November 15th, at Kilcolgen, county Galway, was opened on Monday at Ardrahan. Twelve other persons were charged witn similar Offence. Mr. William St. George gave evidence as to the defendants having Incited the people to erect a hut on his property for an. evicted family. After an adjournment for nearly two hours, during which nego- tiations were proceeding, it was announced that an understanding had been arrived at, the defendants undertaking to remove the hut within the week on the condition that the prosecution was withdrawn. The Court assented to this arrangement.

div.head: MIL VILIJAM O'BRIEN, M.P., INTER-
div.p: MIL VILIJAM O'BRIEN, M.P., INTER-

VIEWED. Forithe greater part of Sunday Mr. William O'Brien. M.P., was confined to bed at the residence of Dr. Kenny, MP., suffering from physical prostration. Replying to a representative of the Press, he saicl4-1 have come out of gaol in the best possible spirits, but the demonstration from Tullamore here on Friday has tried my strength a great deal. I dotr't yet know sufficient of the history of the past three months, while I have been in gaol, to justify mein determining upon any particular line of action, nor do I care to speak upon matters concerning the immediate future without deliberation and consul- tation with my colleagues and leader. However, of one thing 1 am certain: my movements in the near future are of no great importance, as far as the struggle in Ireland is concerned. The people are fight- ing with a spirit equal, if not superior, to anything I ever anticipated. From what I have learned of the country in the short interval since nay release I have no fear as to the determination as well as the mar- vellous patience of our people. They have acted with remarkable courage throughout the whole country, while at the same time they have afforded evidence of patience and self-control to a marvellous degree under circumstances of fearfel provocation. If I may judge of Mr. Balfour's success by any damage he has inflicted on the National League, I find that he has not succeeded in suppressing one single branch of any consequence. Upwards of 1.500 branches bold their meetings un- disturbed, while of the 300 or so proceeded against by the Government. nearly everyone of them continue to hold their meetings and boldly face the imprisonments and the tortures of the Government. Mr. Balfour, to hide the evidences of his defeat, is driven to the mean policy 41 prosecuting a few newspaper eoitors and newevendors. Lord Randolph Churchill predicted several months ago that when Parliament met there would be no trace of the National League; but I think he will find, when Parliament does meet, that it is more vigorous than ever, and that nothing short of suppress- ing civil society in Ireland will suppress the National League. On the other hand, Mr. Balfour seems to be still more unfortunate and more unsuccessful in his endeavoursto grapple withthe plan of campaign. Take, tor instance, the Kingston estate, in connection with which my prosecution and imprisonment arose. The tenants, who had adopted the plan of campaign, de- manded a reduction of 20 per cent. My offence was that I saved a whole country side from being evicted un- til the justice of their demand might be tested by a Tory tribuna/. Well, the Tory Government appointed the worst land sub-commission that they could get to try the merits of the dispute, and the only reprimand this Tory-born Commission administered to the tenants was a vote of censure for demanding so small a reduction. On she average the commission gave a reduction of 221, per cent., whereas the tenants sought only 20 under the plan. In the same manner we had the intelligence telegraphed to us last evening that on Lord de Freyne's estate, which was one of the earliest to adopt the plan of campaign, the landlord has shown his confidence in Mr. Balfour's policy by complying in full with the demands of the tenants. I find that quite recently a similar settlement was effected on the Ely estate,, and peace restored to a district that had been long disturbed. Immediately on my release in Tullamore, when I heard of Mr. Blunt's statement to the magistrates at Gal- way, I made reference to my haying received the same statements from Mr. Blunt some weeks before my imprisonment. The central idea in Mr. Blunt's mind at the time in visiting Ireland seemed to be for the purpose of warning Mr. Dillon and myself against what might endanger our lives, and even if Mr. Blunt bad not given me the warning, I should arrive at the same conclusion from my experience of the policy Mr. Balfour has pur- sued; for it is quite evident, whether he formed the design to kill Mr. Dillon and myself and a few others or not, he had at all events determined on a policy of bar- barous treatment for his political opponents in prison, with the chances of its taking the life of those leaders among them whose physical condition may not be able to bear up against it. The recent prosecutions against so many Roman Catholic priests prove the complete and absolute failure of every endeavour to muzzle them by intrigue, and I think nothing could better illustrate the desire of the Government to outrage the feelings of the people into such violence as may afford some justification for their barbarous and inhuman policy. Since my release I have received very remarkable expressions of sympathy. Of course, they have been innumerable from our own people in Ireland, for no matter who the individual may be, these demonstrations of sympathy might be prospected with as much certainty as we could predict that the sun`will rise 14-morrow. But the warm and kindly expression of feeling that I have received from England have taken me, I may say, by complete surprise, and I can only regard them as evidence of the strong sympathy with our cause which has grown up in England and the closer relations brought about already between the two peoples by Mr. GlAstone's policy.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.
THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC. 4
The Gloucester Boardof Guardians, on Tuesday, decided, by 18 votes to 8, not to prosecute .340 families who re- fused to have their children vaccinated.

It was reported to the Leeds Sanitary Authoiity on Monday that smallpox had broken out at Horsford and Armley. Since the outbreak in Leeds seven cases bad terminated fatally. The smallpox epidemic has reached Louth (Lincoln. shire), and on Monday three cases were reported; in different parts of the town. The medical officer of health complains of the great difficulty of securing com- petent nurses. Smatllpox in the Ashton-under-Lyne district continues to increase. Two new cases were reported on Monday, making a total of 13. The authorities have opened a temporary hospital for the reception of non-pattper eases. Twci of the nurses in the workhouse have beer. attacked with the malady. The Sheffield Guardians beld a special meeting on Mon- day to decide on exceptional measures for the suppres- sing of the smallpox. Dr. Barry, Local Government Board inspector, was present. It was resolved to ap- point 24 additional vaccination officers, and to make house-to-house visitation for the purpose of securing vaccination. _

Another case of smallpox has occurred in Milton- street, Doncaster, where there have already bees three cares, one of which proved fatal. A boy at Hexthorpe is suffering frem the disease, but in his case it is not known how he caught the infection. The disease has also broken out at Epworth, a youth having brought it from Sheffield.

The number of cases at Hoyland Common have in- creased during the past week, and a complaint bas been lodged with the Parochial Committee stating that it is being spread about by the action of the Salvation Army. The first victim was supposed to have brought it from a Salvation Army Meeting at Sheffield, and he was visited by some of the members of the Army, who took it, and so it spread. On Monday, a married woman named Graham, who lived at 9, Prospect-place, died from a very malignant attack of smallpox. She began to be ill on Wednesday, and was prematurely confined of a child, which howed signs of smallpox. The woman died within 24 hours. Mrs. Graham lived near Hooper's, where one fatal and two other cases have occurred. Clubs are being formed in the Plant Works to pay men who are obliged to ab- stain from work owing to the existence of smallpox in their homes. .

The Medical Officer of Health for Leeds has presented, a report on the smallpox epidemic in 'Leeds, which is' assuming serious proportions. In response to a telegram from the ex-Mayor of Leeds. the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company did not run an advectised excursion train from Sheffield on Saturday. The Midland Company would have stopped theirs, but the message did not reach them in time. For the present they will not run any more cheap excursions from Sheffield.

div.head: HORRTBLE DO RESTIIit TRAGEDY AT CARLISLE.
div.p: HORRTBLE DO RESTIIit TRAGEDY AT CARLISLE.

• A domestic tragedy was perpetrated on Saturday at Carlisle. Richard Glaister, between 30 and 40 years of age, was formerly traveller for a London firm, and whilst in their service he fell from his gig and hurt his head. After leaving London he went into the grocery trade, but failed, and has lately been out of a situation. It stated that he had differences with his wife, and that she'had arranged to leave him and go home to her mother. About noon on Saturday a railway lurryman went to their house in Westmorland-street, Denton- ,to remove some of the furniture, and as he obtainmo answer to his knocking, and the neigh- 'xiurs had mot seen the Glaisters astir, the window was forced by a joiner, who, with Mrs. Glaister's brother, entered. A horrible spectacle awaited them in the bedroom. At the foot of the bed Mrs. Glaister was lying, cut and stabbed in the face and breast in many places, and With a deep wound in the chest. She was dead. At the head of the bed was seated her dead bus. hand, with'his head nearly severed from his body. He was grasping in his band a'bread knife; with which it is supposed he had first of all murdered his wife, who was ninth cut in struggling to defend herself, and then cur his own throat. Before committing the murder he had written two letters, one of them dated as far back as Tuesday, in which 'he said, "It's her cursed temper and tongue that have caused the affair, tosay nothing of her hands." 'ln a -second letter, dated Friday, he says. "I've lived ms 'long as •could, and no longer than I could have peace in this world. I now fly to the :lest to get rest and peace for my poor shattered head mid mind. May God have mercy upon my soul."—The coroner's inquest was held on Saturday night —John Wallace MI, next-door neighbour, deposed that at a luarter to eight on Saturday morning he heard screams in Glaister's house, and heard Mrs. Glaister call out. Murder !" He afterwards beard her say, "I'm done." He thought something was wrong, but did not give an' alarm, because lie did not know whether he "had the law on his side?' At the time he believed Glaister was trying to strangle his wife, but as he subsequently heard a gurgling noise he thought she had recovered.—The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful Murder" against Richard Glaister, and found that be had committed "Suicide While temporarily insane."—lt transpired that a second large knife, newly sharpened, had been found concealed in the mattress of the bed, bathed not been used.
THE .nTICIDE OF AN ADMIRAL. SHOCKING ItEVELTIONS:_

On Saturday the inquest on the body of Rear-admiral Versturme was held at the residence of the deceased, Arwenack Mansion, near Falmouth. Mrs. 'Versturme, who was greatly affected, deposed 'hat She and her husband dined together on Thursday evening. They were 'very happy, and the deceased lens in good spirits. After dinner they went into the d raw i ng- room. Having a sore throat she asked her husband to excuse her singing to him as was her custom, and said :he would play the piano only. She went to the piano. and her husband at the same time walked over tc the fireplace and put the small brass poker into the lire, as she supposed to snake a 'blaze. • Shortly after- %n-axes, as she was In the act of opening the piano, she beard a " stuttering noise, which caused her to look round. Shen then saw that her husband had Ole red-hot poker in his hand. Something in his face tarmed her, and she rushed across the room and seized i.he poker. lathe struggle which ensued for the possession of the weapon she burnt her bands, and then she fainted. kfter that she remembered nothing more. She always lived On the best of terms With her husband. There were, however, some family, troubles which had upset her heehand lately: and .at the dining-table, when she wee trying to cheer him up, he remarked, "You are the most cheerful companion any man could have." Witness added that in the, desperate struggle for the poker her nusband seemed bereft of his senses, and seized the !Amp, the shovel, and.litt fact, anything be could lay Isis hinds on. Ellen Davis, the only servant in the house at the time of the tragedy, said Rise heard groans proceeding from Use dramiee,-reem. and hurried thither. She found her mistress on the finer in front of the fire and unconscious. A little distance from Mrs. Versturme lay her master, with a pokes Ist his hands, "struggling and bangine himself about." She took the poker from him, and threw it to the end -el the room. A lighted lamp wasalso on the door, and this he; master was "hugging" to him. She threw a rug over the lamp in order to put it out. She could not hear Ler Mistress calling her, as the kitchen was too far from the drawing-room. . .

Dr. Dunmore denosed that-on his arrival he found the deceased on the door of the drawing-room in a perfect state of frenzy, tie was, in fact, suffering from a paroxysm of suicidal mania, There were four punctured wounds in the abdomen, two of them going right through the integuments. and all with an appearance of burning. The heated poker had penetrated to the peritoniurn. Blood was towing from his mouth, caused by his swallowing broken pieces of glass and china. Witness knew Admiral Versturrne had been in a despondent frame of mind owing to family troubles, but he had never shown any sign of suffering from mania or deli- rium tremens.—The 3ury returned a verdict "That de. ceased died from the effects of wounds self-indicted while in a state of temporary insanity."
THE FATAL FIRE IN HOUNDSDITCH. THE INQUEST.

An .inquest was held on Tuesday at the Coroner's court, Golden-lane, London,, on the bodies of Judith Salzedo, 73, her daughter, Sofia Salzedo, 39, and grand- son, Mordecai Salzedo, three, and Rosetta Borginsky, 40, who perished in the terrible fire at Hutchinson-street. Hounsditch, on Friday last. Jacob Salzedo, butcher, said three of the deceased were his relatives, Judith Salzedo being his mother. They lived over the shop kept by Mrs. Borginsky, who as- sumed the name of Phillips. Mrs. Phillips did not do much trade, and kept but a small quantity of oil in the shop. Both Mrs. Phillips and Mrs. Salzedo's furniture was insured. The Salzedos had two rooms on the first floor, and the floor above was occupied by another family. P.C. Webber, who was supported by a crutch, deposed that he first saw the fire through the shutters. He burst the door open with his knee, and sent for the fire brigade. He heard someone screaming upstairs. He could not go upstairs for smoke. The evidence of the firemen showed that when they arrived the house was well alight, and flames were burst- ing from the windows, while those saved had previously jumped out on to sheets. , Engineer Pierce described the position of the dead bodies, and said he believed Mr. Phillips was trying to save Mrs. Zalzedo at the time she died.
After an address from Mr. Langhatn, the Coroner, the Jury returned a verdict of "Found dead."

Montague Edward Dickson, with several aliases, de- scribed as a traveller, was committed for trial at Greenock, on Monday, on a charge of staling mails from the Belfast mail steamer. The accused is well known to the Belfast police, and he has been identified as having travelled by the steamer on the morning of the robbery. He has also told several stories, which are found to be incorrect, and in a hag belonging to him some skeleton keys were found..

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. Hemming. Q.C., having accepted an appointment which precludes practice at the bar, has resigned the office ofootussel for the University of Cambridge. Mrs. Whittaker. wife of Waiter Whittaker, a brick- setter, of Organ-street, Leigh, has given. birth to four children—ail girls. Three, however, were stillborn. The mother and the fourth child are doing well. The man who murdered a woman named Etty Moore, at Portsmouth, on the Bth of December, and afterwards blew his brains out, has been identified as William Bingley, the son of a publican at Batting Parva, Leices- tershire. In a few days DP. Schliemann will start from Athens for Alexandria. Having recently discovered one of the oldest temples of Aphrodite in Greece, in the Isle of Kedge, he now intends spending three months ha Egypt for the purpose of archteological exploration. The journey will be made together with Professor Virchqw. The 815 express from Manchester to Birmingham was in collision at Macclesfield Station on Monday. Engine No. 1,553 was doing some shunting at a goods siding 50 yards from the platform, when the express came out of the tunnel and dashed into the tender of the abunter. Both engines were seriously damaged, the shunter being thrown off the rails. A breakdown gang are engaged 'clearing the road. The express was crowded with pas- sengers, none of whom were seriously hurt. EXT'RAORDINARY SUICIDE or A WOMAN. Intelli- 4zence has reached Canterbury of a very deter- mined case of self-destruction by the wife of a farm labourer residing at Ash-next-Sandwich. Some time ago two of her children were carried off by an epidemic, and a day or two since another died. These repeated losses would seem to have affected the mother segreatly as to induce her to fasten two heavy clockweights round her neck, and jump into e. large tank of vsater, 'from which her lifeless body was subsequently recovered. Four railway accidents occurred on Saturday night, near Newport, Monmouthshire. Hannah Evans, 84, was crossing the railway at Maindee, when she was knocked down by a Bristol passenger train and killed. Michael Collins, 'fish hawker, was killed by a passenger train whilst walking along the line towards Abernan Station. Robert Hamilton' chief engineer of the steamer Galtea, whilst crossing the dock railway at Newport had his foot out off by the engine. David Jones, carpenter, was terribly crushed between waggons near Cwmbran. The Post Office authorities have some reason to sus- pect that the extraordinary numerous thefts of postal orders in this country, which reached portentous dimensions last year, are the work of a regular con- federacy or conspiracy among the younger members of the service. It is possible that some remarkeble dis- coveries will be made shortly. In the meantime it is believed that the head-quarters of theoonspiracis are not, hi London, but one of the larger cities of. the North of England. Cotomar. Deemsce.—With the exception of Queens- land. all the Australasian Colonies have now agreed to the recommendations of the British Royal Commission upon Colonial defence. The Commissioners recommended that the Colonies should contribete to the Imperial Ex- chequer in order that. England should build ships of war for the protection of harbours of commerce and coaling stations in the colonies, and Great Britain has been called upon to construct several war vessels. These will be commanded by British officers, but will be subject to the control of the several Colonies. Impacitim Team IN THE Mresernist—Great activity is appearing among the railway waggon and carriage building companies In South Staffordshire and War- wickshire districts. they declare that trade is better than it has been for ten years. Alt the works are fully employed, and some of them employ eight hundred and others a thousand workmen. The orders are chiefly for theindian States Railway, and the South American Re- public.: Five large Indian orders are to be decided this month. The contracts are mostly for waggons and carriages of iron and • steel, and this activity is greatly assisting the iron and steel masters. DISTRESSING ELOPEMENT. A commotion has been caused in the West-end of London by the elopement of a sham clergyman with a young lady of tender years and high social connections, to whom the rev. gentleman , had been engaged to act as private tutor. The pair were traced to Paris, and it turned out that the pseudo clergy- man had deserted a young wife and child, wilt= he had left behind in London under circumstances of a most distressing character. There was a violent scene at the apartments in Peels where the fugitive couple were found, and but for the intervention of the servants the indignant father would have laid violent hands upon the betrayer. When the whole of the circumstances were explained, the misguided and repentant young lady placed herself under ker parent's control, and re- turned to London. LORD RIPON ON ELEMENTARY EDIYCATION.—The Mar quis of Ripon distributed the prices at the third annum- meeting of the Airedale Pupil Teachers' Prize Scheme Association, held at Eeighley on Saturday afternoon. His Lordship remarked that in elementary school; pupil teachers constituted a most important element, and the managers of those schools had as their primary duty the fulfilment of a public trust, and were bound to lay aside to a great extent personal considerations, and to•elioose those boys and girls who were most likely to make efficient pupil teachers. The, work of the elementary school teacher he looked upon as being of the first public importance, end alluded to the necessity for having thoroughly trained pupil teachers, speaking in terms of praise of the work carried on by the association, which he described as good, solid, and valuable. EXTRAORDINARY SHOOTING CASE.—At the adjourned inquest in Chester, on Monday, on the body of George Newns, who died from gunshot injuries received at Trevalyn, near Rossett, on Christmas morning, David Huxley stated that at one o'clock he heard a shot, and going out he found Newns lying bleeding opposite the Griffin Inn. The same forenoon John Player, landlord of the inn from which the shot was fired, asked witness. "How is the man ?" Witness said, "He is shot." Player continued, "And serves him right. I am determinepi not to be annoyed by this or any other man, I am only sorry I did not shoot him dead."—Mr. Churton, on behalf of deceased's relatives, complained that no dying depo- sitions of the deceased were made—Mary Viasrd. ser- vant at the inn, said Player went out of the inn, gun in hand. Newns closed with him, and the gun fell and went off. Player then went into the house and shut the door. Player was a hasty-tempered man.—The inquiry was again adjourned. MR. artrour awn Gnansromasts. —An important letter was received on Tuesday from Mr. John Bright, in reply to • communication from a Bir- mingham elector complaining that in the municipal con- tests the Gladstonrans have given their support to the Conservatives. Mr. Bright, in his letter, says :—'t I can only regret the increasingly bitter spirit manifested by the followers of Mr. Gladstone. They have adopted a policy which has excluded their leader from office and power, and they are furious because we are unable to accept what we deem mischievous and full of peril. In boroughs where the municipal contests have been fought' on party lines it is likely that the hostility of the Glad- stone party to the Liberal Unionists will draw them into an alliance with the Tories. I do not think any arguments of mine or others will prevent this We can only regret it. It is one of the evils which have come upon us from the fact that the bulk of the Liberal party, instead of adhering to and maintaining their own principles, have swallowed doctrines which up to two years ago they condemned and abhorred, and at the invitation of an eminent statesman have, in the attempts to break up Parliament, hitherto only succeeded in breaking up a great political party. We must bear the evils which have been thrust upon us. The country, and what is good in it, will survive the present troubles, and we must have patience." PERSONAL STATISTICS.—The oldest Cabinet Minister is Viscount Cranbrook, G.C.S.L, Lord President of the Council. aged 73; the youngest is the Right Hon. Arthur Jameii Balfour, M.P., Chief Secretary for Ireland, aged 39. The oldest member of her Majesty's Privy Council is the Right Hon. Viscount Eversley, G.C.R., aged 93; the youngest. the Duke of Portland, aged 30. The oldest Duke is the Duke of Cleveland, E.G., aged 84; the youngest, H.R.H. the Duke of Albany, aged 3. The oldest Viscount is Lord Eversley (who is the oldest Peer of the realm), aged 93; the youngest, Viscount Southwea (a minor), an Irish peer, aged 15. The oldest Baron is Lord Cottesloe, aged 89; the youngeet, Lord O'Hagan (a aiiner), aged 9. The oldest Member of the House of Commons is the Right Hon. Charles Pelham Villiers, M.P. for the Southern Division of the borough of Wolver- hampton, aged 86; the youngest, Lord Henry Cavendish- Bentinck, M.P. for the North-West Division of Norfolk, aged 24. The oldest Judge in England is the Hon. Sir Henry Manisty, of the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court, aged 78; the youngest. the Hon. Sir Arthur Charles, of the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court, aged 49. The oldest Judge in Ireland is the Hon. John Fitzhenry Townsend, LLD., of the Court of Admiralty, aged 77; the youngest, the Right Hon: Hugh Holmes., of the Queen's Bench Division, aged 47. The oldest of the Scotch Lords of Sessign is the Eight Hon. John Inglis (Lord Glencorse), Lord Justice General, aged 78; the youngest, the Hon. John Trayner, LL.D. (Lord Tmyner), aged 53. The oldest Prelate of the Church of England is the Right Rev. Richard Dumford, D.D., Bishop of Chichester, aged 1 85; the youngest, the Right Rev. John Wordsworth, D.D., Bishop'of Salisbury, aged 44. The oldest Prelate of the Irish Episcopal Church is the Most Rev. Robert Bent Knox, D.D., Archbishop of Armagh, aged 80; the youngest, the Right Rev. Robert Samuel Gregg, D.D., Bishop of Cork, Cloyne, and Ross, aged 53. The oldest Prelate of the Scotch Episcopal Church is the Right Rev. Charles Wordsworth, D.D., Bishop of St. Andrews, aged 81; the youngest., the Right Rev. James Robert A. Chinnery-Haldane, Bishop of Argyll and the Isles, aged 45. The oldest Baronet is Sk John Buck- worth-Eferne-Soame, of Ware, Herts, aged 93; the youngest, Sir Stewkley F. Draycott Shuckbitrgh '.(a minor), of Shuckburgh, Warwickshire, aged 7. The oldest Knight is Sir Provo William Parry Wallis, G.C.8., the senior Admiral of the, Fleet, of Euntington House, near Chichester, aged 96; the youngest, Sir Edgar Vin- cent, E.C.M.G., Financial Adviser to the Khedive of • Fgypt, aged 30. CALIFORSLA. AND ENGLISH WOVEN. BY HENRY WHITMAN. I see from a recent issue of the "Examiner "that Mrs. Parker's statements, affirming general and un- limited prosperity‘ in California, have not been al- lcwed to pass unchallenged. The lady, as well as myself, is well known in Warrington, and whatever we may say on the subject may influence the unde- cided; hence the great necessity for care in giving advice. California is, from England, near upon a three weeks' journey. It is also costly. From this it will be seen how hard a matter it would be to remedy any mistake on the part of the emigrant. Mrs. Parker, moving in a circle surrounded by" will, perhaps, not see the same side of the shield as myself; but, at all events, what I have to say will be said in the interest, and for the welfare of ray own class—the poor working-men and women of England. My attention was first drawn to a letter of Mrs. Parker's, which appeared in the Liverpool Mer- cury." There ' California was described as the " Garden of the Lord." • If this be so, I am afraid the Lord takes his pleasures on very unholy ground. For I am sure no state or country inhabited by the Aryan race can have to deplore so much lawlessness, and BO much brazen-faced wickedness as this "poor man's paradise." I wonder if Mrs. Parker saw the recent statements given in a San Diega paper of the " harrowing illustrations of the selfishness and heartlessness of households." If so, she ought also to have seen that in a review of these statements in the " San Diega Union," of December 18th, the writer confessed his inability to " refute the arguments," although asserting that "the mistress takes more apparent thought for the welfare of the servant than the servant takes for that of the mistress." Now, I take it, sir, that between these statements 'lies the truth. Just now the churches, working togethek, are trying to thin the rookeries of New York by helping forward a migratory movement towards Los Angelos and San Diega. This is as it should be; yet it is not infallible in its results, and the poor servants, disgusted with their new sur- roundings, refuse 'to "hang on," and prefer to "go back to the grind of their poverty" Now, if this is so with the New Yorkers, how much more would it be the case with English servant girls ? The truth is, life in any part of California is so very different in its conditions and surroundings, that the pest experience of an English girl goes for nothing. She has, in her daily life and conduct, to reconcile herself to the great necessity of being born again. I cannot deny that prospetity in this world's goods will attend those who bend their backs to the task of winning" the Almighty Dollar; and that alone. For, to win it and to spend it. seems the only aim and object of the native American. But life to be worth living requires something more than this deep-seated craving for dimes and dollars. It is well known that the comforts of domestic life enter largely into the social economy of Eng- lish life. The conveniences of home life, as known in England, are entirely unknown here; hence arises the startling and sad features of the great I social evil. To Mrs. Parker's letters I add this advice. Let no man or woman, boy or girl:come out here who does not contain within him or herself suffi- cient resources for amusement, or intellectual en- joymeat, without having to seek it in the saloon or the conceit hallj Let it not be imagined that even in Los Angeles the streets are paved with gold. I gather that it is not so from the papers. The following I give as a sample : " Famished by tke Roadivay.:—Yesterday afternoon a Mexican named Jesus Ramey= was found close to the railroad track, about midway between this city and San Fernando, in an exhausted condition. He was taken to McClure's vinery, and after he was restored said he had been there for two days without food or water. Ram- eviz was brought to this city this evening and placed In a hospital?' That this state of things is exceptional I am sure, and I only give the extract to qualify or modify the t(lo general statements of Mrs Parker. Los Angelos and its surrounding district deserves the efforts now being made to " boom " it, and men with a little capital may open out for themselves a prosperous career, but it must be its new settlers. Before they can make many visits to their banker there is a heap of hard work. As to ser- vant girls, they must be prepared to accept the condi- tions I have stated above, but I should say if they are doing fairly well at home stay there. I ask to be ex- cused for saying so much of the servant girl, inasmuch ' as most of Mrs Parker's remarks referred to the "lady help." I have no experience or knowledge of such a person, and I affirm strongly that the native American lady will not, nay cannot, recognise her existence. The American lady, as a rule, is a self-made woman, or the wife of a self-made man, and could not tolerate the insular prejudices inbred in the English educated lady. In no land on earth does tradition and caste pre- judice work with such baneful results as in England, and in no land is class separated from clam to such a de- gree. Then how is it likely that an educated "help" scorning to be classed as a servant, will either make or find the conditions of life so satisfactory as Mrs Parker depicts them? She may term it "false feelings of gentility"; all the same it is there, and bars the way. I see in a further issue of the "Examiner," December 10th, your report of a lecture given on Otis very impor- tant subject by the same lady, in which she gave a list of wages of the artizan class which ranged from L 1 a day to 8s a day. This is simply misleading, and I have been asked by several Englishmen to give it con- tradiction. There are men known to the present writer , working for five dollars a week. ZI English money. The rule for labourers is about es per day. Those who get .£1 a day would have to be, as in Enzland, in posi- tions of trust. The skilled artisan will earn from two ani a half to three dollars a day. But what of this? He has to pay in this land of Protection, of which I shall speak in a future letter, rather smartly for all he puts on his back. Wool being an imported article, and the ex- porter neglecting to pay the added cost, it results that a forty shilling suit in England costs about eighty in this working-man's paradise. Protection also carried out to its legitimate results causes me to sit shivering on this • first day of the New Year, coal being over 3s a hundredweight. This article, generally sup- posed to have been provided by the Almighty Ruler for the common weal of His people, is enclosed by a ring which nothing can penetrate but the material and sub- stantial dollar. As to rent, I pay five dollars a week, ' the landlord insisting upon a month's rent beforehand. I could go through a tolerably long list, such as having to pay from £5 to £6 for a stove before you can warm youinelf, which if Mrs Parker had known any- thing about lam sure she would have Mentioned. Food alone is reasonable, my family having dined off a good leg of mutton on this New Year's Day which cost under 2s. But enesigh of this. Let me speak of San Francisco itself. Its greatest and first curse is the existence of the "meon-eyed heathen." It is supposed that 100,000 of these pig-tailed invaders are now located on the Pacific slope, and that this city has within its boundaries near upon 60,000 of them. It may be, sir, that your good readers may ask for a little charity to be shown towards these celestials. It cannot be. Their habiW their complete and total want of any- thing like moral laws, place them outside the pale of civilised life, and I know of nothing more likely to bring enmity and hatred against England by native San Fran- ciscan than the fact that the Canadian Government shielded by the Imperial Government is willing, for the sake of gam, to forward or wink at any or all the devices adopted to flood this "garden of the Lord" with Chinese slave women. The question of the admission of Chinese slave women is becoming a serious one, and no one except the Judges seems to doubt the fraudulent returns of their claims to prior residence here. There are about 800 respectable women inChinatown,and24oChineseprostituteswerethere in January, 1887. Since then as manyas 100 more prosti- tutes have been admitted by the United States courts on a claim of prior residence, although only fifty-nine de- parted before August 8, 1882, when that claifn ceased to be a legal one. There are still eighty-one eases to be dis- posed, and if the usual course is followed these will also be landed. San Francisco with all its natural advantages must be held back in its progressive march unless something is done to stop these things from coming in. Disease haunts their quarters. They burrow like vermin, in holes which never see day-light. In a city,not over nice in its sanitary laws, these sly and deceitful children of the sun are allowed to hide themselves away, in such a manner that small pox and the most malignant diseases find among them a harbouring which your readers can- not imagine. Settled as they are, in the heart of the town, the citizens are forced through their quarters, and then in the side walk you see behind the wire netting fixed in the wall, the painted face of what appears a wax doll, but is in reality a human being,otherwise a Chinese girl naming her price, and soliciting the passers by. In any other city this would not be tolerated; hero it is a huge sore festering to such a degree that it must ulti- mately bring about the formation of a vigilance society whose member will have to be banded together for two things: as a defence against cheap labour, and for the suppression of all the social evils peculiar to the pig- tailed race. In my last letter I gave vent to a strong expression re- specting this the city of my adoption. For the benefit of others who may not be altogether of my way of thinking on certain matters, I deem it best to state things as I find them. While I have no respect for the Sabbath, except as a rest day,l know that the great majority of my countrymen and women hold its descration in the ut- most dread. Here, whoever wishes to build a house, slaughter a beast, or open a liquor store, does it; Mrs. Grundy has no home in this country. If you want to do a thing, you do itzight away, and ask no one's opinion. Strolling in the levee the other Sunday morning, I came upon a swell mounted on some logs singing a comic song, the burden of which was •
"So if you meet a tramp that bears misfortune's stamp, If he's worthy of your aid why freely give: Give him a hearty grip, wish him luck upon his trip,

And remember-Sat-the poor tramp ha i to live." This man by interlarding with his song a lot of senti- mental twaddle about the horny handed SODS of toil, managed to get rid of a large bundle of songs, in the short space of time I stayed to listen. There is variety sufficient for all tastes, and it causes all who can be at liberty on that day, to look forward ,to it as the only day of pleasure. No Saturday half-day's holiday. On Christmas Day I attended with my family I their church, and I was struck with the following verse that was sung :- 1 "No more let sin and sorrow grow, _

Nor thorns infest the ground; He comes to make his blessings flow Far as the curse is found." Close to this church were several theatres, all of which are open on Sunday, and I thought of the curse. I wish my friends to forgive me, for, after all, I went to the theatre in the evening. You know, Mr. Editor, I, in a strange land, have not yet gathered any of my house- hold gods about me—my books, &c. As for the Free Library that we have here, I have not visited it yet, al- though it is open on Sundays. I wish in this letter to speak more especially of the sins of this city, as they might affect the new comer;these matters to be only incidentally referred to hereafter. In the second main street of the city are to be found saloons in suchnumbers that I think it almost impossible to count them. Music in each one. Brass and stringed instruments cause the 'street to be, every night in the week, as gay as can be imagined. Electric lights, and the flaring gas, do not act as deterrents to those who have an hour to waste; hence the coast of Barbary is a dangerous one to sail around.

Enter a saloon, and you are immediately attended by a fair sprite, clad in the Bloomer costume. It is sicken- ing, Mr. Editor, but I was bound to see it all. And what is the ending. Take the following scene:—" The next case of drunk to pass the iron gate was Mrs. Louisa Frye, who was picked up out of the gutter in the lowest part of Barbary Coast. Her dark hair fell in tangled, uncombed masses over her bleared countenance and the single garment that covered her person was so bedraggled and limp from the slush of.the streets that it clung to her form as though it had been pasted there. The lan- guage that fell from her lips as the officers performed their unpleasant duty of searching her shocked the ears of even the most hardened habitue of the prison. When they had finished, the turnkeys seized her and dragged her, shrieking, cursing and struggling to the dark cell. As she passed one of the cages a youth of perhaps 17 years of age rose and leaned against the bars. Suddenly his face blanched, and he would have fallen had he not caught the irons. Mother Mrs. Frye turned her bloodshot eyes on his faze. Mother !"Phis time his cry was very shrill, and it must have seared her brain like a red hot iron. She straightened up, gazed into his eyes for an instant, and then gasped out: My God ! Al- fred 1' No need for the dark cell ; the cry of ' mother ' had sobered her."

All this can be avoided; there are a thousand ways for the right-minded leading, as I hope and believe, to com- fort and happiness. But the temptations to go wrong are so many that I tremble at the thought of advising any one to come out here. 2,305, Taylor-street, North Bay, San Francisco, California.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AT NORTHWICH.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AT NORTHWICH.

The annual gathering in connection with the Gladstone Liberal Club, Northwich, took plae3 in the Central Hall of that town on Saturday evening. The proceedings commenced with a tea party, at which about 500 persons were present, and Mrs. Brunner presided at one of the tables. At the sub- sequent entertainment the hall was crowded, and , Mr. Brunner. who was accompanied by Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., occupied the chair. In his introductory remarks Mr. Brunner referred to

THE RESULTS OF THE COERCION ACT: He said it seemed to him that their prospects, as Liberals, had been growing brighter day by day— not only in that constituency, but throughout the length and breadth of Great Britain. Liberals were in good spirits, and they showed it by abstain- ing from black-guarding their opponents. (Hear, hear:and applause.) Liberals had been holding forth before their countrymen sound reason, good argument, and kindly thought; and the men who did that were the people who were on the winning , side; and not those who were desperately angry who called their opponents hard names, aye, •and even put them into prison. Those who were angry, hard, and cruel, felt themselves on the losing side. (Hear, hear.) On the previous day that good friend of Ireland, and he believed of England too, Mr. William O'Brien—(applause)—came out of Tul- lamore Gaol. He (Mr. Brunner) asked them to consider who could possibly be the better for the three months Mr. O'Brien had spent in prison. (Hear, hear.) Mr. O'Brien entered the prison a man of fragile frame and delicate health, and he had come out with a constitution still further in- jured, and broken health. That was all the differ- ence. There was not a man or woman either in Ireland or Great Britain, that had been converted to Coercion. (Hear, hear.) Those who were Liberals three months ago had been confirmed in their Liberalism, and those who were in favour of coercion were now beginning to doubt about it. So the sole benefit Mr. Balfour had got by putting Mr. O'Brien into prison was that he had injured Mr. O'Brieu'a health, and that was no good to anyone under the sun. (Applause.) At a later period of the evening Mr. Brunner spoke in favour of

FREE EDUCATION. There was, he said, a conspiracy to destroy the na- tional system of education, commenced under Mr. Glad- stone, in 1870. There was a lama, number of people who were extremely anxious to go back to the system that obtained before that time. For instance, it was pro- posed that no man who subscribed to a school should be called upon to pay School Board rates. As they knew, most of the rich people belonged to the Church of Flag- land all the large subscriptions therefore would go to the Church schools; and the poor would have to keep up the poor schools. This was the bad old system— that the poor have thepoor things and the rich have the good things. He asked the electors not to permit this system of 1870 to be injured. His opinion of a proper sort of school was one which WEIS built at the common expense and managed in the cominon interest by repre- sentatives of the people, and not by the representatives of any section amongst the people. (Hear, hear.) The ideal school was a place where those who were at work had no other thought than the education of the children in the school. If the people would take his advice, they would not have the schools used for teaching Wesleyan- ism, Primitive Methodism, nor the doctrines of the Bap-, tists,or any other religious sect whatever; but have the rich children and the poor children taught what *ill make them brighter and happier children, and make them more useful to their parents and better citizens of this great empire. Let the schools be free from all sus- picion of religious or political proselytism. Let them not, if they could help it, allow their teachers to be ap- pointed because they were Liberals, or because they were Tories; but appoint them because they were good teachers, and for no other reason. He heard some time ago about a school which was not a hundred miles from Northwich, where the tea- cher did not think it beneath himself or beneath the dignity of his position to pick out the nastiest and most .currilous bits about Mr. Gladstone .from the London cerrespondenc,e of a Tory newspaper, and to give these choice morsels as a dictation lesson to the scholars. (Shame.) He had got his eye upon him—(Mr. King: So have I)—and he told that gentleman that not haying heard this in a public way he could not use it, but if he could find out man honourable way so as to bring it for- ward in an open honourable way, he would bring the matter before the department in London. (Applause.) If a schoolmaster of Liberal politics prostituted his prin- ciples in that way, he should call him a snob, and refuse to shake hands with him. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner advised the ratepayers of Northwich to establish a School Board; and said that when we got a proper system of education, it would be possible for all their children, girls as well as boys, to begin in the schools at a penny a week, or nothidg a week, please God, and by- and-bye to go from these free schools to such a school as Witton Grammar School, then to such a school as Owen's College, Manchester, and finally to London University or at any rate the best school in the land. (Applause.) They would make use of Witton Grammar School as one of the steps in the educational ladder, which he hoped would some day be free from the bottom to the top. (Applause). The first portion of the entertainment consisted of a series of views, thrown on a screen by limelight, illus- trative of "Ireland ; its beauty and its blight." The pictures were shown by Mr. Horace Handley, of Run- corn, assisted by Mr. J. Rhodes. Portraits which had been copied from original photographs by Mr. Handley, were also thrown upon the screen, and included gr. Gladstone, Mr. John Morley, and other Liberal and Irish leaders, together with Mr. Brunner, Mr. A. Fletcher, Mr. H. Bratt, &c.

The Financial Reform Almanack has attained a unique position as a standard work on matters of Znance and fiscacreform ; and the issue for the current year fully maintains its high reputation. Attempts are made now and again by Tory orators and journalists to show that it is not infallible; but it does not pretend to be, and the fact re_ plains that, despite trifling errors as to matters With regard to which it is difficult to obtain cor- rect data, it is so wonderfully accurate as to be the established authority amongst the politicians 13t the day. There have been important additions - 'made in the Almanack for 1888, particularly as - to information relating to the Irish Question. The 'subject of hereditary pensions occupies the public mind more than it has ever done before, and the editor has therefore acted wisely in reproducing the Alphabetical Pension List. We cannot imagine MY reader, be he Liberal or Conservative, study- ing this list without feeling that it is a discredit to be nation to have so many "gilded flies" fatten- ing at the expense of the rest of the community. Why should civil servants have enormous pensions, or for that matter any pension at all? They are inr the most part well paid for their services, and they should themselves provide for a rainy day. Why, again, should such large sums be paid in the way of pension, when a reform of the service has to be instituted? It is stated that the clos- ing of the Ecclesiastical and Prerogative Courts has cost no less than £1,750,000 in pensions! Legalised robbery of this kind bars the way to effective reform. What is the. use of a statesman scheming to get rid of drones, if the drones are still Permitted to. cling leech-like to their fainting e°, untry ? Merchants and tradesmen do not reg- ate ul their . • „ Maness affairs in this way. If they find can so reorganise their establishments as 40 be able to dispense with some of their work- People they send them adrift without pensions. Ile most they can be expected to do is to give reasonable notice of the change that is about to take place. And this course should be taken with Public servornts. It is taken, with one class

- but unfortunately it is the class least able to make provision for the future. Dockyard work- men are sacked" by the hundred, and there is 110 pension for them. Will anybody say that their labour is not as good in its way as that of the black-coated gentry? We are not claiming that Pensions should be given to dock labourers; but We do say that it is absurd, by comparison, to give pensions to officials who get pounds where labourers get shillings for their services.

But of all the wild ways of making ducks and drakes with the money of the pebple, commend us to hereditary pensions. John Bull is a slow, sleepy fellow, and unable to attend to more than one thing at a time.. If he had had less on his hands during the last half century, and been at the. same time wile awake, he would have taken good care not only that no additions were made to the pen- sion list, but that the existing burden was greatly reduced. Take the case of NELSON, who deserved a grant if ever one was deserved; but, after pro- viding for his widow, his sisters, and his neice in a most liberal fashion, are we not justifi.ed in say- ing "Something too Much of this," when we find thatlts,ooo was granted to "his successor to the earldom and to all future inheritors"? The DUKE

ot litaaimououan had a pension of £4,000 a year •granted in 1704-6; and the CHURCHILLS have , been Pocketing the money ever since—or at least uPIO 1884, when no less a sum than £107,000 was Paid to the present DUNE of MARLBOROUGH to in- duce him to commute the pension. Let those 'who have a taste for figures/ compute the value of ',,T4,000 a year lent out at interest from 1706 to 1884, and they will be startled at the vast sum Which has been handed over to the descendants of the General who robbed his soldiers in order to rob the nation, and who resorted to the vilest means in order to acquire wealth in his lifetime. But, Perhaps .the most startling cases are those of pen- aiOns paid to the bastards of CHARLES SECOND Ild their descendants. The first DINCE of itienmoND was the • son of KING CHARLES by LOUIS DE QUEROUAILLE, and he was maintained by an infamous tax on all coals exported from the TYne. This commenced in 1676; but in 1799 it Was arranged that, instead of the tax on coal, die then DUKE of RICHMOND should have £19,000 a year. There has since been further commutation of the RICHMOND pension—nearly half a million having been paid in this way. The first DUKE of S. ALBANS was another illegitimate son of en.truEs the SECOND, the famous NELL GWYNNE • being the mother of the "nobleman." In 1832 it was estimated thrt the emoluments or pensions then enjoyed amounted to £640 a year, apart from the 1:96.; received as Master of the Hawks. Another cf CHARLES'S amours resulted in a DUKE of GnArrox, and how much that family have-bled the State it is hardly possible tp say ; it certainly amounts to some millions—principal and interest It is a matter of coon?, to say that the nation at the present day would not permit the imposition of any such charges the remissness is in not dealing with those that exist. As we have already Pointed out, some of the pensioners, seeing rocks

ahead, have taken a lump sum, and ended the claim. But the lump sum is in every case too big a lump. Justice demands that the Legislature shall at once pave the way for a speedy abolition of the pension list. There are too many aristo- cratic paupers; it would do them good to throw them, after due notice, on their own resources; whilst it would be a great relief to the honest men and women in the laid, who find it a hard struggle to earn a living in a legitimate. way.

MB. BRUNNER, M.P., always shows a lively appreciation of the signs of the times in the matter of education. He foresees that a period is approaching when an effort will be made to make our education more and more sectarian rather than more and more national. Speaking on the subject, at Northwich, on Saturday, he described what was taking place in some quarters as "a

conspiracy to .destroy the national system of education commeliZect under Mr. GLADSTONE in 1870." It may seem strange that such a state- ment should be made in view of the fact that a Conservative like Lord RANDOLPH CREECH= has declared himself in favour of Free Education. But there are politicians who will turn in any direction rather than that, if it invnlves unsec- tarian teaching; and one of the most frequently urged proposals amongst those who prefer the crooked path to the straight is that subscribers to denominational schools should be exempted from School Board rates. These people foresee a time, not very distant, when it will be impossible to find a town of the size of Warrington without a School Board, and they are laying their plans accordingly. It has an innocenb look with it—this idea of ex- emption of rate for those who• subscribe to a par- ticular school; but what does it mean? It really means that the poorest neighbourhoods—where Board Schools usually flourish—will be most heavily, taxed. As Mr. BIItNNER puts it, "All the large subscriptions would go to the Church Schools, and the poor would have to keep up the poor schools." It would put a premium, in fact, upon. sectarianism the very thing we re- quire to get !rid of in connection with State- aided education. To quote Mr. BRUNNER again:—

"The proper sort Of school was one which was built at the common expense and managed in the common interest by representatives of the people, and not by representativei of any sections amongst the people." The payments of the State are for secular teaching pure and simple, and, whatever change is made, care should be taken that there is no depar- ture from this sound principle. It would be absurd, after fighting -for generations against the State endowment of particular sects to turn round and become party to the endowment of every sect. For this is what it would come to,,eif a citizen otherwise liable to pay School Board rates, was to be permitted to pay, that rate to whatever school best pleased him., A system So irregular, capric- ous, and one-sided stands self-condenined. Still it is calculated to serve sectarian rather than educa- tional ends,. and we need not therefore be surprised that it finds favour amongst the supporters of class legislation. There is some danger of Dissen- ters Who have well-established schools being tempted into acquiesing in a proposal of this kind before they have well considered whither it will lead them. Let them take courage from those who, like the member for the Northwich Division are sounding the alarm, and, planting their feet firmly by a principle,, are determined to stand by it. Mr. BRUNNER'S ideal is 'a noble one. He says :

When we got a proper system of education, it would be possible for all their children—girls as well as boys—to begin in the schools at a penny a week, or nothing a week, please God, and, by-and- bye, go from those free schools to such a school as .Witton Grammar School, then to such a school as Owen's College, Manchester, and finally to London University, or at any rate the best school in the land. This is what should be, and it is possible of attain- ment under a truly rational system of national education. Already we are on the eve of State-. aided technical schools; which must of necessity be unsectarian. Why then not lead up to them in the right way, by making provision for elemen- tary education being free Said unsectarian ? The laws of evolution apply everywhere,. and the right course is to aid their operation.

IT was fitting, and yet in some degree 'singular, that the centenary of the birth of BYRON should have been celebrated, on Sunday, by the Greeks in this country rather than by the English. The influ- ence of BYRON as a poet is undoubtedly on the wane amongst his own countrymen. As he himself says, he awoke one morning and found himself famous; and he swam for many summers in a sea of glory. He took care by means that were glorious and inglorious to be always in evidence. It thus happened that he occupied an altogether too large space in the lives of our grandfathers but the•average is struck by the negligence of the grandchildren. There will be a reaction after this depreciation, and then BYRON will have found his level. The Greeks are grateful, and they revere his memory, because he stood by them in their darkest hour. He fired them with enthusiasm when they most needed to be fired; and he did more than urge others on; he showed that he was ready to practice what he preached. He took up the Greek cause calmly but earnestly, and met his death by fever in the swamps of Mossolonghi at the moment when, as he believed, he was About to lead the troops to victory. His devoting himself to the struggle for the independence of Greece was Ino mere whim. He know that it might cost him his life, and he made provision for ensuring that it should absorb the remnant of his fortune. BYRON was a man of the wnrld as well as a poet, and his letters at this period show that he, was fully cog- nisant of the difficulties and dangers which were before him. His great fear was that ha would not be physically equal to the task he had assigned himself; and, as the event revealed, there was no shrinking at the prospect of death. The Greeks do well to be grateful; they know how much BYRON helped to direct attention to their cause, to stimu- late their own countrymen, and to excite the sym- pathy of England. It is natural that they should love the poet; for some of his most beautiful verse was inspired by the glory of Greece in the past and the bondage of Greece in his day. He did not live to see independence achieved; but he believed in it; ho pointed the way, and showed how it might be achieved. He was a strange creature, a com- pound o'f contradictions, a sun in the firmament, with spots. large and always visible. If he did not live well, he died well, and, "after life's fitful fever, he sleeps well."

• Pending 'the appeal in the Bell Cox case, fresh proceedings are to be taken, which will probably result in the reverend gentleman being again sent to prison. And why not? Catholic priests are not the only clericals who can be said to break the law.

Reports have been received from Ottawa that Mr. , Chamberlain will probably succeed Lord lAmsdowne as Governor-General of Canada. Well, we can, spare Joseph for a time. If he stays long enough amongst Colonists who have Home Rule, he will perhaps come back a Home Ruler.

The "Star," the new evening paper, isstfed in London, , and edited by Mr. T. P. O'Connor, is , proving a great success; it is evident that there is eoom for Radicalism in London. But why is the figure of Lucifer given as the head-piece? We can surely spare the Prince of Darkness when we are looking for "light, more light."

Somebody with more money than wit has left -ClOO a year for a sermon on the death of General Gordon ; and, this was "earned" on SUnday, at St. Paul's, Eaton Square, London, by the Rev. Horace Waller. Gordon was a hero, but it is the reverse of heroic to keep his memory green by preaching a i hundred pound sermon every year. Eloquence n such a case should have its stimulus in the heart —not in the pocket.

The Ship Canal Company are not disposed to pay fancy prices for the land they acquire, as wit- ness the arbitration' at Chester, this week. The verdict is one which is calculated to give money grubbers pause; they will not rush into arbitra- tion when, they find they can do better with- out, to say nothing of being landed in the pay- ment of costs.

• And hurrah for the Ship Canal Company in another matter; they are taking steps to induce local authorities to see to means for- preventing the pollution of the Irwell and the Mersey. Some 58 authorities were represented in a Conference on the subject, which was, held in the Manchester Town Hall, on Tuesday. That looks like business. Lord Egerton of Tatton was quite right in saying' that, "if the present pollution went on the docks would become a pestilential place." If the mak- ing of the Canal do but tend to the cleansing of the rivers, that, alone will be a good return for all the capital invested.

Miss Milly Hylton, a young actress, playing.. a prominent part in a Birmingham pantomime, has been severely assaulted by roughs, on the ground, it is stated, that she declined to pay black mail for applauding her. If this should prove to be true the ruffians deserve a special punishment, for they were trying villanous means to propagate a vicious system. English people are not very demonstrative; but it is generally understood that such applause as there is, is honest, and has been legitimately earned.

" Man " has been the subject of discussion at tin!) Frodsham Wesleyan Mutual Improvement So- ciety. There is nothing like having ample room and verge enough. The members have good au- thority too, for selecting such a subject ; for is it not Pope Who says,--" The proper study of mankind is man ?" It does not tran'spire that there were any ladies present. Had there been, the man who read the essay might have been reminded that Nature tried her 'prentice hand on man, "and then she made the lasses 0."

The Liberals of St. Helens are neither dead nor asleep. Some of the moneyed men have stepped aside, for a time as Liberal Unionists; but the mass of the people are enthusiastic in demanding Home Rule for Ireland. On Wednesday evening, the Volunteer. Hall was crowded; there was a good audience and a g00,..11y array of speakers, in- cluding three members of Parliament—Mr. Neville, Mr. Brunner, and Mr. Woodall. Resolutions ex- pressing confidence in Mn Gladstone and faith in the principle of Home Rule were carried unani- mously.

The Conservatives are in a cleft stick in the matter of the negotiations in 1885 as to granting Home Rule; and the Nationalists are not disposed to let them go. Speaking at Leamington. on Wed- nesday evening,, Mr. Justin McCarthy repeated, with emphasit, the statement that the Conserva- tive party negotiated with the Irish party, through Lord Carnarvon en Home Rule, and other gen- tlemen on the subject of coercion. It is,a matter, of course, to say that the Tories will turn to Mime Rule again the moment they think it will serve their purpose to do so.

Ismail Pasha must be laughing up his sleeve at the easy way in which he has " done ' the English Government and " spoiled" the Egyptians. When he was Khedive he was so extravagant, profligate, and tyrannical that he had to be deposed. After robbing Egypt;ltight and left, he has had the im- pudence to make a claim for five millions, an.d our Government have arranged to give him about one half. He ought rather to have been beaten with many- stripes. It is to be hoped that the Radical members of the House of Commons will have something to say when Parliament meets about this shameful piece of jobbery.

• The Toriee are. being so closely watched at home by_the Liberal Unionists that they are not per- mitted to go. far wrong, as yet, in matters of fin- ance; but they are making a mull of it in the gov- ernment of India. Lord Ripon managed things so well when he was Viceroy that be was enabled to effect large remissions of taxation, and, to reduce the salt duty. Just now the veryreverse operation is taking place. And salt, be it remembered, is a prime necessary of life in India as in England. This comes of "annexing" Burmah, and meddling and muddling on the north-western frontier.

• Assuming that the following story is true, and it is too. good not to be true, Leo XIII is a wit as well as a diplomatist :—When the present Pope Of Rome was acting in the capacity of Nuncio at Brussels,. he was invited to a dinner party by a well known nobleman. During the repast, he was asked by a noble guest to admire "a very lovely Venus" on the lid of a snuffbox, the betitled gen- tleman expecting to amuse the company at the ex- pense of Monsignor Pecci. "Very pretty" said the Nuncio, quietly returEdng-the box. "Is it the portrait of Madame Is Marquese?" The laugh was not with the nobleman. "The biter was bitten."

On Thursday, the Widnes magistrates were engaged in hearing an adjourned case involving serious injury to a labourer named James Lawton, who had been struck on the forehead with a brick. It was suggested that Thomas Kelly, the man who was charged with the offence, should be discharged on the understanding that the injured man would receive Ra and have hie doctor's bill paid; but the bench very properly declined to take this course. In the end, Kelly was committed for trial. It may transpire that he is, not the culprit; but somebody threw that brick, and the case should be bottomed. "A regular brick" is admirable, but an irregular brick—on the forehead—is not to be tolerated.

The correspondent of the "Pall Mall Gazette" who calls attention to a new reading of Tennyson in the Poems now being issued by Messrs. Macmi- llan is curiously" out of it." He says the, seventh verse of " Lady Clara Vera de Vere" originally ran:—
• Trust me, Clara Vere de Vero, From yon blue heavens above vs bent, The grand old gardener and his wife Smile at the claims of long descent. _ _ _

For "The grand old gardener" there now appearsl "The gardener Adam," and it is suggested that the change is not only for the worso,,but that it has been done, under, political pressure), to avoid any sug- gestion of the Grand Old Man. This is really to abuse the poet laureate. The fact is the altera- tion is not new; we find it in copy of Tennyson's poems which now lies before us, and which was published in 1871—long before Mr. Gladatone was spoken oratithe Grand ()Id Man. Further, the alteration is a distinct improvement; "The ex- dener Adam" is strong in its simplicity. "The grand old gardener *i,sjuvenile ; it is not at all Tennysonian,

WIDNES Elms LIBRARY ',Earl:rim—The third of the series of free lectures, organised by the Free Public Lib- rary Committee, was given in Lacey-street School, on Monday evening. There was a capital attendance, and Mr. E. Carey occupied the chair. The lecturer was Mr. Thomas Snape, who had selected as his subject "Ex- plorations in Central Africa," which was admirably illus- trated with magic lantern views of maps, landscapes, Szc. Mr. Snape at the outset mentioned that until 40 years ago the interior of Africa was as a sealed book— an unknown land to the inhabitants of the other quarters of the globe. Since 1849 to the present day, however, a succession of heroic explorers had brought to light the hidden resources of the hitherto mysterious land. Mr. Snape then dwelt in detail with the discoveries that had been made, particularly by Livingstone and Stanley, and graphically described the difficulties, dangers, and priva- tions that each had undergone in the search after know- ledge. Africa, he said, was not the dreary waste that it had been considered by many, but a rich and fertile land intersected by mighty rivers, and capable of great development for traders. Gold was not found in any large quantities in Africa, but copper and iron were plentiful, and there were large quantities of soda, which was a matter of importance to Wituesians. Vegetable products were very prolific, and were in many instances as valuable as they were prolific. He predicted a great future for the so-called "Dark Continent."—A cordial Tote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Snape for his inter- esting, instructive. and eloquent lecture, on the motion of Mr. R. 1-1-. Davies, seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe. Thanks having been accorded to the Chairman, the proceedings terminated: _

At Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. James Handley, three men named George Seymour, James Crank, and George Meek, were•charged on remand with having stolen 236 poundsweight of rope of rope, valued at £4, the pro- perty ofitessrs. Hazlehurst and Son,, soap manufac- turers.—Xim Dunbavand, master of the flat "Julia,' belonging to the prosecutors, stated tikat the flat waB lying in the Bridgewater canal on the night of the 30th December, and when he left it in the' evening every- thing was safe. Next morning he cliwovered that the forecastle had been broken into and the ropes stolen.— John Allen, watchman, deposed that- the prisoners bad been employed at the works and left-about midnight on the night of the robbery.—Martlin. Alice Jackson who cohabited with Crank in a house.l Nelson-street, said on the niglft in question Crank and Seymour brought large quantity of rope into the house and placed it in the pantry. Two other men were standing otitside at the time. On the 3rd inst the ropes were placed into the midden at the back of theshouse, and Meek said "I will go and report it at the Town Hall."—P.C. Kettle said about a quarter to twelve on the night of the 3rd inst, he met Crank and Meek-cnming down High-street. Crank said he "had seen a ghost or something," and went on to give a circumstantial account of how he had found the ropes in his entry, and he had soiled in Meek in order that he might have a witness. He was then on his way to report the matter. The following evening P.C: Kettle apprehen4d both Crank and Meek', and dur- ing the night he occupied a cell between the cells they respectively occupied. He heard Crank shout "I shalt ' let on in the Morning to know nothing of it," and Meek replied "I wonder who told of us; if I knew I'd make them pay for it."—SuperintendentHollingworth deposed that when he charged the prisoners Crank replied that Seymour had brought the ropes to his house and Sey- mour retorted" Could I carry the ropes myself?" Crank replied "No ; there was another man with you with a monkey jacket on." Meek stated that hp knew nothing of the ropes until the 3rd inst.---The prisoners were com- mitted to the &assizes for trial. .
