,WOUNDED WITH A BRICK AT WIDNES.

_ Xt Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday; Thomas Kelly, a labourer, who lives in Milton-road, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the .14th January, done grievous bodily harm to James Lawton, labourer, of 23, Sankey-street.—Mr., J. W. Knowles, who appeared for the prisoner, contended that the offence was a misdemeanour, and the par- ties could mutually and legally settle the case. The prosecutor was willing to accept 'compensation for the injuries done to him, and had no desire to bring any charge whatever against the prisoner. Under those circumstances Mr. Knowles asked that the prisoner should be discharged.—Mr. G. Pilkin,gton said the Bench must hear the case before they decided upon the appli- cation.—The prosecutor deposed that on the night a the 14th inst he was drunk and went to the backyard, where he was rendered unconscious by a blow on the forehead. He did not know who struck the blow. He had never to his knowledge seen the prisoner before that morning. —By Mr. Knowles: The prisoner's friends had asked to settle the case for £2 and paythent of the doctor's bill, and he was agreeable. He had never authorised any- body to make a charge against the prisoner, and did not wish to make a charae against him. Annie Lawton, wife of. the prose- cutor, said when her hustind went into the yard, she was standing . in Ipe doorway with a lighted candle in her hand. She saw the prisoner in the yard about two yards from the back gate, and there was another man in the entry. The prisoner raised his hand, and threw a heavy brick at her husband. The brick struck him on the • forehead, and knocked him down. She screamed out murder, and the men ran away. She fdloWed, and gave the prisoner into the custody of P.C. Cummings. Her husband had not been able to work since he was injured.—John Melia, a lodger at Lawton's house, corroborated.—Pr. Hutchinson de- posed that he visited the injured man at twenty minutes oast mid-night on the day in question. He was suffer- ing from a dangerous contused wound on the right fore- head. The doctor stitched and dressed the wound, which was an inch and a half in length. He had lost a great quantity of blood, and was net yet fit for work.— P.C. Cummings deposed' to receivibg the prisoner into custody from Mrs. • Lawton. When charged he replied "I am innocent." The brick produced weighed lOilbs, —Mr. Knowles contended that the evidence of identifica- tion was of such a character that no jury would convict upon it.—The Bench declined to allow the case to be, compromised, and committed the prisoner to the Assizes for trial. He was, however, admitted to bail, himself in £BO and two sureties of £3O.
ST. MICHAEL'S ROMAN _CATHOLIC CHURCH,
DITTON.

In this church, on Sunday, two sermons were preached by the Rev. Father Boswin, g.J., on the five martyrs of the Society of Jesus, who have lately been beatified by His Holiness Pope Leo XiII. The sacred edifice had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, the words, "Hail, blessed martyr, hail," being hung between the two pillars at the entrance to the sanctuary, while a picture of blessed Edmund Campiau, the first martyr of the society in Eng- land, was exposed to the veneration of the faithful. In addition a large number of bannerettes were dis- played. The powerful rendering of the "Hymn of triumph," by the entire community, and by the school children, both morning and afternoon, was very effective. The boys' singing deserves especial praise. At the morning service, which was well attended, the reverend father pointed .out that the true idea of " martyr " embodied all that is most high-minded, noble-souled, devoted, for which reason the Catholic Church holds in veneration the memory of those of her children who have suffered the death of martyrdom. In particular, they were that day keeping the feast of five such blessed martyrs of the reign of Queen Elizabeth, viz. Edmund Campian Alex- ander Briant, Thomas viz., John Nelson, and Thomas Woodhouse, all priests of the Society of Jesus. The cause for which these martyrs went into dpath was their steadfast profession of that supremacy of the Roman Pontiff in spiritual matters over the Universal Church, which was proved from Holy Writ and tradition; but while firmly holding this tenet of faith as an inviolable article of Divine truth, they did not fail to give abundant proof of their loyalty to their country, and to the Queen in the matters of this world. Nevertheless, they were unjustly sentenced, on the 10th Novem- Ltr, 1581, to undergo the extreme penalty' im- posed on traitors to their country. Since that day, when the full profession of the Catholic faith was treated as treason, many things indeed had changed for the better in the position of the Catholic Church in this country. And, as a very striking, proof of this amelioration, the Catholics of England thankfully acknowledged the distinguished part her Majesty the present Queen of England took in the late celebration of the Jubilee of his Holiness Leo XIII. In the afternoon

the preacher gave a summary account of the suffering the five martss had to endure. The acoustic properties of the church have been im- proved by the erection of a handsome sounding board over the pulpit. The board is a most skilful auctimpos- ing piece of work, being 14 feet high, and about ten feet high at the base, tapering as it reaches its sumnsit. .Like the pulpit, the base is octagonal in shape, being beauti- fully carved underneath, and artistically decorated at the edge with wooden fretwork. Resting on the base is another piece of skilfully executed work, also octagonal in shape, but of less diamater. Six of the sides are two church doors, in the Gothic style of architecture, which are supposed to represent the twelve gates of heaven, and at each of the corners is a small spire. The designer is the Rev. Father Richartz, who is now at Portego, and the constructor is one of the lay brethren of the College, Brother Egger.

div.head: PROPOSED TREAT TO AGED PERSONB AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED TREAT TO AGED PERSONB AT RUNCORN.

A meeting of tradesmen and others wae held in Westminster Cocoa Rooms, High-street, on Monday evening, for the purpose of considering a proposal to give the annual treat to the aged poor of the town. The attendance was not encouraging. Mr. S. C. Beckett was voted to the chair, and there were present Messrs. J. Johnson, F. N. NormakS... ll. Da- wson, S. Coventry, J. E. Meredith, G. Howard, and W. Pownall (secretary). In opening the proceedings, the Chartman said he understood there was a feeling in the town .that the treat to the aged people should not drop throughif there was any way at all by which it could be givem . His principal reason for being present that night was from the fact that the previous treats had always been enjoyed—(hear, hear,)—and because he thought the aged'people ought to be considered at this time of the year. 1114 u-es an unfor- tunate thing for them that the Young •Men's Christian Association was defunct; but still bethought they might do something which would show that the., aged people were not forgotten. (Hear, hear.) He had thought that possibly the chairman of the Commissioners would under the circumstances of the absence of the Young Men's Christian Association, have seen his way- to take that matter in hand; bat Mr. Dobson had been seen and had said that he could not see his wayto do so. The ques- tion, therefore, to be considered was whether the gentry and tradesmen of the town would come forward and assist, and whether the committee, u hen appointed, would meet with the sympathy of the gentry, public, and tradesmen to enable them to carry out the project. Another plan would be to send a request from that meet- ing to the chairman of the Commissioners, asking him, as the head of the town, to call a meeting with a view to making arrangements for the purpose of giving the treat. Mayors of corporate towns.had taken up such matters. • The Secretary said he had..seen Mr. Dobson, who told him he hardly saw his way to call a meeting. Mr. Johnson thought the , chairman of the Commis- sioners would have - felt• it an honour to call a public meeting, for such a purpose, as their- poorer brethren de.., mandeir their sympathy at that festive season of the,' year. (Hear. hear.) Mr..F. J. Norman saidthat Mr. Dobson had informed him with considerable three that it was not a matter fOr the Commissioners to take, in hand, but for the rate- I payers. Mr. Beckett had referred to mayors taking such a matter up in other towns, but it was very differ- ent there, for the mayors did it entirely at their own ex- pense. (Hear, heart), Mr. Dobson was anxious and willing to do all he, COUla • bat could not provide the 'treat at his iswn expense and could not use his position , as chairman of theCom4sioners to call a town's meet- ing for the purpose, of considering the question. He suggested, however, that the committee which acted last year should be re-appointed, and take the, matter in hand, and he would lend the Commissioners' room, and do all he possibly could to assist them. Hear, hear.) Arrangements had been made for a football mate) in aid of the scheme, and he thought the subscriptions which were given last year would be repeated in this cam (Hear, hear). Mr. Dawson $ The treat has usually cost about £3O or thereabouts. • The Secretary $ £35. On the proposition of Mr. Johnson, seconded by Mr. Norman, a committee composed of the following gentle- men was formed ~Messrs. S. C. Ileckett, F. I, Norman,

IW. H. Rogerson, J. Johnson, G. Howard, W. Shaw-, Smith, .1. E. Meredith, S. A. Dawson C. Pownall, S. Coventry, W. Littler, T. Bowyer, T. Cook,. J. B. Knive- ton, J. Ballamy, J. Yarvrood, J. E. Langshaw, and W. Towns. Mr. Norman was elected treasurer, and Mr. W. rownall secretary. It was decided to call the committee the Aged Persons Treat Committee.
It was agreed to hold another meeting on 'Workday next.
WIDNES TRADERS ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of this association was held on Tuesday, at the luncheon rooms of Messrs. Gas- kell Deacon and Co.; Mr. E. K. Muspratt, president of the association, occupied the chair; and there were also present Messrs, T. S. Timnsise T. Brock, J. W. Wareing, R. Cook, F. H. -Mort, and H. Wade Deacon (hon. see). The Hon. Sec. submitthd the following report of the Executive Committee :—lt will be remembemdthat the London and North-Western Railway Company in their bill of last session introduced a clause under which the , company would have hail powers to make certain charges for the use of wagons when supplied by the com- pany for the conveyance of coal, slack, and various other substances. The Executive Committee considered the proposed charge to be excessive, and recommended that the bill should be opposed, if necessary, and the As- sociation adopted the recommendation. As the commit-, tee found that the railway company would not withdraw or modify the objectionable clauses, a petition was lodged in the House of Commons against the bill.. The clause was also petitioned against by others, and was eventually rejected by the committee of the House of Commons. The committee was very pleased tothe able to report that the St. Helens traders Joined the Widnes traders in the costs connected with the opposition, as did also some non-members in Widnes. The Govern- ment-again brought in a Railway and Canal TrafEe Bill.• The committee did not approve of some por- tions of the bill, and would have joined other bodies of traders in protesting against them, but it. was soon felt that the Bill would not be passed last ses-- sion and the opposition did not take definite form.. in 188 g the London and North-Western Railway Company introduced into their bill clauses wider which they would have been autrised to construct new docks at Garston,• and to increa.4 the charges in connection with the old dock. As the railway company would not promise to withdraw the clauses to which are association objectede• a petition was prepared, when ultimately the clauses were withdrawn. The railway company had now intro-- duced almost exactly similar clauses into their bill of this year, and the committee recommended that unless satis- factory arrangements could be made with the railway company a petition on behalf of the traders be lodged against the bill. The committee was authorised to make a levy of not exceeding 3d. in the 2, but on the St. Helens traders joining the Widnes traders it was found that a levy of Id. in the '2 would be sufficient, and eto, this sum • was fixed upon. The costs of opposing the London and North-Western Railway Company had not. yet been paid, but after paying these costs it was esti- mated that there would be a sufficient sum left to pay the costs if it were decided to oppose the London and North-Western Railway Co. this year. The committee, however, might be disappointed in this hope, and they asked for power to make a levy of ld. in the £in case the money should be required. The balance in hand at pre.sent was £412 7s. I.W.

' sdr. Timmis, as chairman of the Executive Committee,- moved the adoption of the report, and expressed the hope that the St. Helens traders would again join them in opposing the London and North-Western Railway Company. It was possible that the Garston traders would also join them, and the association's expenses would be considerably diminished. Mr. Cook seconded the motion, which was carried. The Chairman remarked that the next business was- to grant authority to the president to sign a petition on behalf of the association against the clause in the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company's bill of this year relatiug to Garston Docks, and to authorise theicom.- mittee to oppose the bill.'

.. - The Hon. Secretary said the committee did not see any. reason to object to the Company making a new dock,. but objected to several other arrangements, one of which, was the proposal of the company to alter the tolls and charges connected with what Oas known as Garston Oldi Dock, placing it on the scale of 1867, and cutting the Widnes tradei-s out of the privileges which they had ob- tained under the Trassfer Act of 1864. A special section of the Act of 1867 in favour of Widnes traders was. also omitted from this bill, and he, author- ised by the committee, had seen Mr. Simpson respectmg it, and that gentleman said that the. bill Would practically make them liable to increased charges. Another bad effect of the bill if passed. as at present would be this. The shipowners of Liverpo* said they would not come to Garston if the clause waaa not erased, and the consequence of that would be that Widnes traders would have to pay a rate of 38 4d instead of Is 3d per ton. . _

Mr. Timis observed that his firm could buy tallow at. 2s 6d cheaper at Garston than they could at Liverpool. The Chairman said they might ask the Liverpool ship owners if they would oppose the clause, and then tke. association support them if they would. Mr. Brock said the fact was the Railway Compasy were trying to get in the thin -end of the wedge. They- tried it on every time they went to Parliament. The association had opposed their objectionable clauses time. after time, and they had been withdrawn; and he had no doubt that in the present case the same would be the res.ult.
The resolution asked for hy the chairman was then passed on the motion a Mr. Brock, seconded by -Mk. Mort.
A resolution'was also passed authorising the com- mitte to make a levy of id in the R. Votes of thanks to the Executive Committee and the secretary concluded the proceedings.

REFUSING TO QUIT AT WESTON.—Elizabeth Wilkinson, a married woman, was charged with having on the 13th inst. been drunk at the Dock Hotel, Weston, and refused to quit when requested by the landlord.—The case was proved by P.C. Hamersley and the landlord.—The wo- man dbenied that she was drunk, and said she had sent her boy for a quart of ale. The boy put a shilling on the counter in payment, and the landlord picked it up and denied having done so when asked for change. She then I put a shillinc, ' down and ho only gave her a .penny change.—A fine of 55, and costs 14s, was imposed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.

In drizzling rain the Mossley skipper (Mayall) started the oval from centre, and it was soon apparent that the greasy nature of the leather affected accurate passing. Ashton charged the kick-off down, and the game rested in Mossley territory. Barnes fafied to take a pass here, and Joe Winterbottom temporarily relieved to half-way. "Morris," by a judicious kick, forced the visitors back, and from a pack here, Pointon tried to relieve, but found the tackling of the West Lancashire men too safe to allow of any liberties being taken. Joe Winterbottom now got away with a, good run to the Warrington quarter-flag, and Cox returned a kick of Massey's with little interest. Billings put in some tricky work, and almost got clear, but Warren was safe, and a rush by the home team for- wards again forced the Mossleyites to act on the defen- sive. Warren almost got, in after a grand run, but spoiled what appeared a certain cliance of scoring by passing forward. From the pack following the visitors slightly relieved, and "Morris" endeavoured to force a way, but Meakin was too bold an obstacle to pass. Bill- ings here passed smartly to Lawton, Frank Turner hold- ing him before he threatened danger. Lawton after- wards put in a neat run and kick to the opposing quarter- flag, but Frank Turner, by a grand dribble, tran.sforred operations to the Mossley lines, being ably assisted in this smart play by Warren, Dillon, and Littlewood. The ball, however, went dead. Winterbottom re-started, and Barnes, by a good kick, again forced the Mossleyites back, and Coxe having his kick charged down, the visitors were again obliged to adopt the saving clause., Barnes made his mark from the recommencAirnent, and from his kick a scrimmage was formed close to the visitors' goal. Give-and-take followed, and Lawton re- lieved the pressure a little, but Fair. Turner and Dillon dribbled back to the Mossley linos. Joe Winterbottom now got in a good run to the " wirepu,Uers' " twenty- five, and Barnes relieved his side by a lofty kick to Poin- ton, Jolley holding him before he could get away. Nothing daunted by tho hard lines they had experienced on former occasions, tho home team played up with re- newed vigour, and Nevins was applauaed for a smart return. The game raged fast and furious, and after some loose play in neutral territory, Massey pit in a huge kick, and Cdxe mulling, Jolley raced up, secured posses- sion, and scored a brilliant try. No goal resulted from Fair. Turner's kick. Barnes again made his mark from

the kick-off, and brilliant play by the opposing centre was applauded. After a grand dribble Povey looked like scor- ing another tangible point, but half time was called, with the score—Warrington one try two minors, to Mossley nil. Frank Turner started the second half, and the first to show up was Barnes, who put in a dodgy run to the opposing t went-five, :Lawton bringing him down. The visitors now invaded the Warrington quarter' but the game was not doomed to stay here long, for "Mor- ris "put in some useful work, whichfound play at centre I flag. Hayes saved a rush of the Mossley forwards in daring style, and Nevins only feebly responded to a hulikick of Coxe. Fair. Turner was next instrumen- tal m taking play to the Mossley quarters' but all efforts , to score by either side were fruitless. Ashton passed smartly to Povey but no headway could be made and a kick by Joe Winterbottom was well returned by Massey. Povey was again to the fore with a neat dribble. Ex- change kicking by Nevins and Lawton was now in- dulged in. but the game was here delayed by Massey be- ing slightly disabled. Frank Turner was repeatedly to the fore with • sterling work, and Rowan negatived a smart run by Jolley to the Warrington line. A fierce pack here ensued, and it looked as if the visitors were go- ing to equalise at last, but all doubts werOet aside when Littlewood came through the pack and dribbled to the opposing quarter flag. This brilliant piece of play was heartily applauded by the spectators, and directly after- wards no side" was called, there having been no ad- dition to the score during the second half, and Warring- ton for the third time this season atoned for their defeat in the first engagement by one try and two minors to Mossley nil. The general play was far below that seen on the pre- vious Saturday, the whole team seeming to lose that combination which has been so apparent during the last few matches. This, no doubt, must be attributed to • the greasy nature of the leather, and it is certain that if Warrington had made the bast use of the chances that were put in their way the score would have been largely augmented. None of the backs showed anything like their true form, whilst the forwards have been seen oI better advantage. If special praise ought to be made this division, Dillon, Littlewood, Povey, and the brothers • Turner deserve it. On behalf of Mossley, Billings was : the mainstay of his side time after time, and his tricky , play gained for him a host of admirers. The other backs were of medium character, whilst the forwards were, no doubt, handicapped by the unfavourable state of the .round. Umpires were dispensed with, and the deci- -40.19 of Mr. Trevor Smith gave general satisfaction, this arrangement working admirably. The following were tlee teams —Warrington:: Full back, W. Nevins; three- • quarter backs, J. Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and J. T. Massey; half-backs, J. E. Warren and " Morris" ' • for- wards, H. Ashton, Fair. Turner. Frank Turner, W. Dil- I lon, T. Davies, W. Hayes, W. Povey, T. Craghan, and • R. Littiewood. Mossley: Full back, Coxe; three- quarter-backs, Lawton, Joe Winterbottom and Poin- • ton ; half-backs, Billings and James Winterbottom; for- wards, Mayall (captain), Newby, Firth, Corscadden, t Hobson, Mitchell, Walker, Rowan, and Walker.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Warrington managed on Saturday to retrieve the de- feat which Mossley had subjected them to at their pre- vious meeting, but the contest was a hardly-fought one all through. The ball was mostly kept in Mossley quar- ters, but the visitors occasionally brightened up, and it was only by strong defensive play that they were pre- vented from scoring. It cannot be said that either club displayed very high form. Mossley seemed to rely mainly on the scrimmages, and went in for very little passing.. Warrington improved upon this to some extent, their winning point being scored by Jolly at three-quarters, but the passing was not very skilfully managed. It was neither sharp nor accurate enough to be really effective, •but this defect was no doubt largely, due to the slipperi- ness of the ball.

_ It wag a pleasure to the Warrington spectators to see that Gilbert was again able to take a place at half-back on Saturday. With regard to Rigby, however, another of last season's crack players, we are sorry to hear that he still keeps in a very precarious condition. We hear that he is to undergo a serious surgical opera- tion, which, we trust, will have the desired effect. The match against the Old Boys proved to be one of the best and most pleasant gamee played on the Run- corn ground this season, and as usual was of the most exciting character. in fact the game with the Old Boys is one of the most popular on the list. Both teams play the game in its best and most scientific sense, and the consequence is that there is a minimum of packed scrim- mages, and the passing and dribbling is a treat to wit- ness. On Saturday the ball travelled from goal to goal with great rapidity amid ever varying incidents, and although the advantage was clearly with the home team the visitors were frequently dangerous, but they could not oven succeed in recording, a minor. For Runcorn, I the whole fifteen played well to a man, but Stubbs deserves credit for the two tries he scored in completion lof grand work by Speakman and Davies. The latter was in especially fine form; in fact, a good judge remarked that had he been in the same condition at Salford, the latter would have had to retire beaten _... • _ _

It is pleasing to notice that tho claims of Runcorn as the premier club in Cheshire are fully recognised by the County Committee. To-day (Saturday), against Northumberland, Davies, Speakman and Cawley are chosen to officiate as three-quarter backs, the clever cap- tain, H. Hughes at half back, and amongst the forwards are W. Huges, Faulkner, Wainwright, and Clarke; while Broady, who is on the reserve, will take the place of Lings, of Sale. The supporters of the Widnes team agree in stating that on Saturday the " Chemicals " played up better than on any previous occasion against Walkden. Both in the pack and on the loose the forwards were much better than their opponents while the back play was very effec- tive, and the score done goal, one try, and four minors ,to one minor clearly indicates the respective merits of the two clubs. Several changes had been made in the , organisation of the Widnes team. Sam Binghant and Plumpton exchanged places, and Barker and Farrell did likewise, and each did remarkably well in their new positions. Farrell and Kiddie were the try getters, and ' Sampson had hard lines in not also being successful. The whdle of the team played so well that it would be in- vidious to particularise, and it is to be hoped that equally good form will be displayed against Aspull at Widnes (to-day).
KICKING.
BT NAB &6il:-IBBBN.

"Kicking, a splendid vocation ; Burns is wrong when he wrote, Man was made to mourn'; more correct to say, 'Man made to kick.' Old author wrong in defining man as a creature that laughs' ; substitute kicks' for laughs.' "heat thing to kick—a ball, commonly called'foot- ball'; made of cow-hide, with ox bladder inside, tightly laced; sometimes made of india-rubber; cow-hide best; may be obtained at any sadler's establishment for 7s 6d and upwards.
" AAfew things the young men of England should not kick :
• (1) Don't kick each other; shins and ankles not good footballs; in fact not balls at all, but oft produce bawls and brawls..

(2)' Don't kick your wives when you marry. Horrible idea this ; but the thing,nevertheless, has been done; have seen references to same in reports of police courts and - quarter sessions. (3) Don't kick "against the pricks." Pricks, the suggestions of conscience as to duties,— the stern inalienable duties of life; pricks, kicked against, come through the boot; hurt the foot; wound difficult to heal. (4) Don't kick over the traces. Seen the horse half broken in, discontented with its position, accomplish this; but horse very uncomfortable afterwards. (5) Don't kick the beam ; this done by an empty purse , at quarter .day. Heavy debts and nothing to pay; 'debts' come down, nothing goes up.' (6) Don't kick the bucket—at least, until you are obliged. Bucket contains the meal and water; meal and water spilt, horse must die. In any case, better to leave the bucket and its contents for spine other horse, if not personally required,
LECTURE ON " CALIFORNIA " AT WAR-
RINGTON.

On Monday evening a lecture on " California :the golden gate to happyindependencelfor men and wo- men," was delivered in Bold-street Wesleyan School by Mrs. M. E. Parker, of Penketh. Councillorß. W. Francomb presided, and there was a fair attend- ance. In the course of the evening a collection was taken in aid of the" Poor Children's Penny Dinner Fund.' 5 After a short address by the chairman, Mr.: Parker, who was received with applause, said that she had spent five months in the beautiful State of California, when, for the third time in her life, she was appointed a temperance delegate to go to America. Having referred briefly, but in an inter- esting manner, to the journey across the Atlantic, the unveiling of the Statue of Liberty, a visit to the home of W. L. Garrison, the birthday of the Quaker.poet, Whittier, and to other matters connec-

- ted with her sojourn in America, she mentioned that the journey to California from New York oc- cupied six days. At Passadena, the "'city of beautiful homes," in Southern California, the cli- mate was most lovely. A month ago they closed their last drinking saloon. When she was there they were lamenting very much that they had a drinking saloon, and every week meetings were held in the churches by the temperance women, ' but about a month ago she received a paper which told her that the churches had held thanksgiving I services because of the last drinking saloon having been closed. So they would see that Passadena was a safe place to send their sons and daughters to, for ,there was no place where drink could be had for love or money. She wished the same could be said of Warrington. (Laughter and ap- plause.) In California they did not need any penny dinners. She never saw a poor person and she never saw a beggar, but so long as they had the drink traffic she supposed they must have penny dinners. (Hear, hear.) She did not recommend any to go to San Fran- cisco. That city had something like 40,000 Chinese who lived in what was called " China town." They had re- duced wages there but further south wages were higher. San Francisco was something like London—a place where all nationalities met. The fertility of the Califor- nian soil was wonderful, five and six crops sometimes being taken in a year. Strawberries and green peas might be had all the year round. With regard to wages the following might be taken as an average :—Joiners, £1 per d,ay ; gardeners, 12s 6d per day; builders, £1 per day: blacksmiths, £2 10s. per week; boot-makers, Bs. per day; cabinet makers, £1 to £1 ss. ,per day • farm hands, £1 per wet*, with board ; upholsterers and ware- housemen, 8s per day; plumbers, 12s per day; and stone-cutters, 10s per day. Women :—Household helps and waitresses, £36 to £6O a year; nurse girls, £4 per month; seamstresses, 6s per day; and shop:.women, El. 8s per week. House rent was dear but houses suita- ble to live in, so mild was the climate, could be built cheaply, and 7•loths of the mechanics and farmers in California owned their own houses. Many people lived in tents. She also mentioned that education was free, and with regard to the time for emigration she recom- mended the months of November, December, and Janu- ary. The lecture was very attentively listened to and frequently applauded—At its close a voteof thanks was moved to Mrs. Parker by Mr. J. Summersgill, seconded by Mr. Toft, and unanimously accorded.-Questions hay- ingbeen invited Mr. J. Gandy said he had very .great sympathy with Mrs. Parker's object, and be might say that California had been his own youthful ambition. i Mrs. Parker had drawn her pictures n the brightest and warmest colours, but there were objections to Califor- nia. One of these was the presence of insects, such as mosquitoes, which must ho a serious nuisance to English people going there. It was also very common for people to suffer from fever and ague, and then the social state of the country was not to be entirely overlooked. A friend of theirs who had gone to San Francisco had written to the effect that although when in England ho did not believe in a hell, yet he was almost inclined to believe that one existed on the Pacific coast. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Gandy) was very much inclined to believe, from what he had heard of California, that a state of lawless- ness was very prevalent there. (Applause.)—Mrs. Par- ker, in replying, remarked that she had before said that she would not advise anyone to go to San Francisco. She was not sure that there was more wickedness there than, in London, but it was more glaring—there was less re- straint. There was some element in San Francisco which made them feel a long way from home, and the only time she was home-sick was wheirin that city. With regard to insects she never remembered to have been bitten, but she hlcl been bitten in Penketh since she came there. (Laughter and applause.) With regard to the diseases referred to theywere no doubt suffered from in some parts of California, but in Passadena malaria was unknown. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the Chairman was moved* theßev. E. S. Jackson seconded by Mr. C. E. Parker, and carried, the meeting then concluding.

Mrs. Parker has received a lengthy letter from Mrs. J. Mills in which she says :—" In reply to some questions you asked me as to wages rate in Tresno I find on refer- ence to letters from my son (who is settled there on a grape ranch) and also from friends—that the average pay for a man would be 1 dollar or 4 shillings per day, with board, in grape picking, raisin drying, digging, cleaning ditches, Sze. and other ordinary farm or labour- ing work. The work of course varies with the season's and a young man must be ready to work at any thing he can get. if he is to be employed all the year round. Whilst therefore any hard working%teady man can -.get work and save a little, I am, from all I hear, much im- pressed with the special fitness of Tresno county for a class of young men whose fathers if they had to give them a start in England and could fmd them from £3OO to £5OO, of capital would be sorely puzzled which way to invest it, so as to give any chance of good and certain return, or to avoid likelihood of total loss of capital."

MARRIAGE OF MR. G. W. BENNETT, OF - BEWSEY HALL. On Tuesday morning, the Chapel-street Congrega- tional Church, Southport, and its precincts were crowded with a fashionable concourse to witness the celebration of the marriage of Miss Baxter (daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Baxter, Acton Grange, Cheshire, and Mrs. Baxter, Ash-street, Southport) and Mr. William Grange Bennett, son of Mr. John Bennett, Bewsey Hall, Warrington. The pastor, the Rev. J. T. Woodhouse, officiated, and as the wedding party entered the chapel, the organist, Mr. Pollard, played a suitable voluntary, introduc- ing the air of the marriage hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden." The bride, who was given away by Mr. Fairhurst, The Elms, Scarisbrick New- road, wore a travelling dress of brown French cloth, trimmed with velvet, with bonnet and muff (with flowers) to match, and a handsome bracelet of dia- monds and sapphires, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Baxter (sister of the bride) ; and Miss Emily Bennett (sister of the bridegroom) ; they wore dresses of French material in fawn check, trimmhd with navy-blue velvet, with :bonnets and muffs ea suite. Mr. John Bennett, brother of the bridegroom. officiated as "best 'man," and the second grooms- man was Mr T. E. Fisher, Soutffport. The other members of the wedding party were Mrs Baxter, Mr and Mrs John Bennett, Bewsey ; Mr and Mrs William Bennett, Warrington; Mr and Mrs John Appleton. Stockton Heath, Warrington; Mr and Mrs Thomas Baxter, Aston, near Chester; Mr W. J. Bennett, Poulton; Miss Bennett, Padgate, Warrington; Mr Joseph and Mr James Bennett, sad Mr T. Fairhurst. The service was that usually adopted in Congregational Churches, and at its close Mr Pollard played Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." After the customary formalities in the vestry, the party, amid a shower of rice, drove away to The Elms, where a recherché breakfast awaited them. The wedding cake, in two tiers surmounted by a wreathed bouquet, was a splendid piece of work, the bells, baskets, and clasped hands being particularly fins; it was supplied by Mr T. Fisher, Lord-street and Chapel-street, and was greatly admired. Early in the afternoon the newly- married couple, amid showers of rice and old slip- pers, and the heartiest of congratulations, drove to Chapel-street station, where they took train for London, where they will spend the honeymoon.

RUGBY RULES. WIDNES v. WALSDEI4.—PIayed at: Walkden on Satur- day. Owing to the•recent thaw the ground Was in a very slippery condition but despite that drawback Some smart play Was witnessed, and at the close Widnes were declared victors by one goal, one try, and four minors, to one minor. Two 35's were played, Smith kicking off for Widnes, down the slope, at 3-40. The ball was scrimmaged at the home quarter, whence J. Bingham dribbled nicely to within a few yards of the line. There Kiddie picked up and grounded the ball within the en- closure.' Plumpton tried the place, which was rather difficult, but failed to realise the premier point. Subse- quently Widnes pressed hard, but were only able to add two minors to their score before the call for half-time. The kick-off after the change of ends brought the ball into the visitors' quarter. Farrell returned to the cen- tre, and J. Bingham, following up smartly, secured the ball from Price's kick, raced away to the home ,quarter, and there passed finely to Farrell, who dashed over %he line and secured a try behind the pests, from which he placed a neat goal. A few minutes later the home men invaded the Widnes quarter, and obtained their solitary point, a dead ball. This was followed by sterling play in the Walkden territory, Widnes adding two minors, and Sampson, who dribbled the ball admirably over the line, having exceeding "hard hiss" for scoring, the ball being kicked from beneath him just as he was grounding it. Widnes played remarkably well all through the match, winning golden opinions from the spectators. They had the advantage at every point. Barker, Farrell, Kiddie, Smith, J. gingham, and Pen- nington played well for Widnes; arid S. Grundy, Mar- tinscroft, Short, and Rushton for Walkden. Teams: Widnes—Plumpton, back; Farrell, Parkinson, and S. Bingham, three-quarter backs; Barker and Wilkinson, half backs; Smith (captain), Kiddie, J. Bingham,Woods, Candy, Pennington, Barber, Sampson and Wright, for- wards. Walkden—Price, back; S. Grundy (captain), Martinscroft, and Hurst, three-quarterbacks ;J. Grundy and Short, half backs; Rushton, Walker, Gardner Rid; yard, Barnes, Hindley, Williamson, Shiel, and G. 'Jones, forwards. 1, OLD BOYS v. Remeoen.—The Liverpool Old Boys visi- ted Runcorn on Saturday, and the spell of misfortune which has hung around them so persistently for the last few weeeks still clings to them, and they had once more to chronicle defeat, though they gave their opponents an excellent game. Having lost the toss, f . Chambers started the ball. Speakman returned, and, Dolan racing forward sharply, Perry had to kick dead. Hickson dropped out, and Wood tried further toimprove matters, but a strong rushby theßuncorn men, headed by Davies, caused a retrogade movement on behalf of the visitors, and when in the 25 Davies threw to Stubbs, who crossed the line and grounded. Brazendale failed to improve. Following some play in centre F. Chambers, Brodie, and Gilbert got in some clever dribbles, and Hickson after- wards made the position of the Old Boys additionally strong by a Run to the Runcorn 25. After a good struggle, however, the home contingent eased the pressure. Hickson again gave; momentary uneasiness to his opponents, but Speakman put a different com- plexion on the game, and the Old Boys beat a hasty re- treat to their own end. Wood stayed the rush, but Davies immediately afterwards necessitated the saving clause. After the drop out Speakman again got under weigh, but being compelled to part with the leather, Stubbs negotiated, and this player succeeded a second time in scoring, Brazendale this time getting the full worth of the place kick. Fast play was still the order of the day, and the ball travelled the ground rapidly. Hick- son achieved a. "fair catch," and this player and Davies put in some long punts. Play once more settled down in the visitors' half, and a protracted struggle was at last got rid of by Hickson, who was, however, pulled up by Cawley in the Runcorn half. The Cheshire club once more put the visitors on the de- fensive, and Brodie, Hickson, and Perry in turn tried to effect a clearance, and half time was called with the ball in the Old Boys' territory, Runcorn having scored 1-1-2 to nothing. W. Hughes re-started play, and though the argument was still slightly in favour of Runcorn, it was well contested. Davies hereabouts made a brilliant rush, but was collared within a yard of the Old Boys' line. Wood, Graham, and Hickson in turn showed up, and now Runcorn had to turn towards their own 25. Percy made his mark near the centre, but Wainwright and H. Hughes removed the struggle from the Runcorn quarter-flag to the Old Boys' territory, and O'Dwyer made a timely save. Another good rush by the visitors again took play to the Cheshire end, and F. Chambers gained a try, but the ball was ruled back and scrimmaged-. The Old Boys still fas- tened their opponents, and kept up the pressure, but Perry, missing to pick up, let in the home forwards. Give-and-take play was the order, the leather at one minute being at the home end and the next at the visitors'' and all that was scored was an additional dead ball by the Runcorn men' who retired winners of a stub- bornly-contested game by one goal, one try, and five minors to nil. The Old Boys were beaten by the better back play of Runcorn. Teams :—Old Boys: J. B. O'Dwyer, back; F. Hickson, M. Perry, and C. Graham, three-quarter backs ; H. D. Wood and R. Fieldwick, half backs; J. Brodie, E. Bullen, W. Edmunds, Gilbert, R. Goold, L. Chambers, W. Green, J. Kipple, and F. Cham- bers (captain), forwards. Runcorn: J. Brazendale, back; W. H. Cawley, H. C. Speakman, and T. H. Davies,three- quaiter backs; G. Whitby and H. Hughes (captain), half backs; W. Hughes, F. Hancock, J. Gayter, J.Clarke, W. H. Broady, W. Stubbs, G. Wainwright, W. Faulkner, and R. Dolan, forwards. WARRINGTON V. MOSSLEY "A" TBAIM—The return fixture between these teams was played at Mossley on Saturday in very unfavourable weather, a dense fog overhanging the ground, especially in the second half, when the players were almost completely obscured. The field also was in very bad condition, owing to the frost having broken up and by heavy rain. The Warrington men suffered defeat by 2 tries and 4 minors to 5 minors. This is accounted for by the fact that the home team had got their full strength up, and had a decided advan- tage in the pack, which will be readily understood when it is considered that Warrington went with one forward ' short, and had to play Sanson in the scrimmage, Daniels taking his place at three-quarters, besides being short of several of their best forwards. The Warrington captain won the toss, and elected to play down hill with the wind, and two 30's being the time agreed upon, Ken- worthy kicked off for Mossley, Evans returning to Booth who kicked into touch in the Warrington quarters. The Mossley forwards worked the ball to near the Warring- ton line, hit Thornley, Adamson, and Appleton trans- ferred play to centre; and from a line-out Whittle broke away with a grand dribble, forcing the home team to kick dead. Mos,sley dropped out, -Evans' return' being charged down. Daniels sent the ball into touch near the Warrington quarter flag. Pickford dribbled toJolley, but this player got the ball away with a tremendous punt, Dunkerley returning. Booth next kicked to Dan- iels, 'who was held by Golland. Jones, Holmes, and Lloyd broke away with a dribble, Booth saving well. Passing between Antrobus, Evans, and Appleton took place, the latter player being collared by Wood. The home forwards now forced play to the visitors' line, Jolley getting the ball away by a kick into touch, Antrobus following up this advantage by a splendid run three parts the length of the field, play resting in the home 25. Batley, Dawson, and Kenworthy again worked the ball up the field, but the Warrington forwards retaliated with a neat dribble, Pickford saving near centre. Daniels next stopped a dangerous rush of the home forwards, scrimmaging taking place near the Warrington line, a touch in goal being credited to the home team. Jolley dropped out, the ball being taken to the Mossley half. Antrobus again shone with a brilliant run, the full back bringing him down. Evans put in a short kick, and Booth mulling the ball Daniels and Whittle appeared to have a good chance of scoring, but the ball went into touch in goal. Kenworthydropped out, Sanson got possession and when tackled by Mellor passed to Adamson, who kicked down the field, Dunker- ley returning to Sanson, who put in a long kick, the ball going dead. Half-time was now called, the score stand- ing Warrington 4 minors to Mossley 1 minor. On change of ends, Sanson restarted on behalf of the visitors, Booth returning into touch. Whittle passed to Evans, who was held by Wood before he could get away. At this time very little of the game could be seen owing to the fog. Adamson, Dillon, Bate, and Thornley put in a fine dribble from a line-out, Newby replying by a kick into touch. Evans next got in a long kick and Donohue following up prevented a return. Batley and Evans broke away with the ball, Appleton kicking across the field, the WU going into touch. Whittle got clean away with a splendid run, and dropped at goal, Dunkerley returning into touch. The Mossley front rank now pressed Warrington on the line, and after a series .of packs Golland picked up out of a scrimmage and dashed over the line, the referee allowing a try. A good at- tempt at goal was made, the ball striking the cross-bar. Shortly after the drop out a free kick was allowed War- rington. Jolley's kick being returned by Wood. With the exception of a minor for the visitors, the home team continued to have the best of the game, scoring a minor, and, from a scrimmage near the line, Evans secufed a try for Mossley, no goal resulting from the place kick. On the call of time the score stood—Mossley, 2 tries, 4 minors, Warrington, 5 minors. Teams '—Warrington: Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Appleton, Evans, and Daniels; half-backs, Whittle (captain) and Antro- bus; forwards, Adamson, Donohue, Jones, Dillon, Thornley, Bates, Lloyd, Holmes, and Sanson. Mossley: Fullback, Dunkerley; three-quarter backs, Wood, Pitch- ford, and Booth; half-backs Golland and Nield : for- wards, Batley, Baker, Evans, Hallewell, Sykes, Mellor, Newby, and Kenworthy (captain). The first match this season re- suited in a defeat for the Wdrring,tonians by one try and two minors to five minors, and strenuous efforts were made by the home team to reverse this verdict, although they were placed at a disadvantage in not having their full strength in the field. div.head: LOVE AND LEARNING.
div.p: LOVE AND LEARNING.

A well-known, elderly nobleman, of large wealth, ! wooed and won-, a few fears ago, a young and .very beautiful girl. Their life has been as happy as it Is pos- sible for married life to be, when December is united to .May. His lordship is distinguished in scientific circles and possesses high literary attainments. Some time after his marriage he was foolish enough to think that his lovely wife was not sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of reading for her. A month later he inquired about her progress, and found that she had not opened a book. He set up his eye- brows after the manner of old husbands When their young wives have displeased thent. Whereupon she looked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said: "I was made to be loved, not to be learned." She won the day, of course. What is. learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye Would not a husband rather be met with a smile and a kiss, than by a wife who assured him that she " knew her lesson ?" WIAO/TI Is all very well, but winning ways go further. Laughing eyes beat Greek roots all to nothing. A woman's lovely tresses, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are more precious in a husband's eyes than ever so much learning iii- side of it. Therefore, all women should endeavour to preserve their attractions, and welcome their liege lords with loving looks, pleasant smiles, and flowing silken tresses, for after, all a beautiful head of hair is the crowning charm of a wo:nan, charm Which all may possess by using Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or faded hair -to its original color, and make it soft, silky, wavy and luxuriant. It may be had of any chemist or perfumer.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. TKUILEIDAY NIGHT. We are now within measurable distance of a ses- sion that promises to exceed even recent average in respect of episodical interest. The session ahead is not of the kind familiar in the heyday 0f,.11r. Glad- stone's administrations. There is no Land Bill, Reform Bill, Church Bill, or Education Bill which people are looking forward to with the certainty that it will be seriously undertaken, and be added to the Statute Book before the session closes. The ' Government have in hand a measure, the impor- tance of which may compare badly with any of Mr. Gladstone's great bills. But there is a deeply rooted suspicion that the Local Government. Bill is a matter of expediency rather than, of legislative business. The Government want to pass over the cry of the Irish people for Home Rule, and in order to do that they must at least "make-believe" to be engrossingly busy with some other question of the first magnitude. It must be admitted that, regarded as a game of tactics, theyhave managed affairs with exceeding akill. The Reform of Local Government is a substantial necessity, the urgency of which is hidden under the surprising load of ignorance upon the subject which affects the public mind. It has been said that there are probably not six men in any borough in England who could off hand describe the areas of local administration, the constitution of the various governing bodies, and the terms of their election. There is widely spread a vague feeling that local government is in a chaotic state, but there is no sharply defined view on the question such as that which has been imparted on Home Rule, and makes the conclusion of that matter 'in- evitable. If the people could only, within the next fortnight or three weeks, be educated so as to com- prehend all the dark places of that existing system of local government I believe there would be such a cry out for reform that the Government would find no difficulty in shelving Home Rule and carrying their Local Government Bill.

But such a prospect is not probable or possible. The Local Government question is like the late Sir Stafford Northcote, as described by himself. There is no "go " about it. The debates in the forthcom- ing session will be useful as informing the public mind on the question, and leading to a state of things in which promoters of Local Government reform will have behind them the impetus of pub- lic enthusiasm. But the Government are safe in 1 the opportunity of dawdling through a session with the measure, and so effecting the main pur- pose of postponing Home Rule. Where the fighting and the scenes will come ip will be in connection with Irish affairs. Mr. Balfour will have a pleasant time when he is brought face to face on terms of, equality with some of the men whose tongues he has temporarily silenced.,by brute force. Irish members would be more than human if they Aid not "take it out" of the supercilious Chief Secre- tary.. .• . . _ _

J. t is probable also that the relations between the Dissentient Liberals and the growing bulk of the re-animated Liberal party may reach a crisis. Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Henry James, . and Mr. Heneage will doubtless, as last session, as- sert their privilege of ex-Ministers and Privy Coun- cillors by sitting on the Front Opposition Bench, ' cheek by jowl with men in whom they recognise the bitterest enemies, inasmuch as once they were held as intimate friends. As the course of an im- portant debate often suggests necessity for private consultation, the situation plainly has its incon-. yeniences. They were felt last session, through which, almost up to the end, there was always latent hope of reconciliation. Now Lord Harting- ton and his friends have broken the bridge and burned their boats. They are gone qver bodily to the Conservative camp, and could not return even if they desired. It would be just as convenient to have Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord George Hamilton, the Home Secretary, and Lord John Manners sitting-at the end of the Front Opposition Bench, as it is to have the four Dissentient Liberals They cannot be evicted, and must be left to the action of their (mi good taste. Certainly if they remain where they are during the coming troublous session, there will be wigs on the green. - One important factor in Ministerial career during the coming seSsion is to be found in the Budget , prospects. These continue to be bright, and even to improve, Lord Randolph Churchill, in his amiable way, endeavoured to take the wind out of Mr. Goschen's sails by over-rating his probable surplus, with the expectation that when the fact was an- nouneed there would be a reaction in public feeling, and the tax-payer, instead of thankfully welcoming a surplus of two millions, would (having been led to believe there were three) be inclined to say, " Is that all? " One source of revenue that has during the past financial year been unusually prolific still keeps up. This is the Death Duties, to which the fortunes of quite a series of millionaires have Contributed. I hear of one recent windfall somewhat peculiar in its history. Six months ago a retired manufacturer of vast wealth died, leaving the whole of ,his money to his wife, with the understanding bftween them that she, who was childless, should upon her death bequeath the money to her husband's relations. Upon this transaction only the probate duty of three per cent, was paid to the State; but atiortnight ago the woman died also, whereupon there is another probate of three per cent, payable to the Exchequer, and a legacy duty of 10 per cent., that being the per centage payable upon the terms of relationship between the legatee and the beneficiares. Thus, within a period of six months 16 per cent., over one-sixth of the vast possessions bequeathed by the manufacturer, have gone to swell the coffers .of the State. Dissatisfaction is expressed in some circles be- cause of the resolve of the Queen not to open Par- liament in person. It is a matter in which personal convenience has been pitted against what was at one time regarded on the part of the Sovereign as a public duty. The Queen, being at Osborne, must needs, if she open Parliament, travel to London, and spend a couple of nights at Buckingliam Palace, which means a certain expenqe and some fatigue. Probably what weighs with her Majesty more tha:n either consideration, is the strange dread she has of appearing in the streets of London on State occasions. When, in recent sessions, during the Administration of Lord Beaconsfield, the Queen opened Parliament in person, the district between Buckingham Palace and Westminster was as care- fully guarded as are the streets of St. Petersburg when the Czar goes forth. From a strictly business point of view, it LS undoubtedly better that the absurdly-attired Royal Commissioners should take their usual part in the ceremony of opening Parlia- ment. What is of ralich more importance, and upon which the grumbling of Ministers is better justified, is the resolve of the Queen to leave for Italy, within a fortnight of the opening of Parliament. Political crises in redent times have,without exception, found her Majesty at Balmoral, or, more often, at Wind- sor, entailing immense difficulty upon Ministers, whether in esse or in posse. In the present condition of home politics, a crisis may arise on any day- after the meeting of Parliament, and the public sei- vice would seriously suffer by the head of the State being at the time tji a remote Italian town. I met the other night a man whose name was once familiar in Parliamentary. proceedings and in politicartontroversies in-the • newspapers, but who ,h as now so absolutely dropped out of the running that the first sensation on seeing him is of surprise to learn that he is yet alive. The ghosf of the past was Mr. B.P. Bouverie, who for thirty.Nars repre- sented Kilmarnock, nominally as a Liberal. Kil- marnock had grown so attached to its member that for many years it took no notice of the gulf gradu- ally. growing between them. The Liberalism of Kilmarnock in 1874 was very different from that of Mr. Boaverie who had been first elected in 1834. Certainly in the very year that Mr. Disraeli was re- turned at the head of a triumphant Conservative

failed has good temperedly accepted the situatiori. Freed from the trammels of connection with a Liberal constituency he was wont to find in the congenial columns of the "Times " opportunities of attacking Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party. He told me that of late the impulse to restune this correspondence had frequently come upon him. But he was less and less inclined to take active part in polities, and so the letters signed ',E.P.8." nn more enrich the columns of the • Times" with their pungent criticism I rather fancy from an obser- vation he dropped that Mr. Bouverie has kept a diary which cannot fail to be particularly interest- ing. For more than forty years he has been in political, sometime in official, life, and has enjoyed the friendship of most public men worth knowing during the past half century. majority Kilmarnock did its best to strike tbe aver- age by turning out Mr. Bouverie whom it denounced as a Whig. Since then Mr. Bouverie has made- one or two attempts to re-enter Parliament, but haying A recent startling case at the British Museum has opened the eyes of frequenters of the reading-room to an unsuspected companion. It is now made known that here and there among the groups of readers, not the least regular in attendance, and en- grossed in the pursuits of literature, are none other than private detectives. Their use was illustrated in the case referred to, where a clergyman of. the Church of England, greatly desiring, to posses some passages frcm a precious book, cut out the leaves, put them in his pocket, and was promptly Pounced upon by a detective. One social gatherinK at which the presence of detectives is a matter ot course is the reception fa the home of the par6nta of a bride after a wedding. The wedding gifts are spread out in abundance. As a rule twice as maul guests as the house will hold are invited, and ,they stream through the room where the presents are laid out. It is a-revolting reflection that-somewhere ia the crowd is a quiet-eyed man, who keeps his e3reS wide open, especially upon the more valuable articles of portable property. It is a dreadful thing to think that among the invitations sent out by the cheery hosts is one to Scotland Yard, or a private detective office, for the assistance of a spy, But So it is, and I suppose it is necessary.

• ALT,EGED SHOCKING CHILD MURDER AT ST. TTFLENS. On Monday some excitement was caused in St. Helens by a report that a young woman residing it the neighbourhood of Greenbank, a low quarter ol the town, had been apprehended on s a charge o: murdering her infant child under somewhat shock. ing circumstances. At the assembling of the Police Court in the forenoon, a large -number- of - attended, and found 'that the rumour - foundation. The magistrates present weee Mr. Thomas Pilk ington and Mr. A. Sinclair. A young single woman, named Mary Dolan, of 14, Anne-street, was placed in the dock on a charge of causing the death of he' newly-born female child; and further with col cealing the birth of the child. The prisoner, whi appeared to be ins very weak condition, was commodated with a eclat. Chief Constable Wt stated the. charge against the prisoner, and pi ceeded to say that she was 19 years of age and rend with her father 'in Anne-street, GreenbaL. Sbor before six o'clock on Saturday night, from what ha told, he went to the house named. Prisoner was' there. Her father, Daniel Dolan, wentin search of bert and in a few minutes returned with her, and said in JO presence, "Now, Mary, where is the child ?" She Ter plied, "There is no child here; I have not had a ' child. On Wednesday morning last I took cramps; which I had before when I was in Manchester." He (Mr. Wood) get a candle, and asked the accused to accompany h 513; They looked into the pantry and upstairs, but returnee to the pantry, where there was a dolly tub containing dirty clothes and water. - .Ho asked the prisoner to take the clothes out, and she took out two sheets and partly 3 quilt. saying, "There le nothing there," and at the-sani!, time letting the quilt drop into nine or ten inches_ water in the tub. He (Chief Constable) put his hand into the tub, and there found a dead female child, bad, cut about the head and other parts of the body. TM skull was fractured. The prisoner then burst into teare* He said to her, "I will have to take you into custody 011! the charge of having caused the death of that child. Shemadeno reply. He brought the prisoner and Oil dead child to the police office in a cab. He said to thg prisoner on arriving at the station, "I am about W. charge you with a serious crime. You are not bound te say anything in reply to the charge, but whatever i yog do say may be given n evidence against you at yell trial. He then repeated the charge, but the accW,' made no reply. He then told her that she wage charged with concealing the birth of the child, 'Her 'ply was" It must have been struck with the legs oft dolly. It was dead before I put it into the tub. Ja sister did not know it was there, and she must hale struck it with the dolly when cleaning the clothes. 10 one saw the child but myself." The: Chief C,onstabie asked that the prisoner should be remanded until Oa the inquest, which would be held on the following da9o and she was remanded until Thursday. A post-mortem examination subsequently made surgeons showed that the child had been brutallybeell with a blunt instrument on the head, and that bones had been smashed. • INQUEST AND VERDICT. Mr. S. Brighouse' the coroner, held an inquest on the body of the child at the Town Hall, on Tuesday morning. The mother was present in custody, and Chief con- stable Wood watched the proceedings on behalf of the police. Daniel Dolan, a labourer, stated that he was the prl" soner's father. She had been in service for about tesle, years in Manchester, and in Peter-street, St. Helens NI since the death df her mother in August fast she bed kept house for him. He had not noticed nor had sblij told him that she was eneiente. He remembered the Chief Constable finding the body of a child in the pantry of the house, and that was the first time he sac' the child. She had made no complaint of being ill. Ilje daughter was ill in bed on the previous Wednesday, .10 She came down on the Thursday, and on the Saturda/ did the cleaning of the house, scrubbing, &c. When the Chief Constable called on Saturday night, she had gone out, and he (witness) brought her in. He asked ba Where was the child, but she denied having had a child. He could not remember the exact words she used. Father Murphy spoke to him about' the matter On Saturda, morning in Mary's presence, and when he heard about it h e gave information to the police. Chief Constable Wood repeated his evidenee, as stated by him in the police court on Monday. He added di:4 he found the hatchet produced among some coal under the staircase. There. was nothing noticeable either en, the hatchet or the dolly tub. The body was cut and the skull was fra,ctured ; and he did not think the cure had been caused by the "dolly." Dr. MeNicoll, medical officer, deposed to having made a post mortem examination of the body on Mondai efternoon. It was that of a full grown child moderatell nourished. The right arm was nearly severed; in tvio about the elbow, and was only held by a piece Of skin. The right foot was also nearly severed from the leg above the ankle joint. The left arm was nearly severed front the body at the shoulder joint, and the left leg was half Severed from the body at the thigh. on the head there was a scalp wound which had been cloven from back to front, cutting through the bones of the head and deeP into the brain. The child had lived, and had had 3 separate existence apart from its mother. It hathad no He thought the cause of death was heniorThag.,e. probably accelerated by the external injury. He amid not say whether the wounds were inflicted before or after 'death. Neglect at birth would have caused death apart 'from the injuries inflicted.—ln reply to several 'more, witness added that there was no sign that the child had been drowned. It must have bean dead before hew' put in the water.. The injuries were not caused by the &Ilya but, might have been done with a blunt hatchet, such a the one produced. The Coroner remarked that the Chief Constable had other evidence of a negative character, and the conceal: meat of birth was a matter for the magistrates to deal with. He did not think it advisable to call any further , witnesses- after the medical testimony, and he suggested that theeury should return an open verdict.—The jure' returned a verdict to that effect, after some minuted deliberation.

div.head: EetttrS to the Obitor.
div.p: EetttrS to the Obitor.

THE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—l was glad to see from an article that you pub- lished last week, that in Scotland, where the people are proverbially far-seeing, they have secured a consolida- tion of their Public Libraries' Acts, the result of which has been, as you say, a very wise amendment. The amendment of the clause that said that admission to Libraries and Museums should be " free of all charge" is worth repeating. The clause, as it now stands, reads: —"All libraries, museums, or art galleries established - under this Act, or to which this Act applies, shall be open to the public free of charge, and no charge shall be made for the use of books or magazines issued for home reading." Evidently the good people of Scotland are in- dined to put no heti interpretation on the law, but be- lieve that the original intention of the Libraries' Act was to make libraries free in every sense of the word, and to allow the public to enjoy the full benefit by being able to read the books by their own firesides. This, as it appears to me, is another very cogent argument against the somewhat incomprehensible conduct of the Warrington Museum and Library Committee, who seem to think that any interprtation that they, in their wis- dom, may deem fit to plaBe on the law, should as a mat- ter of course be accepted without question by the public, whom the matter so much concerns. The example just set them is a good one; will they follow?—Yours, &c., J. K. G. Warrington, January 28,1888.

HOLY TRINITY DEBATING SOCIETY. Sir.—Ever since I saw it announced in your columns, a short time ago, that. Mr. H. J. Longton, a member of the above society, on account of pressure of business, had to ask to be excused from reading a paper he had promised until a later date, I have been in a feverish state of expectation as to what new theory or discovery we were going to be informed of. Alas for my expecta- tions! The mountain has again been in labour and brought forth a mouse. Observe all ye wise men of the earth, particularly all ye Catholic Unionists, what this sprig of -the local Tory Association has to say upon the causes of poverty and its remedies. "Roman Catholic- ism," says Mr.Longton, "is one of the causes of poverty." Is this legal luminary aware that the first statute pro- viding for poorhouses was passed in the reign of Queen Elizabeth? Were there no poor until then? If so, how were they maintained? Do the cathedrals and colleges of our towns and cities show that they were built in ages of poverty? Nay, who built the church at Winwick, Mr. Longton's, and our parish? To go further, can Mr. Longton point to any Catholic country where there is a greater amount of distress than in this country? Perhaps he will say Ireland. The distress and poverty in Deland ire the direct result of the mis- government of that country by the political friends and allies of Mr. Longton; men who seem to have been of his opinion that all that was required to dispose of poverty was to supersede the Roman Catholic religion by the Protestant one. I would advise Mr. Longton, the next time he prepares a paper, to choose some subject for which he will not require to contradict history, or disgust sensible people of all sects in order to gratify parsons of narrow views and their satellites.—Yours, &c., ANTI-HUMBUG.

div.head: MANCHESTER. SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER. SHIP CANAL.

The work on Lymm section of the canal has now started. Two more flat loads of timber have ar- rived; and on Wednesday morning at 11 o'clock about GO men were started near Lymm, in gangs of six, on "piece work," to remove the surface of the ground so that a line of rail may be laid through the island known as" Wolf's ley." The price paid to those at work is 3id per yard for the outer quarter lengths, and 4id for the inner quarters, the soil to be dug and then wheeled about 20 yards. For the convenience of those seeking employment the con- tractors have erected a convenient raft, so that at any time it can be pulled across the river by a single person from the other side. It consists of a stout rope rove through a pulley attached to a tree on the Lancashire side and a post on the Cheshire side of the river and attached to a raft of plank, which float backward and forward across the river. It is stated that plans are to be submitted to the Lymm authorities during the next few days for a temporary erection on land belonging to Mr. John Jackson, just beyond Statham Pools, by a gentle-. man from the Midland Counties; his object being to supply lodgings for single men, and refreshments, such as tea and coffee, and beer also, it is said, if he can obtain a license. Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor for the Ship Canal, has placed an order with Messrs. Fleming and Fer- gusson. Paisley, for a large and powerful dredger. The vessel is to be capable of raising six hundred tons per hour from a depth of thirty-five feet. and is to cut in advance of bull to make her own flota- tion. Iler machinery will be of the most improved kind.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A FUSTIAN-CUTTING
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A FUSTIAN-CUTTING
FIRM.

At the Borough Court at Warrington, yesterday morning, before Mr. John White, Alderman Harri- son, and Dr. Gornall, a case was heard in which Messrs. James Platt and Son, fustian cutters, were summoned at the instance of the Factory Inspector for having, on the 23rd of December, employed several persons after the hour of seven o'clock in the evening, contrary to the Factory and Shop Act of 1878. Colonel Meade-King, Factory Inspector, appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Mulholland, barrister (instructed by Mr. A. Browne), .appeared for the defence.—Mr. Meade-King said that the defendants were charged with employing a number of women after seven o'clock in the evening. That was the technical charge, but the real chitrge made against the defendants was simply that of being the occu- piers of a factory in which there was a contravention of the Factory Act. The first section of the Act to which he would draw attention was section 13, which provided with respect to the employment ot young persons and women that the period of work should either begin at six o'clock in the morning and end at 6 o'clock in the evening, or commence at 7 o'clock in the morning and end at 7 o'clock in the evening, the latter being the latest time at which young women could be legally employed. Section 83 of the Act provided that where a child, young person, or woman, was em- ployed contrary to the provision the occupier of the factory should be liable.—Ammon Platt, an Inspector ' under the Factory Act, then gave evidence to the effect that on the 23rd ult. he visited the shop of Messrs. Platt and Son, in Turner's-fold, at 7-20 in the evening. He then saw work going on. He took the names of nine people, but the whole room appeared to be at work. He said—" What time do you give up working at night ?" and the workers then commenced to put the candles out. In answer to Mr. Mulholland, witness said that he would not swear whether the women at work had aprons on or not. On the• conclusion of the case or the prosecution, in support of which two witnesses employed by the defendants had been called, Mr. Mulholland referred to discrepancies between their evidence and the evidence give!' by Inspector Platt. He also pointed out, as had been given in evidence, that the foreman of the shop, which is a branch one, had been compelled to leave the shop at six minutes to seven, and even if in his absence someone worked a few minutes overtime, he thought the Bench would not convict on that. He thought the case had broken down, but was prepared to defend it if the magistrates desired. He then called witnesses, who positively swore that on the , evening in question there was no one working when the inspector went into the shop, and that only three •candles, which were necessary to enable the workpeople to leave the place, were alight. After a little consulta- tion, the magistrates announced that they thought, con- sidering the conflict of the evidence, they must decide that no offence had been Committed; but they thought that the foreman should have been at his place at seven o'clock. After the hearing of the case, Mr. 11. J. Long- ton, solicitor, said he understood that it had been I stated that Mr. Meade-Ring had received a letter of in- formation in regard to this case, and he had been in- structed by a client, who said that it had been circulated that he (the client) had given information, to ask Mr. Meade-King to say whethee or not that was the cane. The name of his client was William Hunt, of Lythgoes- lane. In reply, Mr. Meade-Ring said that he had never received information of any kind from Mr Hunt, and Inspector Platte said that he had not received any from that gentleman. The subject then dropped.

MR. O'BRIEN AT MALLow.—Mr. O'Brien,' MT., pro- ceeded from Dublin to Mallow, on Thursday, for the pur- pose of attending a banquet given in honour of his re- lease.
