div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMP ROVEMENT CLASS.—. At the weekly meeting of this class, Mr. R. Proud presiding, a paper was read by Mr. John Jones, entitled "Man." The paper was a good one, and broughkbefore the notice of the members of the class many important and inter- esting points for discussion as well as information with regard to the structure of the human frame: CONCERT AT ASTOI4. —On Thursday evening a concert of a very enjoyable nature took place in Aston School- room' near Preston Brook, the object of which was to assist in liquidating the debt attached to the Union (Congregational) Church, Frodsham. The idea of the concert originated with Mrs William Wilkinson, of Aston Heath, and her daughter, Miss E. Wilkinson, and thanks to the efforts put forth by these two ladies, assisted by the other members of the family, the concert proved a complete success both financially and otherwise. The building, which had been nicely decorated, was filled, a large number of Warrington friends journeying thither in order to be present. Mr. Thomas Rigby presided, and introduced the artistes, who were Mrs John Fair- hurst (Stockton Heath), Miss Dutton, Misses Elsie and Annie Dutton (Brindley), Miss Wright (Halton), and Messrs Earp (Preston Brook). Naar Wilkinson (Warrington), G. Shakeshaft (L)'mm), Joseph Mercer (Warrington), and Mr. Scott.
RECOGNITION SERVICE AT CAIRO-ST. CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.

I On Wednesday evening a largely-attended, ser- vice was held in Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington, for the purpose of welcoming the newly-appointed minister, the Rev. Priestley Prime. Amongst the ministers present, in addition to Mr. Prime, were the Professor J. Estler Carpenters M.A.. of Manches- ter New College; Professor J. G. Odgers, M.A., of Altrincham ; the Rev. H. Enfield Dawson, 8.A., of Gee Cross: the Rev. R. A. Armstrong, BA., of Liver- pool; and the Rev. Henry Gow. Lessons having been read, and a payer offered up by the Rev. Hy. Gow, of Liverpool, and two hymns sung, Mr. F. MONKS, d.P., said he had been asked to give that night expression to their feeling of welcome to Mr. Prime, and he would not refer to the causes which had led 4:42, the change in the ministry further than to say that if Mr. Prime in the course of his ministry should find the deep and abiding affection for the minister that Mr. Pil- cher, Mr. Porter, and Mr. Carpenter did, he (Mr. Monks) hoped it would be an encouragement to him, and strengthen his hands in the ministry which he was about to undertake. He did not know that he could say very much that night, but he might perhaps be allowed to say that if that church had meant anything in the past—as he hoped it would moan something in the future—it was a church in which they all might come from week to week and worship without any fear of any ques- tions being asked as to what was their faith, and what was their position theologicAlly, and he knew that many of them valued that freedom very much. They had inherited from their predecessors a plain and simple building, but one which they reverenced. They had not asked their new minis- ter to sign any test whatever, and they lived from week to week without asking any one to subscribe to any article of faith. They believed it to be far better that they should trust to that freedom which they had inherited: and which they hoped to trans- mit to their successors—that Christian reasonable- ness would always manage to perceive what was progressive in religion, to receive truth from what- ever source it might come, and enable them to settle their differences amoihgst themselves in a spirit o: freedom and Christian charity. They knew also that there were changes in their circumstances and in their conditions"; and he might say to their new minister that they did not expect him to be bound by traditions which had been of use to his prede- cessors. They rather preferred that he would strike out and strive to realise his own ideal of what a Christian ministry should , be, and he thought he was expressing the wish of the congregation when he said that they should only be too anxious to assist him with every means in their power to strengthen his hands, and to encourage him to realise the ideal which he had set be- fore him. They had already had sufficient experience of Mr. Prime to believe that the ideal would be a high and noble one. There was only another word that he would say. That congregation did not confine its usefulness within its own borders. It had sent out a very large number of useful men, who had borne the heat and battle of life outside its walls, and who had taken a ' very active part in connection with the institutions with which that town was surrounded. There was one thing that had been impressed upon many of them and that was that many ministers were frequently tempted to take to themselves work which taxed their energies and caused in some of them an overstraining which they could not bear. He hoped that their new minister, while anxious to take his share in the useful work of the town, would consider his own health, and he (Mr. Monks) was sure he could pledge that congregation to a patient, and he might say to an affectionate extension of their kind- ness to him. He might also say that if there was any- thing which their new minister thought would be of use to the town they would all be willing :to help him to realise it by personal and material support. They had ministers who had done noble work, and, although they- had gone to their long home, their work remained behind them, and every member of that congregation would assist Mr. Prime to continue that good work that the church might stand, not only for freedom of life, but for nobility of life. The Rev. J. E. ODGERS next welcomed Mr. Prime on behalf of the ministers of the provinces of Lancashire and Cheshire. They felt a deep interest in that occasion for they: did not forget that Warrington was once the Athens, the intellectual centre! of their liberal non-conformity, from which a light shone which by God's blessing had not yet been extinguished. They remembered that Mr. Prime stood now in a long line of those whose praise had been in all the churches, and the last of whom had left to his successor a noble work, and he (Mr. Odgers) who had been with that people when they sorrowed for his loss ; and that sorrow was the deepest and strongest token Mr. Prime could have that unselfish, watchful, and loving work in that place, and in the midst of those to whom he would minister, would not fail to bring about its exceedingly great reward. The Rev. R. A. ARMSTRONG said he ventured to wel- come Mr. Prime on behalf of the little group of churches of which the city of Liverpool might be regarded as the 'centre. They had in and about Liverpool a growing group of young ministers of high promise and great vigour whom they hoped to see more and more welded into one body, animated by one spirit, and earnest for all good and noble work, and they all of them felt that this little band of workers would be greatly cheered and strength- ened by Mr. Prime's presence and co-operation in their midst. He could not forbear from giving from the van- tage ground of some 20 years of ministerial experience a few words of brotherly counsel to one entering on the arduous task of the Christian ministry, and what he tie- sired most to say was to so far second the words which Mr. Monks had already uttered, asto beseech Mr. Prime to resist the immense temptationwhich every ardent and eager nature placed in the midst of seething humanity must necessarily feel to enrol himself, in so great a multitude of beneficent engagements, that the one shall clash against the other. Believe him that the longer he remained in their ministry the more he would be convinced that the central and vital work which they had to do to which all else was secondary, was the work which was involved in the conduct of their religious services and the endeavour to utter words of wisdom, of strength, and of uplifting to the brethren assembled with them for common worship. And yet with all that he trusted that Mr. Prime's heart was stirred and would continue to be stirred by the great problem of their changing civilisation, and he would put in a plea with the people to whom he was to minister that they would not only be very patient with hin (Mr. Prime) and his views of the great socal questions of their time, and if they might now and then diverge that they would even be thankful to find that they had a minister of such earnest heart and such living and eager soul that he could not refrain from uttering his word of counsel even when it might seem out of season on those great problems which pressed upon them so heavily for solu- .tion. The Rev. PRIESTLEY PRIME, in replying to the words ef welcome that had been uttered, said that if he could but in some measure live up to the ideal that had been before him he would thank God that he undertook that work. He was proud of his position, and he was proud of the welcome they had given him. He thanked them for it, and felt encouraged for the work. The Rev. J. E. CARPENTER next, in an eloquent ad- dress, delivered the charge to the pastor. The Rev. H. ENFELD DAWSON, in delivering the charge to the congregation, remarked that as much depended on the congregation as the minister. He spoke from a pretty long experience in the work, that his youngfriend, their new minister, was undertaking, and he said that theirs was at least one half of the task of making Mr. Prime's ministry fruitful and happy. He thought there was no relationship in life in which so much depended upon both parties to it as that relation between minister and congregation, except, indeed, it be that most sacred relation between husband and wife. To have perfect mutual confidence and under- standing was everything in both these relationships; to have implicit trust was vital, to have mutual Ramona' attachment and regard was the very heart and soul of the union, as it was between husband and wife. And while it would be their young pastor's work to spare no time or labour in entering their homes and becoming one of themselves, it would be theirs to meet him with the sympathy of true friends. The service was brought to a close with the benedic- tion.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1888.
PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BEITH. IL-WILLIAM HENRY'S HOBBIES."

William Henry is a nice, quiet young man who pays his debts to a fraction, like the Village Blacksmith, and in consequence stares the whole world out of coun- tenance. He manages to squeeze a lot of the juice of enjoyment out of the miserable lemon of life by laying hands on those wonderful things known as hobbies, and using them for his personal pleasure. For fear of being misunderstood, I hasten to explain that William Henry is nothing related to, and has no connection with, the t individual called Bill Harry,who has a separate pawning account of his own. Being of an active temperament, William Henri is always busy, and, if he is not at his daily occupation, he is sure to be either oiling a hobby ready for work, actually working it, or picking up the pieces of it after it has worked. Now, as there are differences of opinion. as to Iwhat hobby really is, it is our duty to inquire into the matter. A lady friend of mine told me that "a hobby is simply a curse upon everybody within the cardinal points of the compass ;'' but as the said lady's husband had for his hobby the rearing of a certain spirited pup which had made ribbons of a pair of her best curtains, I consider her's a bigoted definition.
I humbly tender my own definition that a hobby is that kind of mischief that keeps you out of some other kind.

I asked William Henry the other day for his definition, and he said. "A hobby is an enjoyable occupation, prompted by intellectual superiority and activity, and participated in at seasonable opportunities." I acknow- ledged the truth of this, and illustrated its practical value by a young man that I once knew, whose hobby was to go around dropping wet fizzes through letter-box slits. William Henry hopes thab his hobby will never come down so far as that.

Until a short time ago I imagined my hobby to con- sist of staying at the club 'till midnight, but my guiding star says that was a vice. But to return to William Henry. The first hobby that he can remember was making mud pies. His second bobby was catching those attenuated creatures com- monly known as Harry-long-legs, and bottling them up as a sort of museum. This generated quite a naturalistic taste, and he made rapid strides in this branch of science, collecting moths, beetles, frogs, Sm. His parents saw the innate genius in the boy, and encouraged him by purchasing several works on natural history, such as Robinson Crusoe. In this hobby William Henry com- bined business with pleasure, „Yetting up a sort of minia- ture cattle show in their backyard, and admitting his less gifted playmates at a charge of a handful of rags, or two for a ha'penny, and several small boys mortgaged their Saturday ha'pennies to see this show. But like other joys in this life frog shows are fleeting, and by one of those freaks of the juvenile mind which nobody will ever be able to understand, William Henry suddenly cleared out his stock-in-trade. I shall pass over his earlier hobbies, the foregoing being simply given to prove that he was born for something extraordinary. The next hobby of any consequence fastened on him when he was a young man and it was in the greenhouse line. He read up all the Modern horticulture he could lay hands on, and his inquiries from gardeners of his acquaintance about orchids, bulbs, pruning, grafting, and potting, led many of his friends to suppose that he was about to open a public botanical garden. It is astounding how soon a greenhouse gets too little•for you. William Henry's did, and he added new wing after new wing until it became quite extensive. The potting' business didn't go down so well with him, so he invited an interested frielad to assist him; but they who expect a friend to do their potting gratuitously through an entire season may sometimes see an exhibition of Ingratitude on the part of the said friend. It was even thus with William Henry. He waited patiently, but the potter came not; the gents dried up, and the grubs ate their fill, yet still the ungrateful potter returned not. But William Henry wasn't the man to fret over twenty potters; so he just let the whole affair go by the run, and, between you and me, the whole going concern went by private treaty for the sum of ten shillings, with the watering can and the grubs thrown in. He hasn't bought a single plant since that period of his history. His next hobby was keeping rabbits. As he is always confident that whatever he undertakes will be a success, he bought a good-sized hutch and about a score of rabbits. With the dry part of the feeding he managed first-rate, but he drew the line at gathering fresh herbage, and hence entrusted that part of the feeding duty to a smart boy. After a time the boy took the en- tire management, and William Henry's sole hobby was measuring the ears of his favourites, exhibiting them to his friends, and paying the smart boy on Saturdays. One day he found seven of them dead on the floor, which, coupled with the fact that the smart boy had been recently engaged to play in several football ties with the Blalcey Moor Rushers against the Snig Brook Whoppers, and that the rest of the lop ears seemed in the last stage of consumption. caused Willialn Henry to enter into another private treaty for the sale of a rabbit hutch. For the first time in his life be was shaken as to whether he really possessed a hobby or not, so he con- sulted a phrenologist, who at once told him that his forte lay in music; and then he remembered that his father had once played the harmonium in a Methodist Schobl. and he himself had taken the side drum in a fife and drum band. These remembrances corroborated the delineation of the phrenologist, and William Henry wondered that he hadn't thought of it before. He didn't go shouting around that he was going to learn to play a musical instrument, but quietly bought a violin and bow, and a "teacher without a master," rightly judging that it would astonish his friends when he gave his first solo in public. I don't profess to know any- thing about violins myself. but I have been told that there are a few awkward preliminaries to be gone through before you play a solo in public on that instru- ment. William Henry must have been aware of this fact, and as he couldn't engage another smart boy to learn the instrument for him, he pro- ceeded to learn it himself. If it has been the reader's luck to live next door to a man who was learning to play on a fiddle, he will be able to realise somewhat the sounds that proceeded from William Henry's apartment. I lived next door to him at this time, and I lay claim to being an unprejudiced man my- self. I once was in the same room where he was prac- tising what he called the gamut, and I think I can speak with some authority on the sounds produced. I am always ready to assist a fellow creature (if it can be done cheap), and hearing one day a mixture of screams and groans next door, I rushed in, and breathlessly asked what was the matter. William Henry appeared quite cool, and said he was "just trying the gamut." I then innocently asked him if he was practising an imitation of the human voice in distress, or was trying to give an exact representation of a pig slaughter-house ; but as he appeared somewhat hurt, I didn't press the question further..

The reason he gave up the practice of the violin was very touching. Explaining the matter to me, he said, "When a fellow's friendly neighbours tell him one after another that he is injuring his health by such close ap- plication to music, and one and all advise him to give it up for his own sake, he is bound as a gentleman and a I Ehristiin to do so." He evidently knew his duty (some- times), And up to the present he hasn't let any more musical hobbies loose; if he does I shall advise him, as a friend, to practice on Pendle Hill, where genius can ex- mend in unmolested solitude. If you want to send a ' present to a friend in New Zealand, this fiddle will be sold cheap, minus strings and a few fintings. (Anwr.) Last year William Henry settled down to the study of chemistry. He showed me a quantity of glass tubes, bottles and things, and when I asked if he intended to start in the glass blowing business, and had got these as patterns, he smiled at my ignorance, and explained that he was going in for chemistry as a hobby, adding that was the most intellectual and scientific hobby extant. I was surprised for some weeks at his profound interest in chemistry, but he hadn't made many ex- periments then. As I sat reading at home, Mrs. Bette would start up and exclaim, "[(ugh, there's another dish or something fallen off the shelf next door," or, "Good gracious! what's that 2" I suggested that no doubt they would be fog-signals on the reilway, as we have had a lot of these things liftely. One day I noticed an advertisement in the paper to the effect that a complete set of chemical apparatus would be disposed of for an old sow", and the initials at foot were W. H. I asked oar W. H. if the advertisement was his, and he explained that there wasn't room in a house like theirs to give the hobby of chemistry full scope. His hands looked like those of a journeyman dyer, but he assured me that he had only burnt the legs off two pairs of mints all the time. I couldn't advise any one to buy that "complete set" of apparatus, as I have personally seen odd pieces of broken glass (suspiciously like some in the "complete set ") which have been thrown over the back wall. I forgot to tell you that William Henry is a bachelor. He has a chest of tools, but he cannot do much with with them, not being in his own house. Hill present hobby is to plane one piece of wood into shavings, to cut another into chips, and present them to his land- lady for lighting the fire, but you cannot tie true genius down like that; he is bound to burst out into a new flame before long. There is one hobby. that I think would about settle him. Let him take unto himself a wife, to fix his buttons and make things generally hot for him. I believe that such a hobby would last him a lifetime. although I am not going to stick myself up as a prophet.

In Dublin, on Thursday, three prevision dealers were fined £lO each for selling margarine as butter, and the magistrate stated that in all future cases he would inflict the full penalty. ETRE CHARGB AGAINST A PRISON GOVERNOR.—Major Roberts, Governor of Cork Prison, attended before the magistrates on Thursday to answer a charge of having systematically inveigled girls under thirteen years of age for immoral 'purposes. The Rev. Canon O'Mahony, defendant's accuser, and three girls, who swore infor- mations incriminating Roberts, were in attendance to give evidence; but the case had to be adjourned until Tuesday next, owing to the inability of the defendant's counsel, Mr. Adams, Dublin, attending before that date.
WARRINGTON.
THE LITE CAPTAIN' REYNOLDS.—The bust of the late Captain Reynolds, J.P., is at present on view in the shop window of Mr. Boothroyd, Sankey- street. .

LEGAL APPoiNTstExT.—Mr. Samuel Yearsley, solicitot, Warrington, has been appointed by the Lord Chancellor a Commissioner to administer oaths in the Supreme Court of Judicature in England. SOIREE.—Mr. Percy Randall's second soiree took place at the Conservative club on Thursday even- ing, and was a success, a good number of tickets having been disposed of. Dancing was kept up with vigour until the early hours of Friday morning to music supplied by Mr. Randall's band. Mr. Massey, of the Roebuck, supplied the refreshments. INQUESTS.—On Tuesday afternoon, Mr S. Brig- house, coroner, held two inquests at the Three Pigeons Inn. Tanner's-lane. The first inquiry was with reference to the death of a child named Mary Denton, daughter of James Denton, toolmaker, 34, Lvthgoes-lane. Evidence was give a by the mother, Catherine Denton, to the effect that the child, which was four weeks old, her husband, herself, and two other children slept in the bed, which was the only one in the house. Next rtkerning the child was dead, and it appeared as though she had had a fit. The second inquiry was relative to the death of Ellen Poulter, three weeks old, the danghter of Joseph Poulter, wireworker, 55, Bewsey-road. who died on Sunday morning apparently in convulsions. In each case the jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes.' HOLY TRINITY LITERARY AND DEBATING SO- CIETY.—On Monday evening, the weekly meeting of the members of this society was held in the Schoolroom, Museum-street. The Rev W. E. Glenn presided, and Mr F. W. Wood read a paper on "Notorious High wayrden." The three selected were Robin Hood, Claude Duval, and Dick Turpin. The essayist first pointed out the wretched means of communication at the time these highwaymen lived, and gave an account of Robin Hood, the cele- brated outlaw. An excellent account of Claude Duval and Dick Turpin was next given, together with variousninteresting anecdotes of their ex- ploits. After the reading of the paper a short dis- cussion ensued, in which Messrs Dobson, Rose, Westbrook, and the chairman took part, and Mr Wood having replied the meeting terminated. WESLEYAN T. 3lEETuoi.—On Saturday even- ing the members of the Men's Bible Class, Silver- street Sunday School, were, together with their wives and friends, entertained to tea in the vestry at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel by their. leader, Mr. J. Shaw Green. A large number sat down to tea, which was served by Mrs. Shaw Green, Mrs. Bayley, Mrs. E. Whitehouse, Mrs. Horton, Mrs. Farrell. Miss L. Horton, and others. At the meet- ing which followed a number of short and interest- ing addresses were given by the circuit ministers, the leader, and Messrs. Dallow, Thomas, and Hor- ton, Sergeant Taylor and Sergeant Tudball. The speeches were interspersed with songs rendered by the Misses Forshaw, Horton, Mills, Ratcliffe, Booth, A. Horton, and C. Hedgcock, and Messrs. Cox, Kelly, Guest, Tudball, and Dallow, the members separating at 9-30 p.m., after having spent a most enjoyable evening.

CROS-SLEY-STREET MISSION. —On Monday even- ing, a soiree in connectilin with this mission was held in the Conservative Club, there being about 140 persons present. The Mayor, who was present, said he was pleased to learn that Crossley-street Mission was doing A very good work in the town, and that it was very successful. The room was filled every Sunday night, and this was in a great measure due to their excellent minister, the Rev. T. H. Twist. (Applause.)—The Rev. T. H. Twist moved a vote of thanks to .those who had got up the soiree, especially naming Mr. Wright and Mr. E. Bennet.—ln the course of a few remarks, Coun- cillor J. E. Wright said that a noble work was being done in the town under the ministry of Mr. Twist. (Applause.)—Dancing was then commenced, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle and Mr. E. Bennett acting as M.O s. During the evening songs were sung by Miss Slater, Mr. D. ikin, and Mr. V. Cook. Mr. G. Riley officiated at the piano. Votes of thanks brought the pro- ceedings to a close. LESSONS ON COOKERY.—During the present week lessons on cookery have been given in the Masonic- rooms, Sankey-street, by Miss H. M. Young, of Warrington. The first lecture was given on Mon- day afternoon, when the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) opened the proceedings, and in the course of a few remarks said they all knew that cooking was a very important art. It was as desirable, perhaps, for a lady to thoroughly understand the art of cooking as it was for her to understand anything else. It was just as important to know how to cook as it was to know how to buy a dress. If they got a good material for a dress, if it was badly made, it was very much worse than if they had a bad material for a dress which was well made. So it was with cooking. If they had a good joint of meat, and it was badly cooked, they might almost as well have done without any at all. (Hear, hear.) On economical grounds it was desirable that a lady should know how to cook well, because she could then purchase at almost half the amount of money the necessaries for providing a good dinner than she could if she did not know how to cook. Illness was caused by eating food that had not been well cooked, and it was said that the way to a man's pocket was through his stomach; if he had had a good dinner he was generally in a good humour. and could be prevailed upon to do many things that he would not do otherwise. (Hear, hear.) Among those present on Monday afternoon were the IMayoress (Mrs. Sutton), Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Har- rison, Mrs. Milling, and yrs. F. Monks.

WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Monday even- ing the annual tea party of the elder scholars of this school was held in Wycliffe Hall, Bewsey- street About 350 scholars partook of tea, ranged in classes, and presided over by their teachers. After, tea a miscellaneous entertainment was given, land a distribution of prizes took place. About 90 prizes were awarded for geed conduct and regular attendance. The chair was taken by the Rev. John Yonge, and there were also on the platform Mr. F. Brown (superintendent) and Mr. W. 11, Wallington (secretary). The Chairman remarked that it gave him great pleasure to see so many scholars and friends present; and Mr. Brown, in, distributing the prizes, impressed upon the scholars the neces- sity of regular attendance on Sunday mornings. Instead of there being about a quarter of their number receiving prizes, he thought there ought to be three-quarters. He also invited any parents or friends, who could do so, and who were not engaged in any other kind of Christian work, to come and help in the school, in which they were greatly in need of assistance, especially on Sunday mornings. The progratnme, which was excellently rendered, included recitations by Sam Hayes, W. Mills, R Evans, Plorrie Pemberton, J. Irish, Arthur Penning- ton, Alice Hayes, Ada Pennington, Gilbert Lowe, and Emily Pemberton; songs by Miss Naylor, Edith Wallington, and George Smith; and a reading by Mr. Spencer. There was also a dialogue, " Who's won it," by Owen, Smith, Place, Podmore, Pielden, , and Longshaw.—On Wednesday evening the teawas given to tbe younger scholars, about 200 of whom were present. _

THE WILFUL DAMAGE BY A. TRAMP.—Jas. Sadler, described as a tramp, belonging to Birmingham, was on Monday, at the Warrington Borough Court, charged with having on the 19th inst. wilfully and maliciously damaged a plate-glass window and a quantity of glass and china goods the property of Wm. Nicholson, Sankey-street, and valued at up- wards of £44 168.—William Nicholson, manager of the cabinet making department of Messrs. Robert Garnentt and Sons, Sankey-street, and proprietor of the glass and china warehouse, 19, Sankey-street, said he did not see the stone thrown, but shortly before half-par eight on Thursday morning last he was called to his shop. lie found that s stone had been thrown through the window on to the centre stand, and that a quntity of glass and china goods, including Dresden china ornaments, dessert services, and a pair of Worcester china figures. and other articles, had been broken. On clearing the window on Saturday he found that other articles had been seriously damaged. The stone was found in the centre of the stand amongst the desert service.— Charles Young Price, a lad, said that at a quarter- past eight on Thursday morning he was in Sankey- street opposite the prosecutor's shop, when he saw the prisoner coming up Sankey-street on the opposite side, holding the stone produced behind ' his back in his right hand. When he got opposite the shop of the prosecutor he lifted his hand and threw the stone with great force at the window. A woman flatbed Jane Cartvnight, who was cleaning some steps, said to the prisoner, "What did you do that for ? " and he said, I have done it-for shelter." —P.C. Hennessey deposed that he was on duty at Market-gate, when, in consequence of information received, he apprehended the prisoner, who said, "I' did it to get run in, and I bope the magistrates will give me 21 years." He produced the stone, which he had received from Mr. Nicholson, and it vteighed 31bs. 2oz.—The prisoner was committed to the Liver- pool Assizes for trial, the Mayor remarking that prison life was.too comfortable for a certain class of [ offender& t,
OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
EFROII OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23. Old Broad-street E.C.

At the time of writing the Stock Exchange almost wholly absorbed in the -fortnightly settlement. Never- theless other matters have demanded their share of at- tention, also which in some instances have not been of the most favourable kind. The chief of these have been Mexican Rails which from 52i have gradually fallen several points with the almost certain probability of their falling several more. Statements are being pub- lished which must inevitably send these stocks down still further, and having regard to the very mercurial nature of them holders who can do so should get out of them at once.

Home rails have been exceedingly flat during the past week, and the controversy between Sir Edward Watkin, of the South-Eastern, and the chairmen of the Brighton and South-Eastern Lines does not tend to strengthen these markets. The Brighton half-yearly meeting was held on Wednesday ; that of the South-Eastern the fol- lowing day, and it cannot be said that the speeches of the chairman help to suppress the already bitter feeling. At the South-Eastern meeting the attempt to remove Sir Edward Watkin ignominiously failed, but it must also be admitted that the movement must tend in favour of the policy advocated by the opponents of Sir Edward Wat- kin. The opponents of Sir Edward Watkin demanded a poll, the result of which was that the amount of stock in favour of the directors was 5,654,504 as against 2,296,542. The North-Eastern Railway has also come in for a considerable fall. On Tuesday this fall being one on the day, and the anticipated dividend not coming up to expectations being the chief cause. . .

The foreign market in the early part of the week showed considerable buoyancy, but at the time of writ- ing the tendency has been for lower price. A marked exception to this state of things is the various issues of Egyptians. Unified, Preference, and Domains have all become remarkably firm, due in a large measure to the settlement of the claims of Ismail Pasha by Mr. Marriott. It is true that Ismail Pasha is to receive a very considerable sum of money, and the question must ultimately arise as to where it is to come from. Nevertheless, the announcement of the settle- ment of this disappointing dispute is sufficient for the Stock Exchange. Egyptian Preference are higher than they have over been before. Unifials are also excep- tionally strong. ." Bears," who are on the gook out for a stock, might do worse than sell Egyptian Prefer- ence. •

The mining market remains the most active of the whole. Rio Tintos continue in strong demand. A rapid demand has also sprungup for the shares of the Namaqua Copper Co., which until recently was almost unknown. A fortnight ago these shares stood at 41 premium. On Saturday last they went up 2 and at the time of writing are quoted over 9; with every probability of their touch- ing 10.. . . _

In miscellaneous mining shares Don Pedros are very firm at £2, Centennials and Pinas Altos also being ac- tively inquired for. Mysores have become stronger, and most of the established mining companies are likely to experience a general rise. In miscellaneous securities there is not much doing. Warehouse company shares are almost unmarketable, wholesale trade in the City showing steady decline. In inu.sic hall shares Pavilions are considerably lower since the announcement of the dividead. This was expected to be fully 9 for the half- year, but is only 7, with a:very disappointing future be- fore it. In our opinion, Pavilions shouli Certainly be sold, if only for the close rivalry it has in the futur to endure. On the other, hand, Metropolitan Music Hall shares, which are at 50 per cent. discount, are certainly worth securing at the present price, with a probability of 20 per cent. dividend very shortly.

FIRE IN A COLLIERY.—At the Keltv colliery, Fifeshire, the engineman at the pit bank found the flooring of his gig-house in flames late on Wednesday 'night. He sig- nalled to three men who were half-war down the shaft overlooking the pumping machinery. Thoy stepped off the cage to the platform, and immediately after, the ropes, heated by the fire, snapped, and the cages were percipitated to the bottom of the shaft. Twenty men in .the pit estaped by another outlet. The pit will be stopped for a fortnight, and the damage will amount to about £l,OOO. div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A heavy snowstorm visited Wick on Fridaymornin,g. The. Oxford and Cambridge boat race has been fixed to be rowed on Saturday, March 24th.* • Rear-Admiral Hotham, C. 8., has been appointed Junior Sea Lord at the Admiralty, in succession to Lord Charles Beresford.

On Friday afternoon Lord Cross opened the Perth City and County Conservative Club in the presence of a large assemblage of ladies and gentlemen. Further evidence is forthcoming to support the theory ' that Hannah Bowles, who was poisoned at Camberley, was excitable, and had meditated self-des- truction.

It is stated that pictures, valued at £3o,ooo,which were burnt while being removed, on Thursday, from one part lof London to another, belonged to Lord Rothschild, for whom they were being removed %y Messrs. Agnew. Mr. Gladstone, in a circular letter dated Florence, 24th January, asks his supporters to be in their places at the opening of Parliament, as the state of public affairs appears to render it certain that an important discussion may be expected to arise immediately thereafter. STRIKE OF WEAVERS.—On Friday morning the weavers employed' at the, Albany Mill, Oldham, belonging to Messrs. J. J. Shiers arid Co., came out on strike. On Monday a repre:sentative from the+ Weavers' Amalgama- ted Society visits Oldham to go into the prices paid, which are the cause of the dispute. SUPPOSED CHILD MURDER.—Ott Friday morning the dead body of a female child was found in an old quarry, at Royton, by a man who was passing on his way to Oldham. It was wrapped in some old linen, and is in a very much decomposed state. The top of its head had been battered in. It was removed to the police station at Royton. SERIOUS BOILER EXPLOSION IN LIVERPOOL.—A serious boiler explosion occurred on Friday morning at the works of the Liverpool Forge Company, at the south end o.'! Liverpool. The boiler, which is used for driving a steam hammer, exploded with a terrific crash, and some of the brickwork was blown a distance of 100 yards. pour Men were seriously injured, two of them, Jonathan Bell and. Joseph White, so seriously that they are not ex- pected to recover. ANOTHER M.P. SENT TO GAOL —Mr. Patrick O'Brien, M P., Mr. Thomas Byrne, of Ballina,sloe, and Mr. John Hayden, of Muffingar. were prosecuted at a Crimes Act Court, at Coolderry, county Roscommon, bn Friday, for speeches delivered at Four Roads, in that county, on :New Year's Day, in which they advised tenants not to pay rent. Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Byrne were each sentenced to four months' imprisonrnent, and Mr. Hayden to three months. Appeals were lodged. THE BROOHIANDS POACHING AFFRAY.—At Altrincham, on Friday morning, Edwin Bailey, of Mather-street, An- coats, Manchester, and James Peers, of Regent-road, Salford, were charged with being concerned in a mur- derous attack on Sergeant Cooper and Constable Proud- love at Brooklands, in November last. Bailey had been apprehended the previous day by the Manchester police; ' and Peers was taken into custody at his own home by Inspector Meredith, Sale. On the application of Super- intendent Leighton the prisoners were remanded. MURDER IN LONDON.—Doctor Dartford Thomas, the coroner for Central Middlesex, opened an inquiry on Fri- day afternoon into the cause of the death of LucyrClarke, who was found dead with skull fractured and throat cut, at 86, George-street, Portman-square, on Monday. The first witness called was Francis Clarke, a brother of the deceased, who deposed that he knew the deceased had had some unpleasantness with twe of her nephews in consequence of her having missed some property after they had been to her rooms. Both nephews of deceased, Harry Montagu Chadwick and Walter James Chadwick, gave evidence yesterday and admitted that deceased's pro- perty was taken and pawned. The jury returned a ver- dict of wilful murder against some person or persons unknown. THE ATTEMPTED TRIPLE MURDER-IN NOTTS.—At Not- tingham, on Friday, Henry Redfern, alias Smith, was charged with attempted triple murder near Kegworth, Nottinghamshire. The prisoner lived unhappily with his wife, who went to .her parents. His wife's mother had a conversation with him, and. he shot at her, the bullet going through her shoulder. The prisoner also shot Arthur Bramley, a boy of twelve, above the right ear, and Emma Bramley, his sister. In the girl's case the bullet penetrated through the frontal bone of the face, destroyed the eye, and lodged in the upper jaw, carrying away five teeth. The prisoner was not appre- hended until January 14th, when he was arrested at Sheffield, while at work in an engineering works. The prisoner was committed for trial at the assizes.
FRENCH STEAMER RUN DOWN.-19 PERSONS DROWNED.

PARIS, FRlDAY.—Several of this morning's journals report that the French merchant steamer Suez was run down by a German steamer near Lisbon before day break yesterday morning. Nineteeo persons are stated to have beendrowned. The remainder-12 in number— succeeded in reaching Lisbon.

div.head: 11Di DIRECTORS' REPORT.
div.p: 11Di DIRECTORS' REPORT.

Mr. Dux (general manager) read the report of the di- rectors, which stated as follows :—The directors, in sub- mitting to the shareholders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £16,307 Is 7d brought from previous account, the net balance of profits, after providifig amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and re- bating the current bills at five per cent, is £121,418 19s •Bd. The distribution of this sum, recommended •by the directors, is ifs follows—lnterim half-yearly dividend, at 15 per cent per annum, declared 29th July, £42,000 ; dividend to be now paid at the rate of 15 per cent per annum, free of income tax, £42,000; bonus of lOs per share, free •of income tax, £14,000 ; to property ac- count, £5,000 ; balance to next accouut, £18,418 19s 8d ; total, £121,418 19s Bd. The directors who retire at this time by rotation are. Colonel Gamble, C. 13., Sir An- drew B. Walker, Bart., Mr. Henry Woodcock, -Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley, and Mr. Alfred Hewlett, all of whom are eligible and are recommended for re-election. The directors record with deep regret the I,leath of their esteemed colleague, Lord Delamere. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said he was happy to believe that the figures in the balance sheet could not fail to bring satisfaction. There was only one thing which might tend to throw a shadow over their minds, and that was the two deaths that had taken place—that of their friend, Mr. Pearson, imme- diately beforO and that of Lord Delamere immediately after, their interim meeting in July last. At that meeting they recorded their sincere regret at the death of Mr. Pearson, and they had now deeply to deplore the loss of Lord Delamere. As one who was greatly interested in the bank, and one who, so long as health permitted, ren- dered his services in aid of the interests of the company they felt his loss all the more on that account, and he felt sure that every shareholder who had had an opportunity of judging of Lord Delamere's valuable work would join in that expression of feeling. At the last meeting he was allowed to express the hope that a revival in trade had set in, and that the year now just passed, and which had then Just begun, would show an improved state of things, and that the tide of prosperity which had been hopelessly ebbing so long had at last taken a turn, and was rising steadily if imperceptibly. He had not seen any reason to retract what he then said. The Chancellor of the Ex- chequer had spoken hopefully on this point a few days ago; the Board of Trade returns pointed to a better state of things, and if the war clouds hovering over them dispersed without breaking, confidence in the future would be restored, and a much better state of trade would ensue. Having referred in some detail to the balance sheet, he said that was the twelfth time the' bonus of lOs per ' share had been given to the shareholders. The balance to be carried forward to the next account amounted to £18,418 19s Bd, and this, they would notice, was £2,000 ' more than it was last year. It was satisfactory' to the directors to feel that they had a substantial sum carried forward to the next account. (ApplauSe.)—Mr. N. ECKEBSLEY seconded the proposal to adopt the report, and it was agreed to unanimously.

THE DIVIDEND. Sir G. GRERMALT. moved a resolutioij. declaring a divi- dend at the rate of 15 per cent. per annum, and a bonus of per share.—Captain WrrazNo•roN seconded this proposal, which was agreed to.
Quenutt,LE BALL.-_A ball was held on Wednesday night, under the auspices of the Lymm Quadrille Assembly, in the Drill Hall. The Lymm Quadrille Band supplied the music.

UnovELLowb'MEETING.—The annual meeting of the "Trafford" Lodge of the Independent Order of Odd- fellows, MU., was held on Saturday at the Bridgewater Arms. Annual business was transacted, and it waS unanimously decided to elect Dr. Williamson, of Brook- field, doctor to the lodge. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF Hop.—On Monday even- ing the monthly meeting of the Members of the Congre- gationhl Rand of Hope was held in the schoolroom, sew- road. Mr. Dutton presided. An interesting programme of songs, recitations, &c., was gone through by the members.

rans DISTRIBUTION.—A: well-attended public meeting was held in the Parochial Schools, on Thursday evening, when about fifty prizes were distributed to the scholars. The chair'was occupied by the Rev. W. G. Guest, the rector, and an address was delivered by Mr. C. E. Howarth, jof Manchester. Subsequently a farce entitled "The barber's courtship" was given. MEASLES AND SCARLET FEWER AT SANDY-LANE,--oWiLlg to the prevalence of measles, and at least one case of scarlet fever, the managers have found it necessary to temporarily close the schools. The measles have, within the last few days, spread to such an extent that the authorities have thought it necessary to take decided action. The village of Lymm itself is atpresentunusually free from zymotic forms of disease. Ttre LATE Mn. Mosrox.—The following resolution con- doling with Mrs. Mbston on her bereavement has been passed at a meeting of members of the Lymin Liberal Club;—" That the members of the Lymm Liberal Club respectfully tender to Mrs. Mostoh and her family their very deep sympathy in the loss they have sustained, and desire to record their heart-felt sorrow at losing from amongst themselves so excellent a man and so consistent a Liberal as the late Mr. Thomas Aloston." WARBURTON CHURCII.-At Chester Consistory Court, on Thursday, on the application of the -Rev. Geoffrey j Egerton Warburton, rector of Warburton, and Messrs. ' Newton and Collins, wardens, a faculty was granted to place stained glass in the east window of St.Werlsurgh's, Warburton, representing ttn scenes from the passion of Our Lord (the Crucifixion being in the centre), as a me- moriarof the late Mr. John -Worthington, of Whalley Range. The cost, £3OO, Is to be defrayed by Mr. Wor- thington's widow.

BAPTIST IVIUTITAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society took place on Wednesday even- ing. Messrs. G. Diamond, Bragg, vnd E. Clarke took part in a reading,.Mr. Winstanley- read ' "The psalm of life," Mt. E. 'Clarke delivered an impromptu Speech on "Summer," .followed by Messrs. Diamond and Knowles. A recitation. "How Paddy stole the rope." was given by Mr. Hollingsworth; and a paper was read by the same gentleman,on the "Great advance in machinery during this generatioil," Messrs. Diamond, E. Clarke, and T. Griffiths joining in the subsequent discussion. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT :11..ssocwrioN, On Monday evening the weekly meeting Dithe members of this asso- ciation was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Mr. James Mort in the chair. The subject on the syllabus for the night was the Rev. J. H. Ouston's essay on "Our Eng- lish Bible"' : but that gentleman being too ill to fulfil the engagement it was decided, at 'llae last meeting that the evening should be devoted to Shakesperean readings. Act 4-of "The Merchant of Venice." and the latter portion of Act 3 of "Hamlet," were read in an ex- cellent manner by some of-the members, the reading of the ladies being particularly good.

Robinson, at Heywood, and I damage was done to the extent of £3,000. A ...JUBILEE Carr.—Messrs. Robinson and Cleaver, of Belfast have recently presented to Her Majesty, as a Jubilee gift, a specimen of their linen manuiacture, which shows the perfection to which that industry has been brought in the North of Ireland. The gift itself consists of only two dozen doyleys, but every care has been exercised, and no expensespared,to make it worthy of Royal acceptance. These doyleys have been woven in Jacquard looms and bear a representation of the manu- facturers' place of business (just completed), the front of which contains life-size busts of the Queen, the late Prince Consort, and other members of the Royal family.
